en: 4. Chapter on Abiding (Sthiti):
Oṃ. Now the chapter on abiding is explained. Oṃ.
Having meditated upon the supreme inward light, and having contemplated in the mind the auspicious Gaṇeśa, the remover of the fear of worldly existence; and then [having meditated upon] the God...
Having placed the dust of the feet of my guru upon my head, this commentary on this excellent treatise called *Sthiti* is composed by Bhāskara.

Thus, having explained the origin of the world as being of the nature of non-origination in the section on origination, and having observed that Śrī Rāma attained conviction therein upon hearing it, [the author] thereafter begins the appropriate section on maintenance:
"Now, after the section on origination, hear this, O Rāma: the section on maintenance which, when known, brings about liberation. (MU 4.1.1)
The word *atha* (now/then) serves the purpose of auspiciousness. "This" refers to what is about to be stated. What is this section on stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*)?

It is that which, when known and applied to the objects of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), brings about *nirvāṇa*—that is, absolute dissolution (*atyantika-laya*) into Brahman. Such is it. Thus it comes to be.
He explains the section on stability itself:
"Know this, then, to be established thus: the visible world is 'I' and so forth; it is formless, mere delusion, consisting of unreality. (MU 4.1.2)

Understand it thus for now; you will know the rest by yourself—this is the intended meaning. To the inquiry "How so?", he says: "This. "The world" means that which exists under the name "the world"; this visible reality manifesting before one, the collection of entities that is the object of the act of seeing, and that which consists of "I" and so forth. Of what nature is it? Formless, a mere illusion.
And it consists of non-existence.
Without an agent and without a body, a painting has arisen in the sky; it is without a beholder, yet accompanied by experience—a dream-vision occurring without sleep.

In the sky—that is, in the space of consciousness—a painting, as it were, has arisen, has become manifest. What kind of painting? One without an agent, devoid of a creator; one without limbs, lacking any formal structure. Furthermore, what is it? It is the vision of a dream, having the nature of a dream-vision.
Of what nature is this dream-vision? It is without a seer, devoid of a beholder; yet it is accompanied by experience, being the object of the seer’s own experience.
It has gone; it is sleepless, not seen due to the defect of sleep. Here, by stating its supermundane nature, emphasis is placed precisely on its capacity to cause wonder.
The manifestation of future cities appears like a painting come to life; it has the luster of a fire burning on a monkey's fur and is situated like a whirlpool in water.

And the non-existence of the future city is quite evident. "Monkey-fire" (*markaṭānala*) refers to fire appearing as a monkey; its heat is *tāpa*, and that which possesses the appearance (*ābhā*) of that [heat] is [the object]. For a monkey, through the delusion of fire, seizes some particular fruit. "Established" (*āsthita*) means endowed with stability (*sthiti*).
Though having the form of reality, it is devoid of emptiness, like solar radiance in the sky; it is seen in the void like a network of jewel-lights, yet without a foundation.

It is of the nature of existence because its essence is pure consciousness; it is void because it is nothing whatsoever. For the solar light in the sky, though of the nature of existence, appears as if it were void; thus, it is taken as a metaphor for that [reality].
Like a city of creative imagination, it is maturely experienced yet composed of unreality; consisting of the manifestation of the meaning of a story, it neither exists nor does it not exist anywhere.

Of this discourse being told—of the meaning of that discourse, whatever its manifestation (pratibhāna) or flash of intuition may be, that is its essence, its very nature. For at the time of hearing a discourse, its meaning appears to the listener as if standing right before them;
it does not abide anywhere, because it cannot withstand analytical scrutiny, yet it exists because it is manifesting.
Though devoid of essence, it possesses an exceeding inner essence; like a mountain in a dream, it is a mere void, radiant with form like the elemental ether.

It is essence-less because it lacks the grasping of a solid mass; yet it possesses an exceedingly superior inner essence because its essence is pure consciousness alone. It is radiant in form, shining with a form endowed with the color blue.
Like an autumn cloud standing before one, it is subject to decay yet its destruction is imperceptible; like a color in the expanse of the sky, it appears while being devoid of substantial reality.
This is clear.

It has the form of dalliance with a woman in a dream; though it appears to have an object, it is devoid of any real purpose. Like a painted garden in full bloom, it is sapless despite its appearance of being full of flavor.

It is dedicated to its object, intent on the purposeful activity known as the emission of semen, and purposeless because it is seen at dawn, thus appearing in vain. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is flavorless (*arasa*), devoid of taste; yet it possesses a "flavorful form" (*sarasākṛti*), meaning its appearance is like that of something flavorful.
Like what? Like a blossoming painted garden (*citrodyāna*), that is, a garden in a painting. Even though that [painted garden] is also flavorless, [it appears so].
The state of having a beautiful form is well known.
Though appearing as if luminous, it is devoid of radiance, like a painted sun or fire; it is experienced as something unreal and unsubstantial, like a kingdom of the mind.
This is clear.
Like a variegated lotus pond devoid of cranes and fragrance, it shines forth in emptiness, possessing various colors and consisting of manifested forms.
In the void, which is called pure consciousness devoid of objects, upon the wall of the void; "ākārita" means endowed with form—that whose self (ātman) is such. //MT_4,1.11//
In the ultimate sense, it is spread out with elements that are withered and as fragile as sprouts; it is inert, devoid of essence, and as hollow as the trunk of a plantain tree.
*Tatam* means pervaded.
Pervaded like a circle of darkness visible to wide-open eyes, that which is of an absolutely non-existent nature stood as if it were directly perceived.
Just as those circles of darkness are seen by one with wide-open eyes, so too is that [space] extended; and this meaning is to be understood through gestural representation (*abhinaya*).
Like a swelling bubble, it is hollow within yet throbbing in form; consisting of rasa, it is the essence of reality, characterized by uninterrupted decline and emergence.

It consists of *rasa* (essence/flavor), has the nature of will (*icchā*), and has the nature of water. It possesses the *rasa* of truth; that is, it is that which has the *rasa* of the reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-tattva*). The meaning is that it has attained nourishment through the very reality of pure consciousness.
Like a spreading mist, it is grasped as something existent yet is nothing at all; it is inert, a locus of emptiness, and empty—according to some, like an atom.
Of certain logicians who possess coarse intellects.
Something consisting of the real exists; it is established that the unreal is empty. When grasped, it has the nature of non-existence, like a sword drawn from its scabbard.

This saṃsāra exists as something composed of elements (*bhūtamaya*), established and appearing; by these qualifiers, the entire meaning of the section on stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) has been stated in summary. For it is precisely in the section on stability that such a state of the world is intended to be described.
Śrī Rāma asks:
"At the end of the great kalpa, does the visible world remain like a sprout within a seed? Tell me, does it arise again from that very same source?"
Thus, is this indeed so, or is it not? Speak; tell me.
Are those who have such an awakening ignorant, or are they knowers of that? O Blessed One, speak clearly and according to reality for the sake of pacifying all doubts.
Those whose awakening is of the nature described in the preceding verse—such are they.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"This visible world exists within the Great Destruction like a sprout within a seed; for one who speaks of this as supreme ignorance, it is due to extreme childishness."
Because of extreme childhood and extreme ignorance.
He states the reason for this, because it must necessarily be taught:
"What is that [contact] unconnected? How is this unreal? This is a perverted understanding, produced by the ignorance of both the speaker and the listener. (MU 4.1.20)

What does "incoherent" mean? It means "nothing at all. This is unreal and incoherent. How so? Because [the statement] "contact is present before one's face"—this is a perverted understanding produced by the folly of both the speaker and the listener. The speaker must state that this is incoherent for this reason; for this reason.
The listener should be questioned as to why this [object] is not unreal; otherwise, the implication is that both [the proponent and the opponent] would simply be fools.
He states the consequence:
"The notion that the world exists here like a sprout at the time of the seed—listen now, how indeed that foolish idea is merely the meaning of senseless prattle. (MU 4.1.21)

The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied [from the previous context]. "Asatpralāpārthā" means that whose purpose is like that of idle chatter; that is to say, she is of the nature of idle chatter. "Mūḍhā" means dull-witted. "Katham" means by what reason? The underlying intention is that if no reason were stated, the same charge of folly would fall upon me as well.
The seed itself would have to be visible, as it is the object of the senses such as the mind; for in the case of a banyan seed or grain, the emergence of a sprout is logically consistent.

The domain of the sense faculties, such as the mind, is precisely what is visible; thus, things like a banyan seed or other grains would be seeds. In this regard, it is logical that the emergence of a sprout occurs from a seed in the form of a grain or the like.
How could that which transcends the six senses including the mind, and which is even more ethereal than space, be capable of becoming the seed of the self-existent world?
Those for which the mind is the sixth are "mind-sixth. Such are those sense-faculties. They have passed away; the Self-existent One is pure consciousness alone.
How and in what manner can there be the state of being a seed for the Supreme Self, which is subtler than even space, supreme, and unperceivable by any sense organ?
This is clear.

The existent is subtle and appears as non-existent, for it is indeed non-existent to those who do not see it as such. What kind of seed-nature could there be therein? In the absence of a seed, whence can there be a sprout?

Even that reality which is called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) becomes as if non-existent for those who do not perceive it—that is, for those who lack the knowledge of pure consciousness; this is the meaning. He states the reason for this: "appearing as non-existent" (*asadābhāsa*).
That is, its appearance is like that of something non-existent. Furthermore, he provides a qualifying attribute as the reason for this: "subtle" (*sūkṣma*).

Thus, because of its subtlety, it has the appearance of non-existence; because of its appearance of non-existence, it is non-existent—this is the meaning. In that regard, within that reality called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), what kind of seed-nature could there be? It does not exist; the meaning is that only something gross can possess the nature of a seed. In the absence of a seed, how could there be a sprout—the sprout called the world? It is simply not tenable.
This is the meaning.
In that supreme state, which is clearer than even the expanse of the sky and is empty, how can the world, Mount Meru, the oceans, the sky, and so forth exist?
From the attribute of space, clarity is to be understood as being free from the impurity known as insentience.
How can that which is nothing at all be something? What entity could exist there within what is non-existent? If it were present there, why is it not seen?

That which is pure consciousness (cinmātra), because it transcends both external and internal organs, becomes "nothing" (nakiñcit). In that—within that non-substantial, nothing-like pure consciousness—how can there exist a substantial entity called the world, which takes on some form through the reach of the senses?
Even if it were so, if it exists there as something present, why is it not seen? Well then, [what of its] existence?
The sense is that this alone would be logical for him. Now, if it is asked, "How is it that the existence of the world does not exist?", we reply:

it does not exist because it cannot withstand critical inquiry (*vicāra*). For only that which withstands critical inquiry possesses existence, just as, in comparison with the snake in the rope, the rope [possesses existence].
How or from where could something belonging to the self arise from that which belongs to nothing? Where, from what, or when could a jar arise from the empty space within a jar?
The meaning of this verse has already been established by the commentary on the preceding verse.
How can anything exist within its opposite, as [darkness exists] in light or [heat] in shade? How can darkness exist in the sun, and how can fire exist in ice?

"Something" (*kiñcit*) means "anything whatsoever. The sense is that it is not logical for anything at all to abide in the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*). He demonstrates this very point specifically with the words beginning with "shadow" (*chāyā*).
How can Mount Meru reside within an atom? How could there be anything at all in that which is formless? Where is the unity of those two, being of such different natures, like shadow and sunlight?
Having stated the illustrative examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) specifically, he explains the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) in that very same manner by asking, "From what? What?

"What" refers to the world, which is a certain form (*rūpa*) because it is accessible to the senses. "In the formless" means in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is devoid of form because it is not accessible to the senses. The sense is: "How? This is not logical. [Objection: But surely, if there were oneness, these two could not possess the nature of seed and sprout.
Regarding the statement "it exists," he says here: "that and not-that. This refers to those two forms, which are absolutely distinct from one another.
It is logical that a sprout exists within the acorn and so forth when they possess form; it is illogical that the world, which possesses great form, exists within that which is formless.
This is clear.

That which is invisible due to the power of all the faculties, such as the intellect, in another place or in another person—such a thing does not exist at all; when there is no cognition of that kind, it is simply called "nothing."

"In another place" means in this region or in another region; "in another person" means in you or in other persons. This is also an elliptical indication for time; therefore, it should be understood that "at another time" is also implied. Thus, the meaning is as follows: that invisible entity which is the source of the intellect and all the powers of the sense organs, [is perceived] through cognitions of various kinds in another place and in another person.
Of those various kinds—that is, of those various types—of cognitions, whatever their comprehension may be, therein [the object] does not exist;
that is to say, its object does not exist. Therefore, it is said and declared by the wise that "this is nothing at all."
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:

"He whose understanding is deluded asserts that the effect has attained the state of being the cause [of itself]. By what means, indeed, could that effect arise from that [cause] alone, without its own multitude of causes in the form of auxiliary factors? (MU 4.1.33)

The entity called "nothingness" (*nakiñcit*) becomes the cause of its effect; he who says this possesses a deluded intellect. The sense is that such a person is not a knower of reality (*tajjña*). He denies its causality on the grounds that it lacks auxiliary causes (*sahakārikāraṇa*), saying "that is its effect. [This is because] by their own nature, all things have the form of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) as their essence, being of the nature of nothingness.
The meaning is that there is no existence of a cooperative cause (sahakārikāraṇa).
By this, he states the established conclusion with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Having cast far away the notion of the relationship between cause and effect imagined by those of dull intellect, know that the very world which is real, without beginning or middle, remains as such. [This refers to] those possessed of dull intellect (*durbuddhibhiḥ*).

"Conceived" means delineated by one's own volition (*saṅkalpa*), but not as a relation of cause and effect that is ultimately real regarding the world and Brahman—that is, having set aside or abandoned such a relation of cause and effect. "Know this as 'Thou'" means ascertain it as being true.
Why? Because it is without beginning or middle, since it exists as the witness even of the beginning and the middle; thus, it is devoid of beginning and middle.
That which is well-known is indeed real; there exists a reality called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) that is true and has become the truth.
That alone exists, and not its effect, the world. May there be auspiciousness!
Thus ends the first canto, titled "The Refutation of the Produced and the Producer," in the section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Now, O best among those who know what is to be known, I shall speak regarding this acceptance [of the truth]: in the stainless, great sky of consciousness, which transcends all mental constructs.
If the primordial sprout of the world exists therein, then tell me: by what auxiliary causes does it arise?

O best among those who know what is to be known! Now, having accepted this state of being the seed (*bījatva*), I speak—that is, I declare it. To the question "What do you say?", he replies with the word *samasta*: "in that which transcends all mental constructions" (*samastakalanātīte*), meaning that which transcends all constructions such as the relationship between cause and effect; and "in that which is stainless" (*nirmale*), meaning untainted by the impurity known as the object of thought (*cetya*);
[and] "by means of auxiliary causes" (*sahakāribhiḥ kāraṇaiḥ*). This is a pair of verses.
In the absence of auxiliary causes, the sprouting of a seed or the birth of a barren woman's daughter is never seen here by anyone at any time.
The word *vā* is for the purpose of completing the meter; the word *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction.
And that which has arisen in the absence of auxiliary causes is the very root cause, the Self; it remains thus established in its own nature.
And that which is called the world, as an effect, when it arises in the absence of auxiliary causes, appears as something distinct from its cause;

yet, in that manner, it remains established within its own nature, its own essential form. Thus, the Self is indeed the fundamental cause, being the very essence of the root cause, and not the effect; for it is only when auxiliary causes are present that the status of being an effect is observed.
At the beginning of creation, Brahman itself remains within itself in the form of creation; since it exists as it is, devoid of form, where is there any sequence of produced and producer?
And at the beginning of creation, at the moment when there is an orientation toward the object of thought (cetya).
Now, if earth and the other elements, or something else, having come from somewhere, act as auxiliary causes (sahakārikāraṇa), then the same refutation as before applies here.

"The previous refutation" means that whatever refutation exists regarding the arrival of creation, that same refutation applies to the arrival of the earth and other elements which are considered its auxiliary causes.
He states the conclusion:
"Therefore, the world remains quiescent apart from that [Self] and its auxiliary causes; the claim that it spreads forth [without them] belongs to the child, not the wise man."

Therefore, for that reason, the world exists as the supreme peace abiding in the state of a seed; the claim that it "proceeds" without auxiliary causes—that is, without cooperative conditions—is the talk of a fool, a person of little intelligence. It does not belong to the wise, the learned.
Therefore, O Rāma, he declares that the world has never existed, does not exist, and will not exist; it is only the pure space of consciousness that shines forth in this manner within itself.

O Rāma! Therefore, the world did not exist, does not exist, and will not exist, due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). Again, as to why this [world] vibrates: here he says, "consciousness" (*cetanā*). It is transparent and devoid of objects of cognition. Consciousness-space (*cetanākāśa*) is the space of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-ākāśa*).
Within the Self, in this manner, it vibrates as if, it shines as if, in the form of the world.
O Rāma, when the absolute non-existence of this world is realized, then all this is Brahman; it is not otherwise.
Otherwise, it would be non-existent.

"But surely, why is it that prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and the others do not exist here? What is the use of absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva)? To this, he says: "That which is pacified by means of prior non-existence, destruction, and mutual non-existence is, in fact, not pacified within the mind; for that [mind] does not cease at all. (MU 4.2.10)
By means of prior destruction, mutual non-existence, prior non-existence, subsequent non-existence, and mutual non-existence—

that which is pacified remains indeed unpacified, because it is a real entity (vastu) existing within the mind (citta-manasi) as a formative force (saṃskāra). Therefore, the sense is that absolute non-existence alone is appropriate here.
Therefore, there is no other means for the total destruction of this harmful world-appearance than the realization of its absolute non-existence at all times.

The summary meaning is this: the absolute non-existence of the world-appearance itself is the means for the destruction of the misfortune consisting of the world-form; there is nothing else whatsoever.
That which exists as the awakening of the sky of consciousness, [manifesting] as the world and so forth—this is that very "I," as well as this form, light, mind, mental constructs, and the rest.

That which exists as this beginning of the world is nothing other than the very awakening of the space of consciousness (cidākāśa). By the word "beginning" (ādi), dissolution (pralaya) is included. Through the specific expression "this beginning of the world," he refers to such things as "I am that.
Mental activity (manaskāra) is a mere fraction of the mind (cittakalā).
This is the sun and so forth, this is the earth and so forth, as well as this year and so forth; this is the kalpa, this is the moment, and these are death and birth.
This is clear.
This is the agitation at the end of an aeon; this is that very end of the great aeon. This is the commencement of creation; this is that sequence of existence and non-existence.
This is clear.
These millions of kalpas, these millions of cosmic eggs, these multitudes of Brahmās and Indras, and these powers of Viṣṇu and the others—[all are but manifestations of You].
The powers whose forms are Viṣṇu and others are the "powers of Viṣṇu and others."
These have evolved, and these have further returned; these are the networks of celestial abodes, and these are the divisions of space and time.
These have reached their end; they are dead.
He makes this summary: "The great consciousness, the supreme space, unobstructed and infinite, shines by itself in this way—just as it was previously situated, peaceful."

"Unobstructed" means free from obstruction; "endless" means free from end; "quiescent" means always dissolved within its own essential nature; "the great consciousness, the supreme ether"—in this manner, thus, it shines and vibrates in the form of the world.
These [appearances] are but a thousandth part of an atom of the Great Consciousness; being its very nature, they remain within it, neither coming nor going.

They abide within the Great Consciousness; for this very reason, they are its very nature. These successions of creations are manifestations and radiances whose magnitude is but a thousandth part of an atom. They neither come nor go, because they are eternally established.
That which is itself an internal wonder is projected forth by consciousness; thus this appearance of creation shines as the nature of light, and not as something possessing a material substrate.

By "citā" is meant by consciousness alone. That "wonder" (*camatkāra*) which resides within—consisting of the relish (*āsvāda*) that is the self-reflection of one's own nature—is perfectly emitted outwardly. This emission appears as the manifestation of creation (*sargabhāna*). Of what nature is this? It is "light-form" (*bhārūpa*), meaning its very essence is knowledge (*jñānasvarūpa*); it is not possessed of a wall (*abhittimat*), being devoid of any supporting substrate.
They do not arise, nor do they perish; they do not come, nor do they go; they are as immovable as the inscriptions within a great rock.
The word "creations" (sargāḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
These creations manifest spontaneously within the pure Self, like portions of space appearing within space itself—formless within that which is formless.
By its own nature.
Like the liquidity of water, like the movements of the wind, like the whirlpools of the ocean, or like the qualities of one who possesses them.
This should be applied precisely as an illustration for the preceding verse.
This entire world exists as a single mass of consciousness, appearing thus, infinite, peaceful, and pervasive, including its beginning, its rise, and its setting.
In this mass of consciousness, whose sole nature is knowledge, the reality that is pure awareness, lies this world.
To claim that the world is empty due to the absence of causes such as cooperative factors, yet that a self-existent being is born [from it], is indeed the babbling of a madman.
"Unmattakaphūtkṛtam" means the prattle of a madman.
He describes the fruition [of the practice] with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Free from the stain of all conceptual objects and their parts, having cast off the entire bed of discursive thought, having long since dispelled the deep sleep [of ignorance], free from fear of existence, and gracing the earth—you have awakened. The word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is to be supplied [at the beginning of the sentence]. Therefore, you...

"Bhava" (O Lord)! In response to the inquiry "Of what nature is he?", he states the qualifications beginning with "praśānta" (tranquil). "Praśānta" means one who is profoundly tranquil through the realization of oneness with Brahman. "Sarvārtharūpakalaṅka" refers to one for whom all forms of objects constitute a stain [which has been removed]. "Nirastatalpa" refers to one by whom all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have been cast away without remainder. "Vidrāvitadīrghanidrā" refers to one by whom the long sleep consisting of ignorance has been dispelled.
Therefore, he is awakened, endowed with perfect knowledge; therefore, he is fearless, free from fear. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the second canto in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. The venerable Rāma asks:

"At the beginning of creation following the great dissolution, how does that first Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*) arise as the very essence of memory (*smṛtyātman*) during the creation? And from that, how does the world likewise arise as the very essence of memory?"
The first Prajāpati, Brahmā, has the nature of Śuddhamanu; he is of the nature of Smṛti, that is, the form of memory.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replies:
"O scion of Raghu, it was exactly so at the beginning of creation after the great dissolution; at first, that very first Prajāpati exists as the self of memory alone."
"Thus it is" means that this is indeed the truth.
And since the world consists of his volition, this [world] likewise consists of memory; thus it stands as a city of volition belonging to the former Prajāpati.
Its nature is volition, its nature is memory, and its nature is Prajāpati.
Even though this is established, O Rāma, that state of that former Prajāpati is simply not possible, like a great tree in the sky.
That [cognition] has the nature of memory.
Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Brahman, is it not possible that there is a memory of the past at the beginning of creation? How is it that former memory is destroyed by the delusions of the great dissolution?"
By the delusions of the great dissolution—that is, by the faintings brought about by the great dissolution.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks further:
"O wise one, formerly, at the time of the great dissolution, Brahmā and the others attained liberation in the past; indeed, they necessarily reached the state of Brahman."
Nirvāṇa is liberation.
Who is the rememberer of that prior memory? Therefore, O observer of noble vows, explain this: since the rememberer has attained liberation, the memory has become rootless.
This is clear.

Therefore, in the absence of a rememberer, how could that tradition (smṛti) arise, what would it be, and how? For necessarily, during every great aeon (mahākalpa), all beings are destined for liberation alone.
This is clear.

Whether regarding what has been experienced or what has not been experienced, that memory which arises within the self-luminous sky of consciousness is the matured glory of the world; for in the absence of any visible object, it is indeed the radiance of consciousness.

It is not from itself, nor from assuming the form of Prajāpati; rather, it is regarding an object previously experienced, not one never before experienced. That memory which arises in the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoman*) becomes the matured "glory of the world" (*jagacchrī*);
the sense is that it is not the memory of Prajāpati. Why is this so? To this he says: "because of the visible" (*dṛśya*). For (*hi*), because in the absence of the visible...
In the absence of the object of perception appearing as a mental representation, there is only the radiance of consciousness; it is not the radiance of Prajāpati.
Alternatively, enough with this construction based on memory; for, with the intention that the world exists as nothing but the radiance of consciousness, he says:
"The radiance of consciousness alone shines forth, pure and manifesting without beginning or end; that which is established as 'this world' and as the 'Self-existent' (Svayambhū). (MU 4.3.10)

The radiance of consciousness (*saṃvitprabhā*) itself—shining without beginning or end because it is eternally manifest, and thus devoid of the appearance of beginning or end—is that which shines as this clear world; this is how it stands. It is also established as being "self-existent" (*svayambhū*).
Therefore, the sense is that there is no existence whatsoever for either memory or a self-existent creator.
That innate manifestation of Brahman, established from beginningless time, is the subtle body (ātivāhika-deha) of Virāj, which has the form of the universe.

That which is established from beginningless time, eternally established, which is the innate manifestation belonging to Brahman—the reality that is pure consciousness—that constitutes the subtle body (*ātivāhika-deha*) of Virāj, the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*) who possesses the form of Virāj.
Of what nature is it? It has the form of the universe; its essential character is the entire world.
Within the atom, this entire world shines forth, together with the three realms of existence, endowed with the succession of space, time, action, substance, day, and night.

Substance is the object of action; it is the referent of a word. [The author] will explain later, in the section on Nirvāṇa, that this extends down to the ultimate atom (paramāṇu) and manifests as the three worlds for Indra.
Then, within each atom, there appears that very same interior, shining with a radiant form and likewise surrounded by mountain ranges.

Therefore, for that reason, within each and every atom—that triple world existing inside those atoms—it shines forth in exactly that same form and not in any other; it has a radiant appearance, enclosed by such mountain ranges and filled with such a multitude of peaks; thus, in effect, the triple world shines.
Even there, such a form, extended thus toward every atom, appears as a visible object consisting of light; my friend, this is not real.
Even there, within this threefold world that exists in every atom, its nature is light—that is, its nature is knowledge. He states the result with the words "this":
O dear one, therefore this threefold world is not real—not ultimately existent—because it is of the nature of light, like a dream.

Thus, there is never an end to either the view of existence or the view of non-existence; yet, O sinless one, regarding this [view], the Buddha has arisen—whether for one who understands or for one who does not.

In this manner, there is no end—that is, no finality—to either the view of existence (*saddṛṣṭi*), which is the view of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), or the view of non-existence (*asaddṛṣṭi*), which is the view of the objectified (*cetya*). Regarding this view of existence and this view of non-existence, there is an "arising" (*abhyudita*), meaning an emergence or manifestation.
This occurs either with respect to the Awakened (*buddha*) or with respect to the unawakened (*abuddha*). With respect to the Awakened, it is the arising of the view of existence.
The sequence for understanding one who has not yet awakened from false views should be known.

But surely there is only one appearing vision called the world; so how can it be said that for the enlightened (buddha) there is no end to right view (saddṛṣṭi), while for the unenlightened (abuddha) there is an end to wrong view (asaddṛṣṭi)? He replies: For the enlightened, this is only Brahman—solely peaceful and immutable; but for the unenlightened, it is duality, radiant and accompanied by the worlds. (MU 4.3.16)

This very world appears as real to one with right vision (*saddṛṣṭi*) and as unreal to one with wrong vision (*asaddṛṣṭi*). The meaning is that it is like a single rope, which appears as a rope to one who knows it, but as a snake to one who does not.
Just as this radiant world shines forth, expanded within a single cosmic egg, so too do thousands of millions of others shine within every atom.
This is clear.
Just as there is a figurine on a pillar, and on its limbs another figurine, and on that figurine's limb yet another, so too is the figurine of the three worlds.
The daughter named Trailokyā is the Daughter of the Three Worlds (Trailokyaputrikā).
Just as atoms on a mountain are neither distinct from it nor can they be numbered, so too are the atoms of the three worlds within the vast Mount Meru of Brahman.
This is clear. (MT 4.3.19)
The minute atoms within the flood of the sun's rays can be counted; but the atoms of the three worlds within the sun of consciousness have neither beginning nor end.
This is clear.
Just as atoms move within the rays of the sun, within waters, and within dust particles, so do the atoms of the three worlds move within the space of consciousness.
This is clear.
Just as this elemental space has the nature of being merely the experience of emptiness, so too this space of consciousness has the nature of being merely the experience of creation.
That whose self (ātman) or essential nature (svarūpa) consists solely of that experience of emptiness—this is it.

When "creation" (sarga) is understood as the meaning of the word *sarga*, it leads one downward; but when it is understood as the meaning of the word *brahman*, it becomes a complete source of the highest good.
The highest good is that which consists in liberation.
He expresses this very point with the concluding verse of the chapter:

"Know that the knower of the field (*vijñānātman*), the ruler, the seed of the universe, is none other than the primordial Brahman itself, which is merely the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*). That which is born from it is to be known as nothing but the awakening of awareness within oneself, consisting solely of the realization of consciousness. The *vijñānātman* is whose sole nature is knowledge.
The "Instructor" (śāsitā) is the impeller. His own self (svam), which exists as the Self (ātmatvena) of all, is the primordial Brahman alone, which is the mere space of consciousness (cidākāśamātra).

It is the seed of the universe (viśvabīja), like a seed for the universe; however, it is not a literal seed, because that [literal seed] has been refuted immediately thereafter. That which arises from such a Brahman is that very same thing.

Thus, for this reason, you should know—that is, understand—that the entire range of objects to be known (*vedya*), which constitute the domain of the act of cognition, are nothing but that awakening within your own self, which is the self-reflective awareness (*svaparāmarśa*) of consciousness. (The apparent confusion of genders is intended to indicate the absence of gender. May there be auspiciousness! (MT 4.3.24)
Thus ends the third canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
The ocean of existence is crossed by means of the bridge that is the restraint of the collection of the senses; indeed, it cannot be crossed here by any other action whatsoever.
The "battle" refers to the conflict with the collection of the senses, that is, the aggregate of the sense-faculties; he is the bridge by means of that very [collection].

Through the study of the scriptures, association with the virtuous, and practice, one who possesses discernment and has conquered the senses realizes the absolute non-existence of this flood of the visible world.
He understands; he knows.
All this has been told to you, O best of embodied beings: the nature of the series of waves in the ocean of saṃsāra, and how they come and go.

O best of embodied beings, I have described to you the entire nature of the series of waves in the ocean of saṃsāra, as well as how they come and go within that series of waves in the ocean of saṃsāra. Thus it has been told.
What is the use of saying more here? The mind is the sprout of the tree of karma; when that is cut, the world-branch—the tree of karma—becomes severed.
Of what nature is the tree of karma? It is such that the worlds themselves are its branches; it is like that.
O Rāma, this entire world is within that mind; once the mind is healed, this whole existence consisting of the web of births is likewise healed.
This is clear.
Thus, this mind, agitated by a trace of impurity, arises in the world; apart from the mind, where indeed can a body be seen?
It arises as the world; it is produced as something turbid with a trace of impurity—that is, agitated by even a slight stain known as conceptual construction (saṅkalpa).
Without the absolute non-existence of the object of perception, the demon of the mind does not subside by any other cause, even in hundreds of eons.
The absolute non-existence of the perceptible is the absolute absence of the perceptible.
And this is indeed possible for the treatment of mental disease; it is the supreme, most excellent medicine, whose nature is the absolute non-existence of the perceptible.
In the task of treating mental illness, he is indeed capable and indeed powerful.
The mind takes on delusion; it dies and is born again. Yet, through the grace of someone, it is bound and then liberated once more.
Of a certain unnamed pure consciousness alone.
Thus the entire world throbs within the mind when it is stirred by thought, like a city of Gandharvas in the vast, empty sky.
Slow in reflection, yet filled with the weight of contemplation.
This entire expansive universe exists and vibrates within the mind; it is like fragrance residing within a cluster of flowers, being both identical to and distinct from it.
Sphāra means extensive.
Just as oil is in a sesame seed, or as a quality is in that which possesses qualities, or as a property is in its substratum, so too does this abide in the mind.
This is clear.
Just as a mass of waves in water, just as the delusion of two moons in the moon, and just as a mirage in the heat, so is cyclic existence within the mind.
This is clear.
Just as a web of rays exists in the sun, just as light exists in brilliance, and just as heat exists in fire, so does this world exist in the mind.
This is clear.
Just as coolness is in frost, as emptiness is in the sky, and as flickering is in the wind, so is this world in the mind.
This is clear.
He expresses this very point with the concluding verse of the chapter:
"The mind is the world, and the entire world is likewise the mind; for these two are indeed always inseparable from one another.
When the mind is wounded incessantly, both of them are wounded, but when the world is wounded, the mind is not. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16) Incessantly.

"Excessively" (*atiśayena*). The genitive case in "of those two" (*tayoḥ dvayoḥ*) is used for selection (*nirdhāraṇe*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that the mind alone is to be destroyed by means such as right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). May there be auspiciousness! (MT 4.4.16)
Thus ends the fourth canto in the "Chapter on Stability" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha. The venerable Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, best among those who know the past and the future, how is it that this vast cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) persists within the mind?"
In the mind, which is of the nature of atoms, there is expansion—that is, vastness.
O sinless one, tell me clearly how this expansive undertaking manifests vividly in the mind, by means of a clear illustration.
The undertaking is that which is called the world; it is the undertaking.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replies:
Just as the worlds of the sons of Indu, though bodiless, exist with established firmness within the minds [of others], so too does this [world] exist.
Of those bodiless ones, by virtue of their being dead.
Just as King Lavaṇa attained the state of a Caṇḍāla when his form was confounded by Indra’s magical illusion, so too has this [state] remained in my mind.
He is one whose form is confounded by the net of Indra—that is, by the magical illusion employed by a magician.
For a long time, Bhārgava’s mind remained fixed on this: the desire to enjoy the pleasures of heaven and the sovereignty over all enjoyments.
Of Bhārgava Śukra.
Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, how did the son of Bhṛgu come to possess lordship over enjoyments and worldly existence due to his desire to experience the pleasures of heaven?"
Is the state of being a lord over enjoyments the very nature of transmigratory existence? Is it the condition of being in saṃsāra?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply:
"Listen, O Rāma, to an ancient account, a dialogue between Bhṛgu and Kāla, which took place on a ridge of Mount Mandara, thick with the branches of *tamāla* trees."
This is clear.
In ancient times, on a certain flower-laden peak of Mount Mandara, the venerable Bhṛgu performed severe austerities.
This is clear.
The radiant and highly intelligent young son, Śuka, who possessed the luster of the full moon, attended upon him just as light attends the sun.
This is clear.
In that excellent forest, Bhṛgu remained established in meditative absorption at all times, as if carved out from the surface of a forest rock.
The word "was" (āsīt) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
The child Śukra played with ease upon beds of flowers, amidst silver lotus-pools, and on swings made of Mandāra trees.
He states the reason for this delight as "the fool."
At that time, it is said, Śukra, having fallen into great calamity between the two views of knowledge and ignorance, existed as if suspended between heaven and earth like Triśaṅku.
Within the two worlds, that is, between heaven and earth. //MT_4,5.12//
Then, while his father was established in non-conceptual meditative absorption, he remained undistracted in solitude, like a king who has conquered his enemies.
This is clear.
There he beheld an Apsaras traveling along the path of the sky, like Janārdana beholding Lakṣmī emerging from the midst of the Ocean of Milk.

He distinguishes the apsaras as one adorned with garlands of mandāra flowers, her locks of hair swaying in the gentle breeze, her gait possessing a charming and resonant sound, and her fragrance perfuming the air of the sky.
This is clear.
She was a creeper of the tree of loveliness, her eyes rolling with intoxication, making that very spot nectarine with the moonlight-like splendor rising from her body.
This is clear.
Upon seeing his beloved, his mind became tremulous with joy, like the body of the ocean when the stainless full moon is beheld.
This is clear.
The author declares his attainment of the state of a celestial nymph with a verse at the end of the canto:

Having restrained his mind within his heart when struck by hundreds of arrows from the god of love, Uśanas thereafter became composed entirely of celestial nymphs, as all other mental functions had dissolved away.
In the heart-center, within the seat of consciousness; having restrained it by binding it away from other mental functions—thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the fifth canto in the "Stability" section of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Then, meditating upon her with his mind, with his eyes closed right there, Uśanas alone indeed began this kingdom of the imagination.
Uśanas is Śukra.
For this woman is here in the sky, the abode of the thousand-eyed one; I have now reached heaven, which is graced by the restless celestial beauties.
In heaven, the abode of the thousand-eyed one.
These gods of yours, beautiful with crests of soft māndāraka flowers and possessing bodies that grace the world like streams of molten gold, [are here].
This is clear.
These are those beloved ones with gazes like deer, charming and playful in their smiles, who rain down blue lotuses created by the delight of their eyes.
This is clear.
These Maruts, radiant with the Kaustubha gem and reflecting one another’s forms, possess appearances comparable to the Universal Form (Viśvarūpa) and look like those intoxicated by wine.
Of Viṣṇu, who possesses universal forms; those whose appearance is equal [to his]—they are the Maruts, a specific class of gods.
These are those songs of the hosts of gods, sung in sweet, warbling melodies, which have been heard by bees who have turned away from the fragrance of Airāvaṇa’s temples.
*Kākalīgītāḥ* refers to those [songs] known as *kākalīgīta*.
This is that Mandākinī, where the female swans of Brahmā wander among the golden lotuses, and where the celestial consorts rest in the gardens upon its banks.
This is clear.
These are your world-protectors—Yama, Candra, Indra, Sūrya, Anila, Jala, and Anala—their bodies radiant with scattered, blazing, and intensely glowing rays of light.
This is clear.
This is that Airāvaṇa, whose face was scratched by the tusks of the gods' prowess, and whose clashing tusks pierced the circle of the lords of the Daityas.
He whose face was scratched by the gods, the Suras, with their weapons wielded for the sake of prowess.
These beings who were situated on the surface of the earth have now attained the state of stars in the sky; as celestial denizens, they wear moving, beautiful necklaces, chowries, and earrings.
Those whose place is on the surface of the earth are "bhūtalasthānāḥ."
These are those rows of celestial palaces, adorned with various gardens and jeweled mansions, possessing beautiful golden roofs.
Those [lotuses] whose radiance is a beautiful glow consisting of refined gold.
These are those very waves of the Ganges' waters, strewn with Mandāra flowers, by which the deities are drenched with spray as they strike the surface of Mount Meru.
Those [trees] by which the deities are strewn with the sprays produced by the impact—the striking against—the slopes of Mount Meru.
These are the avenues of Indra’s grove, where rows of celestial nymphs sway upon swings, tawny with clusters of blossoms from the spreading mandāra trees.
This is clear.
These are the breezes from the Pārijāta tree, fragrant with the nectar of the kunda and mandāra flowers, appearing like a mass of moonbeams.
This is clear.
That Nandana grove is filled with throngs of vine-women eager for the battle of scattering frost-like pollen from flowers and wearing garments of fine silk.
The frost is indeed the filaments of the flowers; that very thing is the powdered incense. Their *īraṇa* is their movement or wafting; [the wind] is eager for that.
These two, Nārada and Tumburu, have voices as melodious as the lute; they cause the celestial maidens to dance with joy at the sound of their lovely songs.
This is clear.
These performers of meritorious deeds, adorned with many ornaments, dwell in happiness within celestial chariots soaring through the sky.
This is clear.
These celestial women, their limbs intoxicated by passion and love, attend upon the Lord of the Gods like forest creepers in a grove.
This is clear.
These wish-fulfilling trees have flower-clusters made of moonbeams, bunches of wish-granting gems, and are bristling with clusters of ripe jewels.
This is clear.
Here, first of all, I shall worship and salute this Śakra, seated upon his throne, as if he were a second Lord of the Gods.
The Lord of Gods, Mahādeva.
Having reflected thus, the Lord of Śacī was mentally saluted by Śukra, appearing there like a second Bhṛgu.
Only by means of the mind, and not by means of the body.
Then Śukra, having been honored by Śakra, rose respectfully; taking him by the hand, he was brought near and seated.
This is clear.
"O Śukra, this heaven now shines with its fortune through your arrival; O Śakra, please dwell here for a long time," he said to him in this manner.
This is clear.
Then, having sat down there, that descendant of Bhṛgu, with his face radiant, eclipsed the splendor of the entire stainless moon.
This is clear.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he describes his renunciation of humanity:

"Worshipped by the entire host of gods, that son of Bhṛgu, stationed by the side of Indra, attained incomparable satisfaction for a long time; having utterly abandoned the notion of being a man, he became [fully liberated]."

This Śukra abandoned—completely—that human intellect, the notion "I am a man"; he became perfected. The sense is that he recognized his own divinity alone. May there be auspiciousness. (Śivaṃ) MT 4.6.25.
Thus ends the sixth canto in the "Chapter on Stability" within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Thus Śukra, having reached the city of the gods with his own mind, forgot his former nature and his previous calamity, except for his grief.

Thus it was: having reached the city of the gods with his own mind, Śukra forgot his entire former state, except for his addiction—the attachment to the realm of the *apsarases*. Since that addiction had arisen only in his human existence, its status as "former" (prāktana) should be understood accordingly.
Then, having rested for a moment by the side of the Lord of Śacī, he rose up to roam through heaven, urged by the inhabitants of the celestial realm.
Urged by the dwellers of heaven, urged by the immortals.
Having beheld the splendor of heaven, marked by the tremulous glances of women, he went to look upon the host of goddesses, as a crane goes toward a lotus pond.
*Straiṇam* means a multitude of women.
There he saw that beloved woman with eyes like those of a young deer, who had come into the midst of the forest, just as a bee finds a mango creeper.
That [suffering] was previously experienced in the world of humans.
Beholding her, whose form was graced by shimmering and restless charms, his limbs began to dissolve like a moonstone under the light of the moon.
This is clear.
With all his limbs melting away, he gazed upon that lovely woman, as a moonstone gazes at the cool, playful moonlight in the sky.
This is clear.
Gazed upon by him, she too became intent upon him; at the end of the night, she was called out by her beloved cakravāka.
This is clear.
Surely, that very splendor which belongs to the sun and the lotus in the morning—when they have blossomed through their essence and are mutually enamored—was possessed by those two.
Of those two, Śukra and Apsaras.
Because that region grants whatever is desired, Madana, having rendered her helpless in every limb, surrendered her to Śukra alone.

Of the region—that is, the heavenly realm—because it grants whatever is desired. By Madana, that Apsaras was rendered helpless in all her limbs; she was surrendered, that is, given, to Śukra. This is the majesty of the heavenly realm itself, which grants every wish, that she was surrendered to Śukra by Madana after being rendered helpless; such is the meaning.
The arrows of Love fell repeatedly upon her tender limbs, like torrents from a fresh rain-cloud upon the petals of a lotus.
This is clear.
Shaken by passion, with her curls swaying like a swarm of restless bees, she became the companion of a flower-cluster tossed by a gentle breeze.
This is clear.
Madana agitated her, who had eyes like blue lotuses and a gait like that of a swan or an elephant, just as a flood disturbs a bed of lotuses.
A flood is a mass of water.
Then, seeing her in such a state, Śukra, who was intent on achieving his purpose, summoned forth darkness, just as the Creator summons the dissolution of all beings.
He formed a mental resolve; he brought [it] forth by means of that resolve.
That region of heaven became shrouded in darkness, like the edge of the Lokāloka mountain on the earth, which is enveloped in blinding gloom.
This is clear.
When he, like a sharp-rayed sun to the darkness of shame, had established himself within that circle of gloom, it was as if the god of love had taken his stand within that couple.
When all those beings had departed from that place toward their desired directions, like birds at the end of the day, they returned to the world of mortals.
With her long, white-cornered eyes and her passion thus fully aroused, she approached the son of Bhṛgu, as a peahen approaches a rain-cloud.

In what [context] does the circle of darkness (timira-maṇḍala) exist? It is the darkness that is shame itself. [He is like] the sun with its sharp rays toward that [darkness], because of his power to destroy it.
There, upon a couch prepared in the midst of a white chamber, Bhārgava entered like Mādhava entering the Ocean of Milk.
This is clear.
Clinging to his feet as if helpless, that lovely-faced woman shone like a lotus plant clinging to the foot of a divine elephant.
Helpless, one is dependent on others.
And he spoke these sweet, joyful, and playful words, with syllables modulated in charm, in a voice radiant with overflowing affection.
This is clear.
O moon-faced one, behold: why does this bodiless god, having drawn his bow into a circle, pursue me, a weak woman?
Is he "Anaṅgaka" because the bodiless one (Anaṅga) has been disparaged?
"Protect me, O Lord, for I am weak, miserable, and here have you as my refuge; know, O virtuous one, that consoling the wretched is the vow of your true conduct."
This is clear.
O Great-minded One, those who are truly deluded, not recognizing the gaze of affection, disregard such endearments; never do those who know the essence of flavor treat them with contempt.
Endearments, being characterized by affection, are disregarded—that is, they are held in contempt.
O beloved, the intimacy of two people who have attained union without apprehension and are mutually enamored eclipses even the tasted nectar of the moon.
The lunar [nectar] is the outflowing ambrosia.
This sovereignty over the three worlds does not so gladden the mind as the mutual joy of affection between two people who have first fallen in love.
This is clear.
O giver of honor, by the touch of your feet I have been comforted, like a night-lotus touched by the rays of the moon at night.
This is clear.
O handsome one, I live by drinking the nectar of your touch, just as the restless female cakora bird lives by drinking the essence of the moonbeams.
This is clear.
Embrace me, who am like a female bee clinging to your feet, with your sprout-like hands, and place me within your heart, which is a true lotus filled with nectar.
"Līnām" means clinging to the feet; "caraṇālīnām" means those who are clinging to the feet from all sides.
Having spoken thus, she, whose limbs were as soft as flowers, fell upon his chest; her eyes, with their rolling bees, were like a cluster of blossoms on a tree.
This is clear.
He tells us in a concluding verse of the canto:
"There, those two, husband and wife, lovely in their dalliance, sported in those forest glades, like two intoxicated bees in lotus ponds shaken by the breeze white with pollen."
This is clear. May there be auspiciousness. MT_4,7.30.
Thus ends the seventh canto in the "Stability" section of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Thus, through those beloved advances long imagined by the play of his mind, the sage Bhārgava’s union with her became a source of satisfaction.
"Sasamāgama" means a coming together with that apsarā.
Then, with her who was adorned with garlands of *mandāra* flowers and intoxicated by the nectar of the gods, he was accompanied by that second [companion] who was like the spotless moon.
He dwelt upon the banks of the celestial river amidst golden lotus-ponds where intoxicated swans sported, accompanied by kinnaras and cāraṇas.
The divine liquor is nectar.
The gods, together with the playful one, drank the yellow elixir flowing from the moon’s crescent while dwelling within the bowers of the *pārijāta* creepers.
This is clear.
He sported for a long time with playful ease upon the creeper-swinging platforms in the beautiful Caitraratha grove, together with groups of attentive Vidyadhara maidens.
This is clear.
The expanse of the Nandana grove was brought to a state of extreme agitation by the attendants of Śambhu, just as the ocean is stirred by Mount Mandara.
Together with Śukra and the Pramathas—the attendants belonging to Śambhu—the expanse of the Nandana grove was brought to a state of intense agitation.
And he wandered through caves entangled with networks of young golden creepers, and through the lotus ponds of Mount Meru, his passion having become like that of a madman.
An error was committed—that is, a delusion was produced—by Śukra as the agent. By Śukra of what kind? By one whose passion was intoxicated, that is, by one whose passion was excessive.
In the forest groves of Kailāsa, that lover spent the night—white as the moon—with her amidst the songs of the Gaṇas.
The meaning is: by means of group songs (*gaṇagīti*), that is, by diversions consisting of songs performed by Gandharvas and others.
Having rested upon the plateaus of Mount Gandhamādana, she was adorned by him from head to foot with golden lotuses.
From the feet to the extremities of the feet.
O Rāma, he sported with her, laughing, upon the shores of the Lokāloka mountain, which are captivating with their various wonders.
This is clear.
In the groves between the Mandara trees, together with the young fawns, he dwelt for sixty years, having fashioned for himself a celestial palace.
"Kalpitam" means constructed or brought into being by imagination; "amarāmandiram" means the abode of the gods; "yena" refers to that by which [it was so made]. Thus it is he.
On the shores of the Ocean of Milk, half of the Kṛta Yuga was spent by him in the company of his wives, together with the inhabitants of Śvetadvīpa.
This is clear.
Through his playful creations of celestial cities and gardens, he has come to imitate Time, which brings forth the creation of infinite worlds.
This is clear.
Then that Śukra dwelt again in the city of Purandara for eight cycles of four yugas in happiness together with the deer-eyed woman.
This is clear.
Due to the exhaustion of his merit, he then fell to the circle of the earth along with that very proud woman, his form stripped away.
This is clear.
With all his limbs mangled by others, robbed of his chariot and his joy, he was overwhelmed by anxiety and ruined like a soldier struck down in battle.
He for whom the delight of chariots was taken away in the grove that delights in chariots; in the case of the warrior, he is one from whose excellent chariot the joy of battle was snatched away.
As he lay fallen upon the earth, his body shattered into a hundred pieces along with his long anxiety, like a waterfall crashing against a rock.
This is clear.
When their two bodies had perished, those two minds, shrouded by latent impressions, wandered in the sky like two birds without a nest.
This is clear.
There, those two entered the moon’s lattice of rays; having quickly attained the state of frost, they then became rice plants.
The state of being frost, that is, the condition of dew.
That best of brahmins ate those cooked *śāli* rice grains in the Daśārṇa country, and the king ate those born from the womb of Śukra’s wife in the Mālava country.
"From semen" means belonging to semen; that is to say, having as their cause the seeds which are the material basis for it. "Those whose [semen] is in the womb of a woman"—those [beings].
Formerly, Uśanas was born among the Daśārṇas from the best of the twice-born; and his wife was born among the Mālavas from King Uttamasaubhāgya.
Her woman is Śukra’s woman; that is to say, an apsaras.
There the boy grew up, and there that woman grew up; they were like a former couple born upon the earth after having fallen from heaven.
This is clear.
Then Śukra, bearing the name Sāraṅga, became sixteen years old; a glorious young Brahmin, endowed with youth, remained in his father’s house.
She bears the name "Sāraṅgā," thus she is called Sāraṅganāmabhṛt.
That maiden Mālā, the daughter of the asura, grew up in the king’s palace like a creeper in a choice forest, her eyes like bumblebees.
This is clear.
Then the auspicious princess Mālā constantly worshipped Śaṅkara, thinking, "May I obtain my former, perfected husband."
This is clear.
Then, at the sacrifice of the King of Mālava, she beheld Sāraṅga, who had arrived at the assembly of brahmins together with his father.
This is clear.
Seeing him, she of faultless limbs, permeated by former affection, shone with her body moistened by love, like a moonstone that has beheld the moon.
By "former affection," meaning by the affection from a previous birth; she was "cultivated" or "perfumed" [by it].
Then, in the midst of the sacrificial assembly, that garland, the daughter of the King of Mālava, chose the son of the Daśārṇa Brahmin as her husband.
This is clear.
When he had gradually completed his marriage, the lord of Mālava, worn out by old age, handed over the entire kingdom to him and departed for the forest.
Worn out by old age, decrepit with age; having bestowed, that is, having given.
Together with her, that Sāraṅga ruled the kingdom in that pavilion of Mālava for a hundred autumns, as exceedingly happy as Śakra himself.
This is clear.
Then, after a long time, due to the fickleness of the mind and by the power of destiny, that husband and wife came to dislike one another.
This is clear.
But Sāraṅga, worn out by old age, his body ready to fall, assumed the color of withered leaves due to the weakness of his breath.
Due to the slackening of the breath, that is, due to the slackening of the vital wind (vāta).
Due to his detachment from wife and people, and due to the extreme onset of old age, he—free from desire and with all doubt stilled—rejoiced in death.
This is clear.
Then, in that sapless kingdom which proclaimed an excess of suffering, delusion reached a state of extreme density, like a vetāla spirit in a forest.
This is clear.
One who has fallen incessantly into the blind well of delusion due to attachment to enjoyments, who lacks discernment, is ignorant, and is devoted to the company of the wicked; //MU_4,8.35//
This is clear.
Just as a frog seizes a crying, helpless moth that has swallowed a firefly, so does Death seize this person whose heart is gripped by craving.
One who possesses nothing is incapable.
Then, having experienced the fruit of his own auspicious and inauspicious karma in the next world, he was born as a fisherman among men due to the power of that evil disposition.
Due to the power of evil intentions, that is, due to the power of negative latent predispositions.
There, performing the labors of a fisherman for a hundred autumns, he attained a state of world-weariness because his mind was worn out by suffering.
This is clear.
Reflecting thus that "saṃsāra is suffering," he then leapt toward the sun; by means of that act, he was born as a great king in the Solar dynasty (Sūryavaṃśa).
Falling [into distress], he goes for refuge.
Then, by the power of his virtuous state of being, he attained some degree of knowledge; having cast off his royal body, he became a teacher who instructs all.
This is clear.
For he, having achieved success through the mantra, then became a Vidyādhara; for one kalpa he enjoyed the city of the Vidyādharas.
This is clear.
Having brought about the time of the end of the kalpa by means of her body in the form of the wind, when creation had begun once more, she was born again as the son of the sage.
This is clear.
Then, through association with sages, he established himself in fierce asceticism and dwelt in the thicket of Mount Meru for the duration of a Manvantara, blameless.
This is clear.
There, a son of a deer in human form was born to him; through affection for him, he again fell into a state of supreme delusion in an instant.
From the female deer, from the presence of a doe.
"May this son have wealth, virtues, and eternal life for me"—with such incessant anxieties, he abandoned his established state of truth.
Abiding in truth, and being devoted to the Dharma as that which has become reality.

Because he had strayed from reflection on the Dharma and was preoccupied with thoughts of wealth for the sake of his son, Death carried him away as his lifespan was exhausted, like a wind sweeping away a snake.
This is clear.
With his consciousness departed along with his singular preoccupation for enjoyments, he attained the status of the son of the Lord of Madra and became the sovereign of the Madra land.
The state of being the son of the King of Madra; the state of being the daughter of the King of Madra.
Having ruled the kingdom in the land of Madra for a long time and having destroyed his enemies, he reached old age here, just as a lotus withers before the frost.
This is clear.
But he abandoned that body of the King of Madra along with the latent impressions of his asceticism; therefore, he was born as an ascetic, the son of a forest-dweller.
"He abandoned the body of the King of Madra"—this is the connection; by that abandonment of the body.
Having reached the bank of the great river Samaṅgā, O Rāma, that ascetic of great intelligence performed austerities, free from all distress.
Samaṅgā is a particular river.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he describes the state of Śukra’s happiness:

"Having followed the succession of bodies with a mind rendered helpless by various states of birth, that son of Bhṛgu remained in happiness on the bank of the excellent river like a firmly rooted tree. (MU 4.8.51)
On the bank of the Varaṇa river, on the beautiful shore of the excellent river named Samaṅgā. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the eighth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
As Śukra was reflecting thus, a vast period of time consisting of many years passed in the presence of his father.
This is clear.
Then, after a long time, his body—withered by wind and sun—fell to the earth like a tree whose roots have been severed.
This is clear.
But the mind, with its restless range, wandered through those various and most diverse states, like a deer among the rows of forest trees.
This is clear.
His mind—wandering, distracted, and agitated as if cast upon a wheel—found rest on the bank of the river Samaṅgā.
For that which is placed upon a wheel revolves.
Śukra remained there, bodiless, experiencing that state of worldly existence—which is both fragile and yet very firm, and dense with endless occurrences.
That state of transmigratory existence belonging to the ascetics on the banks of the Samaṅgā—that state of worldly existence—[he perceived] as Videha, being devoid of the gross body.
Standing upon the peak of Mount Mandara, the body of that wise one became withered by the spreading heat until it was reduced to mere skin.
This is clear.

Due to the joy arising from the cessation of the suffering of physical exertion, he seemed to sing a soft, low melody (*kākali*) in the form of the whistling sound of the wind flowing through the apertures of his body.
That was his body. From the destruction of that suffering and pain of movement comes bliss;

for that reason, he seemed to sing with a *kākalī*—a voice of song exceedingly subtle. Of what nature was it? It was of such a form as had the specific sound of a *śītkāra* produced by the wind flowing through the apertures of the body.
Like a sigh of breath through the recollection of life, it released its vapor; having been stirred by the play of fierce winds across the forest lands.

Of what nature is the vapor? It is that whose swelling—its increase—is caused by the recollection of those vital breaths (*prāṇas*) which previously existed; that is, by their moment-by-moment remembrance. Furthermore, in this context, "vapor-ness" (*vāṣpatva*) should be understood as frost.
She seems to mock the wretched mind, which clings only to the body as it wallows in the pits of worldly existence, with her row of teeth white as an exceedingly brilliant cloud.
Abiding in the stages of existence, in the pit of the form of an apsaras, in the pit.
She displayed her own natural emptiness before his eyes through the beauty of the hollows of her mouth, which resembled the dilapidated wells in a forest.

Furthermore, of what nature was she? With her own pair of eyes (*akṣṇoḥ*), her face itself was a forest; by means of its appearance as an old well—that is, by way of its resemblance to a pit—she displayed her own body as empty. That is to say, she showed herself thinking, "I am indeed empty.
And in the mouth of a dead body, a cavity arises because only the flesh remains.
Scorched by the heat and drenched by the weight of the rainwater, she was as if defiled by the dust raised by the wind, like one stained by evil deeds.
The word "sā" (she) is a reference to her own body.
Trembling like dry wood, making clattering sounds as it falls, it is pierced by the downpour of a mass of raindrops at the arrival of the clouds.
"Vinunnā" means impelled; that is to say, moved.
On the bank of a mountain river, flooded by the torrential downpour of the rainy season, she stood like a forest rock, hissing with loud gasps from the wind.
That [forest] in which there is a loud whistling sound like that of the wind; it stands like a forest-stone, as if possessing forest-stones.
Crooked, with strings of dried entrails, foul-smelling and making a jangling sound, she is like the lute of the Goddess of the Forest, her belly made of empty skin.
The lute of the forest-goddess is the *araṇyalakṣmīvīṇā*; [he is] like that.
"Surely, how was it that such a body of his was not devoured by wild beasts? To this he replies:
"Because that holy hermitage was free from passion and hatred, and because Bhṛgu was a man of great austerity, it was not devoured by beasts or birds. (MU 4.9.15)

And the state of being free from passion and aversion belonging to the meritorious hermitage is to be understood through the fact that the living beings residing there are themselves free from passion and aversion.
He tells us this very same thing in the concluding verse of the canto:

"The mind of the descendant of Bhṛgu practiced asceticism, its slender body made lean by restraints and observances; then his physical form, its blood drained away by the wind, lay for a long time upon the great rocks."

The mind of Śukra, the descendant of Bhṛgu, whose slender body was emaciated by restraints and observances, practiced asceticism. Then that body, its blood having been removed by the wind, rolled upon great rocks. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the ninth canto in the "Stability" section of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Then, after a thousand divine years, Bhṛgu, the Supreme Lord, desisted from his meditative absorption due to his supreme awakening.
From what kind of meditative absorption? From supreme enlightenment—that is, from a form of knowledge untainted by the impurities of the knowable—and not from a state of unconsciousness.
He did not see his son before him, whose face was bowed down by humility, who stood like merit incarnate—the very limit of all virtues.
This is clear.
He saw before him a great skeleton, appearing as pure Time alone, like misfortune embodied or poverty personified.
Time is black; it is a skeleton, a mere carcass; it is misfortune, the reversal of fortune.

He describes the skeleton: its body dried by the heat, with partridges quivering from the openings of the skin, and frogs resting in the shadows of the hollows of its completely parched entrails and belly.
*Tittirayas* are a particular kind of insect.
The forest insects sleeping within the hollows of the eyes, and the swarm of cocoon-spinning worms impaled within the cage of flies.
In which [place] there were swarms of flies seated in the shape of cages within fly-cages, and in which there was a multitude of silkworms woven together.
With his body washed by the stream [of tears], his chain of dried bones laughing aloud, he abandoned his former longing for enjoyments that yield desired and undesired fruits.
The meaning is "as if laughing, laughing."
With his bright, well-formed head, possessing the luster of the moon, he emulated the beauty of a linga-head drenched in camphor.
With the luster of the moon, that is, with the radiance of the moon; the *liṅga* is the Śiva-liṅga.
With his neck straightened, completely withered and white, reduced to mere bone, and stretching upward toward his head, he seemed to lengthen his very form.
"Followed by the self" means by one's own self; "followed" means connected with it.
He bore a face whose contours were defined by the bridge of his nose, which was as pale as a lotus stalk and from which the flesh had been stripped away by the constant flow [of blood].
Having established the sequence of boundaries means having established the sequence of limits.
Surely, with her long neck extended and her face turned upward, she was looking as if for her life-breaths departing into the belly of the sky.
"Surely" is used in the sense of deliberation (*vitarka*).
With his shanks, thighs, knees, and staff-like arms having attained double their length, he seemed to be measuring the boundless space out of fear of the exhaustion of a long journey.
The quarters of space were unappeased.
With his belly deeply sunken, reduced to mere skin and withered, it seemed to demonstrate the extreme emptiness of the heart of the ignorant man.
This is clear.
Beholding that withered skeleton, like the tethering post of an elephant, Bhṛgu rose up without reflecting on what had preceded or followed.

What was Bhrigu doing? Out of affection for his son, he failed to reflect on what had occurred before and after [the event]. For even among yogis, at times, due to the power of *prakṛti*, there arises a loss of reflection on what preceded and followed the fall of the body;
however, in their case, that state is merely momentary. He had "arisen," meaning he had emerged from the reflective awareness of the reality of his own self (*svātmatattva*).
For at the very moment the light appeared, Bhṛgu’s thought instantly dawned: "Has my son been dead for a long time? or "Is this him? MU 4.10.14.

Then, immediately after rising; "simultaneous with the light" means simultaneous with the sight of the skeleton of his son; "of Bhṛgu" refers to what appeared or flashed forth. What was it? "This son of mine"—meaning, from a long time ago—how has he become one whose life-force has departed?
This is the meaning.
Even as he was reflecting thus, the power of his future destiny then swiftly gave rise within him to an exceedingly terrible wrath directed toward Time.

Then, due to the power of what was to be— the power of destiny— for this Bhṛgu, who did not reflect and thus lacked the prior and subsequent deliberation that arises at that moment, there arose an exceedingly terrible anger directed toward Time, which consists of the manifold variety of activities residing in pure consciousness.
"Why was my son taken away at such an untimely hour?"—thus provoked to anger, the Blessed One proceeded to cast a curse upon Time (Kāla).

"At the improper time" means at a time when there is no [fixed] duration, consisting in the non-completion of the lifespan determined for humans in that particular age. This is the intended meaning here: Bhṛgu had attained the state of pure consciousness alone through non-conceptual meditative absorption (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). He then arose from that absorption. Thereupon, through external contact, he began to become slightly affected like a crystal. In that state, he first saw his son dead at an untimely hour.

Having become powerless, he desired to destroy the time characterized by the variety of actions created by himself through his own nature as pure consciousness experienced immediately prior. And as for this arrival of time, how could he—[thinking] "I shall destroy this which was created by myself and accompanies my very nature"—be understood as the arrival of discernment (*viveka*) itself? Let this suffice; there is no need to further unveil the secret.
Then that Time, having assumed an unmanifest form and having swallowed all living beings, approached the sage, taking on a physical body composed of the elements.

He whose form is unthought (*akalitarūpa*). Because it abides as having entered into the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it has not attained the state of being an object of knowledge; such is his form. The physical body (*ādhibhautika-deha*) should be understood as being, in the ultimate sense, of the nature of inquiry itself; but for outsiders, it is of the nature of a deity (*devatārūpa*).
