In response to the inquiry as to what kind of form he approached with, [the author] describes his appearance as an external deity for those who hold external views:
"The glorious one, bearing a sword and a noose, adorned with earrings and armor, six-armed and six-faced, surrounded by a vast army of servants. (MU 4.10.18)
This is clear.
The sky, by means of the leaping mass of flames arising from his body, bore the splendor of a mountain covered with blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees.
This is clear.
The quarters of the sky shone with the circles of fire spat from the tips of the tridents held in his hands, as if they were golden earrings set upon rising.
This is clear.
By the wind of his noose, the mountains—whose peaks were strained—moved as if mounted upon a swing, reeling and falling.
"Strained peaks" means pulled-up peaks.
The orb of the sun, darkened by the radiance of the circle of his sword, shone as if it were obscured by the smoke from a world consumed by the fire at the end of an aeon.
This is clear.
Approaching that great sage who was enraged and as deep as the ocean agitated at the end of an aeon, the mighty-armed one spoke to him with words of consolation.
That is time.
O Sage, those who have understood the nature of the world and have seen both the higher and the lower are not deluded even by a reason; how much less so, O Supreme One, without a reason?

"Seen" means experienced as one's own true nature (*svarūpa*). "The high and the low" refers to the reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-tattva*) abiding in the form of both the transcendent and the immanent. Those by whom [this is seen]—they [are the ones].
"You are a brahmin of infinite austerity, while we are merely observers of destiny; therefore, O holy one worthy of worship, you are honored by us, and not according to our own will."
"Of infinite austerity" means of immeasurable austerity; by virtue of that state of having infinite austerity.
Do not exhaust yourself with penance against one who has not been consumed by the great fires at the end of the eon; what can you burn with a curse that I am not already burnt?

The meaning is that there can never be a burning of that which is "who I am"—that is, of the nature of the manifold activity of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), because time itself is incapable of such combustion. The form *dhakṣyasi* is the future tense (*lṛṭ*) of the root *dah*, meaning "to reduce to ashes."
Circles of transmigratory existence have been devoured; tens of millions of Rudras have been swallowed; multitudes of Viṣṇus have been consumed—by whom, O Sage, have we been cursed?
This is clear.
"For we are the eaters, O Brahmin, while you and others are the food; this is indeed our own destiny, for it was not by our own will that this came to pass."
The desire or longing of both us two, of you all, and of ourselves.
Fire ascends upward by itself; waters flow downward by themselves; food goes to the eater by itself, and creation likewise goes to its end by itself.
The time of the end.
O Sage, this form of the Supreme Self is thus; here, the Self itself manifests within its own self by its own power.
It unfolds through various activities; it shines forth.
By the vision that has destroyed all taints, there exists here neither an agent nor an enjoyer; yet by the vision that has not destroyed its taints, there appear to be many agents here.
By means of a vision free from stain, which is right view; by means of a vision not free from stain, which is wrong view.
O Brahman, agency and non-agency are merely imagined through incorrect vision alone, and not through correct vision.
This is clear.
Flowers in groves of trees and living beings in the worlds come and go here of their own accord; yet the causality of fate is postulated.

In this world, the causality of fate (vidhi) is imagined by the deluded and conceptualized through mental construction; however, in the ultimate sense, no causality belongs to anything at all, because only the solitary, pure consciousness alone exists.
Just as there is neither true agency nor non-agency in the movement of the moon reflected in water, so it is with time regarding creations.
Of me, who am Time, whose form consists of the manifold variety of actions.
In this world, the mind, through its false delusion, creates the conceptualization of agency and non-agency, just as one with impaired vision perceives a snake in a rope.
This is clear.
He states the conclusion:
"Therefore, O Sage, do not give way to anger; such is the course of calamities. Let it be exactly as it is; look at the truth with an undisturbed mind."

Such is indeed the course of calamities; the sense is that these come upon everyone. Let things remain exactly as they are. You have become agitated; look at the truth. The meaning is: do not fall into agitation regarding the web of good and evil that comes with the natural flow [of events].
We do not act out of a sense of power, nor are we overcome by pride; rather, we abide solely in our destiny through the force of our own inherent disposition.

We are not established in our restraint toward the Blessed One for the sake of power—that is, for the purpose of exercising authority—nor do we remain there having been brought under control by pride; rather, we remain in that restraint solely out of our own nature, arising spontaneously from a sense of decorum (*hevāka*). The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever here that depends upon us.
A wise person, under the influence of destiny, should conform to the necessary activities of worldly conduct as determined by fate, without being shrouded in the great darkness of egoism.
"Fixed" means fixed by the scriptures. Of what nature is the wise one? He is one for whom there is no egoism—that is, for whom egoism itself is darkness (tamas). Such is he.
Only that which ought to be done is performed by those skilled in action, having resorted to the state of deep sleep and being free from any desire whatsoever.
The sense is that the wise perform everything entirely without any expectation of results.
Where is that vision consisting of knowledge? Where is your greatness? Where is your fortitude? Since the path is well-known to all, why do you wander like a blind man?
It was experienced immediately thereafter, in all that is well-known in the world.
Even while maintaining in your mind the stainless vision of the three times, why do you become deluded like a fool, failing to investigate the course of the world?
The state of perceiving the three times without impurity, and being the locus for the investigation of what precedes and what follows.
O Omniscient One, why do you wish to curse me in vain like a fool, without considering the state of my son, which has arisen from the ripening of his own karma?
This is clear.
O Sage, for all embodied beings here, the body is of two kinds; do you not know this—the one physical body and the other called the mind?
The body is the gross body; the other is the second [subtle body].
In this regard, the body is utterly insentient and solely intent on destruction; the mind, however, being constantly active, either perishes through its miseries or does not.
When the mind is fixed upon exertion in the form of resolve, it does not waste away through hardship; or rather, even by that [hardship], it is not exhausted.
O virtuous one, just as a chariot is driven by a skillful charioteer who exerts some effort of his own, so too should this body be guided by the mind.
It is carried away; that is, it is led toward the place desired by itself.
Having conceptualized what is unreal, the real body is destroyed in an instant by the mind, just as a clay figure is destroyed by a child.
"Non-existent" means not being present; "existent" means being present.
In this world, the mind alone is the person; what is done by it is said to be "done. Bound because of conceptualization, when that conceptualization ceases, it is liberated.

"Due to the cause of conceptualization" means because of the cause known as *saṅkalpa* (volitional construction); "the cessation of conceptualization" means that in which all conceptualization has subsided.
"This body, this eye, this limb, this head—this [entirety] which undergoes such vast transformations is designated as the mind alone."
What is the nature of the mind? It is that which possesses this expansive transformation. "This" refers to that which is expansive and characterized by the tendency to radiate outward (*sphuraṇa*).
Such is the mind as it is described by the wise. What is that? It is that which arises [in the form of]: "this is the body," "this is the eye," "this is a limb," "this is the head."

For it is the mind (*manas*) that lives as the so-called "living being" (*jīva*); the intellect (*dhī*) functions as the determiner; and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) exists because of its nature of self-conceit. Indeed, it is this [mind] that comes to possess manifoldness.

Live, O mind, performing the activity of living; by being determinative, that is, by acting as the agent of determination; and by possessing self-conceit, that is, by acting as the agent of the conceit "I am the body. Through the latent impression of the body, you perceive multiplicity—in the form of various individual souls and so forth—as if there were other earthly bodies existing apart from yourself, even though they are but your own thoughts.

If one perceives, experiences, or observes other earthly bodies belonging to others as if they were one's own, through the power of the mind and the latent impression that "I am the body," then that mind is composed of untruth; by abandoning the identification with the body, one attains supreme bliss.

If the mind correctly perceives the truth, then, having abandoned the conception of a body— which is composed of unreality and has the nature of unreality— it attains supreme bliss, which consists of pure consciousness and is the form of ultimate liberation.
He states the result:
while you were established in meditative absorption, that mind of your son has gone far, even further away, along the path of its own desires.
Since the mind alone is the agent in all cases, for that reason [it is so].
Having abandoned this body of Uśanas in a cave of Mount Mandara, he departed for the abode of the gods, like a bird flying up from its nest.
The *Auśanasa* is that which pertains to Śukra.
There, in groves of mandāra trees and in dwellings of pārijāta trees, in the thickets of the Nandana garden and in the cities of the world-protectors;
This is clear.
O Sage, for eight cycles of four ages, that one of great splendor enjoyed Viśvācī, the celestial beauty, just as a bee frequents a lotus.
This is clear.
Then, when his own merit was exhausted—though it had been fashioned by his own volition born of intense spiritual urgency—it vanished like the nocturnal mist.
This is clear.
With his floral crest withered and his limbs perspiring, he became languid in his bracelets; he fell down along with her like a fruit ripened by time.
Having abandoned that divine body in the sky itself, and having reached the elemental ether, he was born upon the earth.
This is clear.
There was a twice-born man among the Daśārṇas, a lord of the earth among the Kosalas, a fisherman in the great forest of Aṅga, and a swan on the banks of the triple-pathed river.
This is clear.
The king of Pauṇḍra was Saura of the Solar dynasty; among the Śālvas was Daiśika; the glorious Vidyādhara was Kalpa; and then there was the wise son of the sage.
In the Pauṇḍra country, a king born of the Solar dynasty was born; among the Sālvas, a teacher born of the Solar lineage, a preceptor, was born.
Then, among his mothers, that protector of the earth became a young ascetic known as Vāsudeva, dwelling on the bank of the Samaṅgā river.
This is clear.
Under the influence of various latent impressions (*vāsanā*), your son wandered by himself through endless births, even among those that were most perilous.
This is clear.
While providing an explanation of other words, he recounts his previous births prior to those born as an ascetic on the banks of the Samaṅgā:
"In the Vindhya forest he was a cowherd; among the Kekayas, a Kirāta; among the Sauvīras, a feudal lord (sāmanta); and among the Traigartas, a local guide (daiśika). (MU 4.10.63)
*Traigarta* means belonging to the country of Trigarta.
The bamboo thicket is for the Kirātas; the deer is in the Cīra forest; the reptile is beneath the palm trees; and the wild cock is in the Tamāla grove.
This is clear.
This very son of yours, having become the best among those who know mantras, formerly recited the lore that bestows the station of a Vidyadhara.
He muttered prayers; he recited the mantra, the vidyā.
Therefore, O Blessed One, that great Vidyadhara Brahma moved through the sky, adorned with necklaces, earrings, and armlets, dancing with a multitude of graceful gestures.

"O Blessed One, O Brahmin! This is your son; by means of that recitation, he became a Vidyādhara. In response to the expectation of what kind of Vidyādhara he became, [the author] states the qualifiers beginning with "hāra."
The sun to the lotuses that are the heroines, like another god of the flower-bow, he was the beloved of the Vidyādharīs and the ornament of the city of the Gandharvas.
This is clear.
Having reached the end of the eon at the locus of the twelve suns, he was reduced to ashes, like a moth in a fire.
This is clear.
Then, in the vast sky devoid of the creation of the world, that latent impression of his wandered like a bird without a nest.
This is clear.
Then, when time had arrived—initiating the manifold undertakings at the commencement of the cosmic display of saṃsāra, following the reversal of the night of Brahmā—
That mental impression of his, having been stirred by the wind, attained the state of a Brahmin once again and was born today upon the surface of the earth.
In the Kṛta age, that is, the Kṛtayuga. This is a pair [of verses].
O Sage, that young Brahmin named Vāsudeva was born among the wise, having studied the entirety of the Vedas.
This is clear.
"O great sage, having been a Vidyadhara for an eon, your son now practices austerities, situated on the bank of the river Samaṅgā."
This is clear.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he describes the entering of the womb of an old woman:

"Driven by the persistence of various and uneven latent tendencies, he has gone into the world among the wombs of the aged, into the hollows of *khadira* and *karañja* trees as terrifying as caverns, and into the most dense forest regions. (MU 4.10.74)
In the state of old age and rebirth, amidst the terrifying thorns of the *khadira* and *karañja* trees, and within the various perils of manifold suffering—may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the tenth canto in the "Stability" chapter of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the illustrious Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Today, on the bank of the excellent river, where the wind resounds with the gurgling roar of a surging mass of wild waves, your son is performing penance.
He performs penance at the confluence of the Varataraṅgiṇī and the Samaṅgā.
Wearing matted hair and a rosary, having conquered the delusions of all his senses, he remained there for eight hundred years steadfast in his ascetic practice.
This is clear.
O Sage, if you wish to see that son who is but a delusion of the mind, then quickly open the eye of discernment and look.
The mental delusion in the form of one's own son is "the mental delusion of one's own son"; that is to say, [the delusion] that it is one's own son.
When this had been said by Jagadīśa, who regards all with an equal eye, the sage reflected with his eye of knowledge upon what was intended for his son.
This is clear.
And in a moment, by the power of his visionary intuition, he beheld the entire account of his son reflected upon the mirror of his intellect.
He beheld; he saw with the eye of knowledge.
Furthermore, at the time when Mandara’s ridge was situated at the peak of Time, Bhṛgu came from the bank of the Samaṅgā river and entered his own body.
At the time, at a very short time; situated at the limit of time, standing before time.
Looking at Kāla with a gaze smiling with wonder, the passionless sage spoke these words to his beloved, who was herself free from passion.
Because time operates with impartiality, there is freedom from passion.
Bhṛgu said:

"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, we are but children, untainted [by worldly knowledge]. O God, only those like you possess the intellect that perceives the three times without impurity."
"Childish" means ignorant; this [term] is connected with the second half of the verse.
Though it exists as reality, this course of the world—rich in transformations and appearing in manifold forms, yet possessing an unreal nature—produces delusion even in the wise.
The course of the world is the construction of the world.
O Lord, you alone know that form which resides within you and which constitutes this mental activity that creates a magical illusion.
That which exists within you, that which dwells in your midst.
"O Blessed One, it is said that death does not exist for this son of mine; therefore, seeing him dead, I have become filled with agitation."
Because Śukra was long-lived.
"O Lord, although my son’s life was not yet exhausted, Time has carried him away; by the power of destiny, the desire to curse you has arisen within me."
Regarding the phrase "due to necessity": the desire for your curse that arose within me was itself nothing but necessity; therefore, the sense is that there is no fault whatsoever on my part.
But we, who have understood the course of saṃsāra, do not fall under the sway of joy or resentment when encountering either misfortune or prosperity.
The word "having reached" (prāpya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. That is, "having reached adversity" (āpadam) or "having reached prosperity" (sampadam).
"Anger toward one who acts improperly and favor toward one who acts properly—this worldly condition, O Blessed One, is established as something that must be practiced."
Therefore, the sense is that I became angry because I suspected you of acting improperly.
"This must be done, this must not"—such is the course of the world as long as one lives; as long as fire persists, so long are its perceptions of heat, burning, and the like observed.
This is clear.

O Teacher of the World, for one who regards the state of the world as something to be abandoned—thinking "this is to be done" and "this is not"—the total renunciation of that very [state] is itself what must be abandoned.

For one for whom the worldly order (*jagatsthiti*)—consisting of the notion that "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done"—is itself to be abandoned, even the abandonment of that [order] must likewise be abandoned, because the very act of abandoning it retains the nature of the worldly order. Therefore, the intended meaning is: "I have not abandoned my former state."
O Blessed One, since we became agitated and departed without having considered that this was merely a mental fabrication, we are subject to censure for that reason.
*Tānayīm* means pertaining to a son; *vācyatām* means the state of being subject to censure, namely, the fitness for reproach consisting in being the cause of your anger.
"O Lord, I have now been reminded by you of what was intended for my son; therefore, this son of mine was seen by me on the bank of the Samaṅgā."
This is clear.
I think, O all-pervading one, that among the beings in the world there are not two bodies; for the mind alone is the body, by which this world is brought into being.

O All-pervading One, I think that in this world there are not two bodies for living beings; for indeed, the mind itself is the body, by which mind this world is brought into being—that is, it is manifested through mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Kāla said:
"O Brahman, you have spoken correctly; for us, the mind alone is the body. Having formed a conceptual intention, it creates the physical body, just as a potter fashions a jar."
This is clear.
Through delusion, the mind—by means of conceptual construction—creates an uncreated form and destroys what has been created in an instant, just as a child [imagines] a Vetāla.
Out of delusion, that is, from ignorance.
And likewise, during states of agitation, radiant powers in the form of dreams, false cognitions, and so forth, resembling cities of the Gandharvas, are seen in the mind.
This is clear.
But relying upon this coarse perspective, O great sage, it is said that for a person there are two bodies: the mind and the physical body.
Vision that takes the form of coarse perception is "coarse-perception-vision"; [refer to] that.
O Sage, these three worlds are merely a manifestation of mental ideation; they have arisen as something vast that is neither existent nor non-existent, and nothing else.

This world is nothing but the mental activity of the mind—that property known as "thinking. Of what nature is it? It means that it is neither existent nor non-existent; it is indefinable (*anirvacanīya*). Furthermore, of what nature is it? It has appeared as if expanded, having manifested with a tendency toward vibration; however, the use of the word "as if" (*iva*) indicates that, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it has not arisen at all. [The following explains] the meaning of the word *mātra*.
He speaks with his own throat, not otherwise.
Through the creeper-like limbs of the body of consciousness, fueled by the latent impression of duality, this manifoldness has arisen from ignorance, like the appearance of two moons.

Due to the latent impression of duality—the latent impression of difference—which acts as a branch of the body called "mind" (*citta*), and which is powerful, nourished, and real, this manifoldness in the form of the world has arisen and become manifest. How so? Like the appearance of two moons;
just as the appearance of two moons arises from ignorance, such is the meaning.
Due to the manifold latent impressions of duality, the mind perceives everywhere a multitude of distinct objects, such as jars, huts, and cloths.
"Extensive" means vast; "everywhere" means in all places and at all times.
"Emaciated, extremely miserable, and deluded—I am such a one. Cultivating these and other such mental states arising from its own conceptual constructions, the mind enters the state of saṃsāra.
The state of saṃsāra, the nature of saṃsāra.
"This thought is an artificial form; it is not I, and thus I do not fall [into delusion]. Through the abandonment of that [thought], the mind becomes tranquil—the eternal Brahman.
Through the abandonment of that, there is the abandonment of mental construction; it is eternal and beginningless.
With the words "Just as" (*yathā*) and so forth, ending with "free from affliction" (*nirāmayā*), he explains one analogy in detail:
"Just as in the vast, expansive ocean, which is spread out and possesses many waves, and which is graced by rows of many billows consisting of gentle ripples. (MU 4.11.29)
In the Self, which is like water—equal, clear, pure, sweet, cool, indestructible, vast, of great majesty, and manifest; //MU_4,11.30//
The triangular wave, contemplating its own form by its very nature, constructs its own conceptualization through the thought, "I am triangular."
Thinking, "I am falling away and my form is utterly destroyed," one goes to the *talātala* hell by means of that very mental disposition directed toward the surface of the earth.
And when it has been forcibly raised upward, one conceives, "I have risen"; through various conceptual constructions, one conceptualizes that state along with its designation.
When the reflection of the sun appears, it is conceived as "I am luminous"; when a mass of dust falls, it is conceived as "I am defiled."
Enveloped by a net of jewel-like rays, he shines with radiant splendor; yet, pierced by the weight of frost, he experiences the sensation, "I am cold."
With its body blazing with the reflection of the constantly moving forest fire, it trembles, thinking, "Alas, I am being burned! and it quivers as it swallows the fish.
With the reflections of its shores, mountains, birds, forests, and trees, the great ocean shines, as if possessed of the intense activity of thinking, "I am."
With my flickering body destroyed by the arising of stainless radiance, I cried out as if seized by a scream, "I have been reduced to pieces! (MU 4.11.38)
And those waves are not distinct from the water of the ocean; nor is there any single form among them that, while existing, is composed of non-existence.
Nor do those qualities such as inferior length and so forth exist in each of those [waves], nor are they not present there; they are like waves situated in the ocean, yet not situated therein.

Merely through being fragmented by their own mental constructs while remaining within their own inherent nature, they are lost and yet not lost, born again and again, and though born, they are repeatedly destroyed.
Through mutual contact, they reach a state of manifoldness; yet they remain free from affliction, consisting solely of the single-natured commonality of water.

In that which possesses many waves— that is, in the essence of water characterized by many waves— consisting of gentle vibrations, having the nature of gentle water-movements, and graced by many circles of billows; in such a watery self, just as that well-known wave, triangular in shape, manifests its own form— the triangular form— to the perceiver, revealing it by its very nature.

By means of its own [arising] from itself—by means of a non-distinct conceptualization (*vikalpa*) in the form "I am triangular"—it performs the conceptual construction, the construction of the triangular form.

It does not perform only this; rather, it performs other actions as well, as he says: "And falling away," and so forth. That triangular wave, thinking "I have fallen away," is for that very reason falling away.
Then, by means of that [meditative] cultivation (*tādṛgbhāvanayā*), one goes to or reaches *Talātala*, which is called *Talātala*, and to the *Bhūtala*.

"Risen" (*utthita*) means that the triangular wave has been cultivated as "I am risen upward. For this very reason, it is "risen" through those various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*), namely, conceptualizations of rising; it is "with designation" (*sābhidha*), meaning accompanied by verbal expression; and it is "that state," meaning the state of rising.

He conceptualizes by means of conceptualization; he brings it to completion. "With the sun" is clear. "With the jewels" is clear. "With the waves": *āttamīnaḥ*. That which is seized (*ātta*) by fish (*mīnaiḥ*) is *āttamīnaḥ*. "Reflected" is clear. "Stainless" (*vimala*): that which is stainless is the shimmering (*ullasana*).
From that, what has arisen is the destruction (*dhvasta*), the vanishing (*dhvaṃsa*). He whose body is restless (*lola*) because of that [destruction] is so described.

"He" refers to the one previously mentioned. "And not waves"—those [waves] were mentioned before; the singular number used previously should be understood as referring to the genus (*jāti*). Therefore, the plural usage is employed here. "And not"—and those waves, in those qualities (*guṇa*), do not exist.
"Merely"—abiding in its own nature, abiding in its own essence. That conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which consists in the attainment of the state of being a wave is the conceptual construction.
By that [wind], they were made deformed and their continuity of water was severed. "Mutually" (*parasparam*) means one another.

Because of that mutual contact (*parāmarśa*), which is staying in close proximity, they undergo differentiation. Of what nature are they? They consist of that very single form which is the commonality of water; for this reason, they are "free from affliction," being devoid of the diseases known as destruction and arising.
Having stated the illustration, he explains the subject illustrated by means of two verses:
"In the same way, in this vast, white, pure, and stainless Brahman, whose sole body is Brahman alone, which is of expansive form... (MU 4.11.43).
Within the All-Powerful One, who is without beginning or end, various powers—distinct yet non-distinct from Him—abide, restless with their diverse modes of activity.
He explains the meaning of the word *sitapada* (white-footed) in his own words with the phrase "in the pure" (*śuddhe*). This means being free from the ailment (*āmaya*) designated as such.

[It refers to] that whose body (*vapuḥ*), or essential nature (*svarūpa*), is solely (*eka*) and exclusively (*kevala*) Brahman. In such a one; in that which is expansive (*sphāra*), meaning having the nature of radiating (*sphuraṇaśīla*), and possessing such a body. In such a Brahman, the powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are not made separate, just like waves.
They exist as distinct entities; this constitutes a pair.
For Brahman, abiding in its own form, attains multiplicity through its various powers; it expands within Brahman like a circle of waves in water.

Brahman is pure, the reality of consciousness alone. In Brahman—its own body, its own essential nature called Brahman—it becomes expanded, being endowed with expansion in the form of the universe. It thus attains multiplicity, the state of being manifold. How so? It possesses manifold powers; for otherwise, the attainment of multiplicity would not be logical—this is the sense. Like what is Brahman expanded?
Like a circle of waves upon the water.
Now, if Brahman alone has expanded itself in the form of cloth and so forth, how can there be a fixed, individual form for each object? To this, he says:
"Because its nature consists of manifold forms, Destiny (Niyati), which produces hundreds of diverse appearances, presides over objects with a fixed form. (MU 4.11.46)

That form which consists of various shapes, because it is endowed with that [power], brings about a hundredfold diversity (*vairūpya*)—that is, it brings about a hundredfold irregularity (*virūpatā*) known as the fixed form of individual entities.

*Niyati* is the power called "destiny" (*niyati*). It presides over the entity and brings it under its own control. The sense is that by means of the power of destiny produced from Brahman alone, each entity possesses its own fixed form.
Having spoken in general terms, he now explains a small portion in detail:

"The power, whose form is latent impression (*vāsanā*), assumes inertia when it is inert, and becomes consciousness when it consists of consciousness, for the Self remains established in its own true nature. (MU 4.11.47)
The power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*), which consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and exists in the form of latent impressions, belongs to that Self which abides in its own true nature.

Having become insentient in the form of the latent impression of dullness (*jāḍya-vāsanā*), it assumes and takes on dullness, by which it manifests a stationary form. Having become conscious in the form of the latent impression of sentience (*cetanatva-vāsanā*), it attains consciousness, by which it manifests a moving form.
He states the conclusion:
"O sinless one, Brahman alone expands in this vast form through various manifestations and movements, like the ocean overflowing."
O sinless one! For that reason, this world of expansive form is none other than Brahman itself manifesting, shining forth.
Like what? Like a full ocean; just as it manifests through various movements called waves, so too does it—this is the meaning.
One assumes diversity for oneself through dwelling in various forms; it is as if the self, by itself and within itself, creates this diversity, like the water of the ocean within the water itself.
It is for the sake of various forms and for the sake of perceiving various forms; it is because of that which is a dwelling, namely play.
Just as various waves are not distinct from the water, so too all mental constructions are not distinct from the Lord of All.
From the Lord of all, who exists as the controller of everything, from that reality which is pure consciousness alone, arise the mental constructions (kalanā) that take the form of the world.
Just as the stalks, flowers, creepers, leaves, fruits, and buds reside within a single seed, so do all powers reside within Brahman.
The powers are the forms of the world; the powers are [the powers].
Just as there is a variety of powers in the Person (puruṣa) due to his being the agent of various [actions], so too is there always every power in the omniscient Self (ātman).

He states the reason for [the Lord's] omnipotence as "omniscient" (*sarvajña*). For if He were not omnipotent, He would not be omniscient; and here, omniscience is grounded in the capacity to be the creator of all things. Indeed, one who does not know everything cannot create everything, since it is observed that in the case of potters and others, their knowledge of the jar and so forth is restricted.
Just as a variegated color is seen in the harsh sunlight, so too does the Lord of Gods possess a manifold power consisting of both existence and non-existence.
This is clear.
This world of diverse forms arises from the non-diverse Śiva, who is of a single color, just as a streak of Indra’s bow arises from a cloud.
This is clear.
From the non-inert, the state of inertness arises, caused by the contemplation of dullness; just as a thread emerges from a spider, or as deep sleep arises from a person.
Of *jāḍya*, which is dullness; that which is its cultivation or conceptualization—that very thing is the cause of her, she who is such.
The auspicious Śiva, though devoid of mind, by his own will expands the power of the mental factors for the sake of his own bondage, just as a silkworm weaves a cocoon from its own silk.
"Mindless" (*acitta*) means devoid of mind due to its absolute purity; "made of threads" (*tāntava*) means connected with threads.
O Brahmin, by voluntarily contemplating its own form as the Self, the soul attains liberation from saṃsāra, just as an elephant [is freed] from its own tethering post.

By means of his own will pertaining to himself—that is, by his own desire—he, having contemplated his own innate body, known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), as being his true nature, bringing it within the range of contemplation as his very self, attains liberation from *saṃsāra*—from that *saṃsāra* consisting of the contemplation "I am the body. Who is he like? Like an elephant; just as the latter [attains] liberation from its tethering post.
"It comes"; that is the meaning. Here, the word "svecchā" (one's own will) denotes mere will (*icchāmātra*).
Whatever the self constantly contemplates, being itself cultivated by that very thing, even the great one is swiftly filled with that power.
Whatever power it may be that he has constantly cultivated and always perfumed, even though he is great and all-pervading.
Cultivated power brings the self to its true nature in an instant, just as a great autumn mist suddenly obscures even the infinite sky.

"Bhāvitā" means made the object of cultivation. "Ātmatām" refers to the state of being that self which is of the nature of power. In the case of the alternative reading "mihikā," it refers to the state of being mist (mihikātva).
The unborn one who quickly attains identity with that power which has arisen becomes identical with it; indeed, once he has reached that very state, he becomes like a tree permeated by its essence.

The Unborn (aja) is devoid of birth; the Pure is the reality of pure consciousness alone. "Stability" (sthitim) refers to the ground that serves as a support; for [the tree] ascends by conforming to the earth which constitutes its support, just like a tree.
There is no liberation for the Lord, nor is there bondage for the Self; I do not know from where these notions of bondage and liberation have arisen in the world.

Of the Lord who is the Self; or of the Self who is the Lord. If so, to whom do bondage and liberation belong? To this, he says "bondage" (bandha). The sense is that since, from the perspective of ultimate reality, the very arising of bondage and liberation does not exist, what need is there for consideration of their substratum?
For him there is neither bondage nor liberation, and he is perceived as being composed of that very [reality]; alas, this world is swallowed by the unreal, consisting of illusion! MU 4.11.62.

For this self, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is neither bondage nor liberation; however, from the perspective of immediate appearance (*āmukhataḥ*), it is perceived as being composed of that—that is, consisting of bondage and liberation. [Objection: If so, how is it that the conceptualization of bondage and liberation exists in the world? To this, he says: here, by the word "world" (*jagat*), the subjects (*pramātāraḥ*) residing within the world are indicated. Oh, what a marvel! The world—that is, those residing within the world—[is thus perceived].

The cognizers have been seized—that is, made permeated by their own mental constructs—by something called bondage and liberation, which is unreal (asatya), meaning non-existent. He states the reason for this by means of a qualification: "consisting of *māyā*. The sense is that it is precisely because they consist of *māyā* that they are seized by what is unreal.
Now, one might ask: "How has the Self come to be as if seized by the conceptualization of bondage, liberation, and so forth? To this, he says:
"When the mind was indeed conceptualized by the timeless (akala) Self, then this Self was enveloped by it, like a silkworm in its cocoon. (MU 4.11.63)

Because it is undivided and devoid of parts (*kalā*), it is "without parts" (*akalena*). When the mind is thus conceptualized—that is, made manifest—by this very self through the process of conceptualization (*kalanā*), then by this very self, like a silkworm (*kośakīṭa*), the self's own true nature (*svarūpa*) becomes enveloped. It is covered by a cocoon in the form of conceptualizations such as bondage and liberation.
"But surely, from what material cause did this mind, fashioned by this Self, emerge? To this he replies:
"Yet these powers of the mind, though non-different in nature from it, emerge from this [Self] in millions of forms, their bodies conceptualized as being distinct. (MU 4.11.64)
They are of non-different form, that is, they are not distinct; yet these [elements] exist as separate entities.
Abiding in that and born from that, they appear as distinct forms like waves from the ocean; abiding in that and born from that, yet appearing as separate entities, they are like rays from the moon.

"Abiding in that" means situated in that Supreme Self; "born from that" means produced from that Supreme Self. These powers of the mind exist as distinct forms. Like what? Like waves. The meaning is: just as waves exist as distinct forms from the ocean, so it is here. He states a second illustration with the words "abiding in that."

In this vast ocean of the Supreme Self, which consists of vibration, whose waters are consciousness, whose expansive expanse is spread out, and which abounds in the essence of pure consciousness alone; MU 4.11.66.
Some of these surging waves stand as the powers of Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra; they flash forth, their very nature manifested from the Self.

In that which consists of vibration (*spanda*) and consists of the self-reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃvimarśa*), for it is precisely this awareness of "I" that constitutes vibration here; in that which is expansive (*sphāra*) and vast; in that in which consciousness (*cit*)—consciousness directed toward an object of cognition (*cetyonmukhā cit*)—is itself the water; in such [a state]; in that in which pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—consciousness not directed toward an object of cognition (*cetyānunmukhā cit*)—is itself the essence (*rasa*); in such [a state]. It should be understood that *rasa* is the quality called "taste," which is the essential constituent of water.

In such a great ocean of the Supreme Self, these certain waves—waves of consciousness—quiver. How do these waves exist? They exist as Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra; they are those which are the movements and vibrations of consciousness (*cid-valanā*, *citspandāḥ*), and they exist as such with those [movements] as their primary quality. Furthermore, how do they exist? Their manifestation is brought forth and made evident from their own nature.
The meaning is that some waves, whose essence has gone [into them], manifest in the form of Hari, Brahmā, and Rudra.
Some, like Yama, Mahendra, Arka, Vahni, Vaiśravaṇa, and others, strike, act, or remain still—these waves of restless craving.
The *eṣaṇās* are fickle desires; those [women] who possess such [desires]. //MT_4,11.68//
Some Kinnaras, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Suras, and others fly up and fall down, like fierce waves surging and leaping about.
"Parivalgitāḥ" means those who have leaped about or quivered.
Some exist in a certain state of form, such as those born from the lotus and others; some have arisen and then perished, such as gods, humans, and others.
Those whose forms remain for some time are "those with forms that persist for a while" (*kiñcitsthitākārāḥ*).
Worms, insects, moths, and the like, as well as pythons, cobras, and so forth—some of these flicker within that great ocean like mere droplets.
The plural number in the word *eteṣu* is for the purpose of completing the meter; therefore, it should be construed as "in this great ocean" (*etasmin mahāmbhodhau*).
Some, such as the *calānana*, *mṛga*, *gṛdhra*, and *vañjulaka* birds, flutter about in the mountain thickets like those on the shores of the coastal forests.
This is clear.
Some have very long lives, while others have extremely short lives; some have wretched bodies due to their own wretched mental cultivation.
Some, due to the void, the unreal, from the cultivation of their own voidness, from their own objects, and from the conceptualization of the void, come to possess a void body.
In the turbulent dream of saṃsāra, some are imbued with a sense of stability; others, struck down by their own conceptual constructions, imagine the world to be firmly established.
"By stability" means by way of firmness; "cultivated" means they have been made possessed of the latent impression that "this saṃsāra is stable."
Some have very slight cultivation, being overcome by the fault of dejection; they are made firm in their suffering by thinking, "I am emaciated, extremely miserable, and deluded."
In this context, the extreme meagerness of meditative cultivation should be understood as resulting from extreme dullness.
Some have attained the state of stationary beings, some have reached the state of gods; some have attained the state of men, and some have gone to the state of Dānavas.
This is clear.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he summarizes the very same meaning previously stated:

"Some remain in the world for many hundreds of kalpas; others, being perfectly pure, go to the Supreme Person. For the cognitions of consciousness—known by the other name 'reflection' (manana)—arise from the ocean of Brahman, restless like waves.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter in the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
O Sage, these cognitions that take the forms of gods, asuras, and humans are non-different from you, who are the ocean of Brahman; this is the truth, and everything else is false.

This refers to those cognitions that take the form of gods, asuras, and humans; their non-difference from the ocean of Brahman is "oneness," while their difference from it is "otherness. The mention of gods, asuras, and humans is made because they are the most prominent [of all beings].

O Brahmin, cognitions taking the forms of gods, asuras, and humans differentiate themselves through false imagination, defiled by their own conceptual constructions; indeed, by the internal conviction that "we are not Brahman," they have descended to lower states.
With the second half [of the verse], he states the reason for its being stained: "It is not Brahman. The word *hi* has the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Even those who have entered the ocean of Brahman, conceiving themselves as distinct from Brahman, become deluded while wandering through the terrifying terrains of worldly existence.
In the terrifying [situations], which are extremely fearsome due to their quality of bestowing suffering.
O Sage, know that these divine cognitions, which are not stained by manifold defects, are either the seed of actions or, indeed, the action itself.
These aforementioned cognitions (*saṃvidas*), which are reflections (*parāmarśās*) appearing in the forms of gods, demons, and humans, are "Brahmic" (*brāhmyaḥ*), meaning they are related to Brahman.

They are "not stained by a single [type of] stain" (*naikakalaṅkitāḥ*); the meaning is that they are stained in many ways. Know this—that these very Brahmic cognitions are the seed, the cause, of actions; or rather, action itself.

Know that this [consciousness] is preceded by the external object intended as an object; for indeed, the arising of an external object is neither observed nor logical without the reflective awareness of consciousness.

O Sage, he explains that these very [powers] are the cause of the entire world: "By means of this internal process of conceptualization (*kalanā*), which is of the nature of volition (*saṅkalpa*), and which is formidable like a handful of seeds for the *karañja* trees of the web of karma."
In this vast world, these rows of stone-like bodies stand, they leap about, they weep, and they laugh.
From the realm of Brahmā down to a blade of grass, like the wind through its vibrations, they surge forth, withdraw, wither, and laugh.

O Sage, by this mental construction— which is of the nature of volition (*saṅkalpa*), which is like a handful of seeds for the *karañja* trees of the web of karma (meaning: that which constitutes the cause of the web of karma),
and which is therefore a source of transformation and terrifying— by this very construction whose form is consciousness, there exist in the vast universe,
from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, rows of stones that are bodies.

They leap about, weep, laugh, rejoice, withdraw, wither, and smile; this is an illustration, meaning that they perform all actions. This is because the aforementioned actions are not observed in dead bodies.
What is it like? It is like the wind. Just as the wind performs various kinds of actions through the vibrations within itself...
It acts; that is the meaning of "so."
Among these, some are exceedingly clear, such as Hari, Hara, and others; some are situated in slight delusion, such as the uragas, humans, and gods.
This is clear.
Some remain in a state of absolute delusion, such as trees, grass, and the like; others, utterly bewildered by ignorance, have come to the state of worms and insects.
This is clear.
Some are carried away like blades of grass, far from the great ocean of Brahman; these have not attained the [spiritual] stages, just like the serpent-people and others.
They have not attained the stages; they have not reached the further shore.
Seeing only the riverbank, some have fallen into despair; those born and those yet to be born are being buried by the old rat of Kṛtānta.

It is by merely beholding the shore, not by reaching it; for if one were to reach it, it would not be appropriate to be repeatedly buried by Death (Kṛtānta). And here, the "shore" should be understood as the nature of resting in pure consciousness alone.
Having reached the interior of the great ocean of the reality of Brahman, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śiva, and the others have attained that state for the sake of freedom from sorrow.
That state of Brahman; for the sake of freedom from sorrow, that is, for the absence of grief.
Some, possessed of only slight delusion, remain established by taking refuge in that very ocean of Brahman, which has never seen the flood of the disease of passion.
"Having relied upon" means having taken as one's own self; the meaning is that some [beings] are of the nature of those liberated while living (jīvanmukta).
Some multitudes of births yet to be experienced, and millions of multitudes of births already experienced; some species of beings remain barren, while others abide in the light of manifestation.
They are characterized by the quality of darkness (tamas) and possess excessive darkness; for this very reason, they are barren, being devoid of the fruit known as perfect knowledge.
Some go from above to below, and likewise from below to the great state; some go higher than high, while others go even lower than low.
Below, there is birth as an animal or hell; above, the great state of humanity or heaven.
He states the final conclusion with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"This activity, fraught with many joys and sorrows, has come into being here due to the non-remembrance of the Supreme State; through the realization of the Supreme State, it goes to its destruction, just as the pain of poison vanishes through the remembrance of the Lord of Birds."
Of the Lord of Birds, Garuḍa—who is the embodiment of the deity of the Garuḍika mantras—may there be auspiciousness! (Śivaṃ). MT 4.12.16.
Thus ends the twelfth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. The venerable Vasiṣṭha said to the venerable Rāma:
"Those who know reality, reflecting upon the courses of the world, set out from that bank of the Samaṅgā river like rays of light flickering."
The *jāgatī*s are those related to the world; they are the *gatī*s, meaning structures or arrangements.
Gradually ascending into the sky and emerging from the hollows of the clouds, they reached Mount Mandara with its golden caves by way of the path of the Siddhas.
"By means of hollows" (*koṭaraiḥ*) means for the purpose of [coming] from the hollows (*koṭarebhyaḥ*).
On the plateau of that mountain, the descendant of Bhṛgu beheld his own body from a previous birth, now withered but still draped in moist leaves.
This is clear.
And she said this: "O father, this slender body is indeed that very one which was formerly cherished by you with pleasant enjoyments."
This is clear.
This is that very body of mine, for which cool beds were prepared with heaps of mandāra flowers upon the grounds of the groves of Mount Meru.
"She" refers to her alone, and not to anyone else.
Behold, this very body of mine, once caressed by hosts of celestial women, now lies upon the surface of the earth, mangled by the mouths of crawling reptiles.
This is clear.
This very body of mine, by which I long sported in the groves of the Nandana garden, has now become a withered skeleton.
The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), as in "the act of sporting" (*vilasitam*).
Because my mental state is devoid of contact with the limbs of celestial damsels and is engaged in the lofty theater of passion, this body of mine here is wasting away.
The *lakāra* occurs in the sense of the state of being dried up.
Having bound those very mental impressions to each of those various amorous pastimes and each of those states, how can you, O embodied one, remain at ease?
Those meditations have celestial women as their object. You are composed because you are free from fickleness. "Dehaka" refers to the body; it is an address to that body, meaning "O little body."
Alas, where have you been shattered? You have come to the withering of an ascetic; you have reached the state of a mere skeleton, yet you, O wretched one, still fixate upon me!
"O wretched body, you that are a skeleton and a heap of bones, do you still cherish me? Do you remember me?"—this statement is made because she is overwhelmed by excessive affection.
I am now afraid of that very same body by which I once took delight in its graceful charms, for it has now become a mere skeleton.
I am afraid of that very body by which I was once delighted in pleasures, now that it has become a mere skeleton.
Behold, where there was once a necklace with the appearance of a net of stars upon my chest, ants are now crawling over it.
They settle down; they cling.
Behold: by that very body of mine, which once captivated excellent women with its luster like molten gold, I am now dragged along by a garland of skeletons.
It is carried away and it is sustained.
Behold, in this forest, the deer are terrified by my gaping mouth—my ascetic’s dried-out hide, my skull-like face with its foul countenance.
They are terrified; by virtue of being possessed of transformation, they are made to experience terror.
Behold how the cave of my corpse’s belly, through its extreme dryness, shines with the web of the sun’s rays, as if illuminated by discernment.
The belly of a corpse—that is, the interior of a dead body—is itself a cave.
With her body intoxicated yet now completely parched, she lies supine upon the forest floor; by the insignificance of her own self, she seems to lead even those dwelling in the sky toward dispassion.
The gods residing in the sky.
On this mountain, my body is being emaciated by means of non-conceptual meditative absorption alone, which is liberated from attachment to sound, form, taste, touch, and smell.

By my body being of what nature? It is such [a body] as possesses a concentration (*samādhi*) within that which is non-conceptual—that is, which has emerged from conceptualization and is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). //MT_4,15.17//
When the vampire of the mind has been completely stilled, the degree of bliss that the body attains cannot be reached even by sovereignty over the entire world.
By means of that which belongs to the world, i.e., that which is related to the world.
Behold: with all worldly toil at rest and every curiosity vanished, the body sleeps happily, with the web of conceptual constructions cast away.
This is clear.
The tree of the body, agitated by the frantic agitation of the monkey-mind, shakes with such force that it cuts away its own roots.
The "cutting of the root" should be understood as having the form of worldly agitation.
Freed from the miseries of the mind, he no longer perceives this body of mine as having the flickering appearance of an elephant, a cloud, or a lion; rather, it remains like supreme bliss.
He does not see—that is, he does not experience—the *vibhrama*, meaning the playful grace or the restlessness, of elephants, clouds, and lions.
I see no other source of welfare for living beings than this state of mindlessness, which is like the arrival of autumn to the mist of delusion caused by the fever of all desires.
This is clear.
Those of great intelligence and tranquil minds who have attained a state of detachment have reached the very limit of the enjoyment of happiness.
This is clear.
By good fortune, I behold this body of mine in the forest—freed from all states of suffering, perfectly tranquil, free from fever, and beyond the activity of thought.
This is clear.
Here Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, it is said that at that time the descendant of Bhṛgu repeatedly took up and experienced very many bodies."
O Sage, since this body was produced by Bhṛgu, what great excellence has arisen in it through that [act], or is it merely a cause for lamentation?
Excellence is the knowledge of excellence.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha speaks further:
"O Rāma, that conceptualization of Śukra which had reached the state of a living being was born as the son of Bhṛgu, the descendant of Bhr̥gu, consisting of the nature of karma."

The *kalanā* is the vibration (*spanda*) known as consciousness (*samvit*), which brings about the manifestation of the *śukra* (semen) and the *jīva* (individual soul). "Of Venus" (*bhṛgoḥ*) is in the ablative case; "that" (*sā*) is the ellipsis to be supplied [referring to the *kalanā*]. It [brings about] the state of the *jīva* belonging to the *śukra*, that is, the condition of the individual soul associated with the *śukra*. (MT 4.15.27)
For she, having first come together from the supreme state and reached the state of elemental space, becomes agitated by the wind.
Entering the heart of Bhṛgu by means of the flow of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, he gradually attained virility and became endowed with the body of Uśanas.
By virtue of being the very first and by virtue of preceding that; having come together and arisen perfectly; the body of Uśanas, which takes the form of the body of Śukra. This is a couplet.
Then, having received the purificatory rites of a Brahmin, she went before her father; after a long time, she reached the state of a withered skeleton.
This is clear.
When that body of Brahmā first arrived, it was then that Śukra lamented for her.
This was the first time; that was the previous [occasion]. Such was that lamentation; such a lamentation was performed.
Though free from passion and though he was without desire, Śukra, possessing a body of equal form, grieved for his own physical frame; for such is the nature born of the body.
This is clear.
However, under the guise of grief, that wise one demonstrated for the sake of attaining dispassion that very separateness between the body and the embodied self.
"But what" (*kiṃ tu*) introduces an alternative view; thus, the sense is that Śukra lamented solely for the sake of benefiting others.

Whether for one who knows or for one who does not know, this sequence continues as long as life lasts; worldly activity proceeds always, either with attachment or without attachment, just like the common world.
Alternatively, in another sense, the connection is "the worldly activity of the body. Or, by means of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the meaning is "of the embodied one" (*dehinaḥ*).

Thus, the meaning is "of the body of the wise one" or "of the body of the ignorant one. It should be understood that the sequence follows from the non-attachment of the wise one and the attachment of the ignorant one.
Those who have fully understood the course of existence and those who are ignorant, following the nature of beasts, remain within worldly conventions like a forest thicket.
The "network of forest trees" is to be understood as a mere simile for the state of being situated.
Just as the worldly person is ignorant, so indeed is the wise one; here, the difference lies merely in their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), which is the cause of bondage and liberation.
The distinction consisting solely of latent impressions (vāsanā) is to be understood in terms of purity and impurity.
For as long as there is a body, so long indeed is there suffering in suffering and pleasure in pleasure; yet the wise, whose minds are unattached, demonstrate this as if they were unawakened.
They show [it] to others and cause them to see it, but they do not see it themselves.
Great-souled beings are always happy amidst pleasures and sorrowful amidst states of suffering; indeed, they are seen to be truly cool within.
They are cool, being free from the agitation caused by pleasure and pain.
The reflections on a pillar tremble, but its stable form does not; likewise, only the active organs of the wise man are agitated, but his steady mind is not.

The "firm body" is the stable form known as the pillar (*stambha*). The term *kṣubhyanti* contains an implied causative sense (*antar-ṇic*); thus, the meaning is that those two do not cause agitation. The "organs of action" are those which perform the function called perception; that is to say, they are the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriyāṇi*).
Through its state of being both moving and unmoving, the Knower of That abides amidst the activities of the world, like the sun reflected in clear waters while remaining fixed below.
"By being unsteady" means by extreme flicker. Of what nature is the Sun? He is one whose "stay"—that is, his remaining—is "below," in the lower region. //MT_4,15.40//
One whose intellect is unawakened remains bound even if he has abandoned worldly actions; one whose intellect is awakened is truly liberated even while still engaged in the play of delusion.
The intended meaning is that, in this context, the states of having an awakened intellect and not having an awakened intellect are themselves the causes of liberation and bondage, respectively.

For one whose faculty of intellect is liberated is liberated even if the faculty of action is bound; likewise, one whose faculty of intellect is bound is bound even if the faculty of action is liberated.
The word "hi" indicates what is well-known.

In this world, the intellect and the senses alone are the cause for the perception of pleasure and pain, as well as for the perception of bondage and liberation, just as lights are the cause for illumination.
In the sense of "manifesting," that is, in making the meaning evident.
Outwardly, observe the conduct appropriate for the world, yet inwardly, be devoid of such conduct; remain as if you were non-existent, with all desires completely stilled.
Within the mind.
Free from all desires, abiding in the Self by means of the self, perform the actions that ought to be done; indeed, let your state remain centered in the mind.

O Rāma! You, being liberated from all desires, should therefore perform your prescribed duties and actions with a mind that abides in the Self—indeed, in the Self and not in objects which are of the nature of the non-Self. Truly, by necessity, that state of "abiding in the non-mind" does not exist as an abiding in the [ordinary] mind.
Do not fall into this pit on the path of saṃsāra, which is a great whirlpool of mental and physical ailments, and which yields only misery—a deep, blind well of possessiveness.
In what kind of place? In the blind well of "mine-ness" (mamatā), on the path of saṃsāra—that is, on the way whose nature is saṃsāra—situated as a pit by virtue of being a pit.
You do not exist in things, nor do things exist in you, O lotus-eyed one; you are of the nature of pure awakening, established in the self—be firm.

You are the witness, whose nature is pure consciousness alone; you are established in the self, having the nature of being pure and enlightened, with the self as your supreme goal, and not dependent on the body and so forth.
He concludes the answer with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"O Great-Souled One, if you have attained the stainless state free from longing, wherein the great darkness of *mamatā* (the sense of 'mine-ness') has vanished, and if you thus prevail over the mind, then salutations to you, the one of supreme intellect, the great and the truly existent. (MU 4.15.48)

That which has dispelled the great darkness consisting of the form of "mine-ness"—that is such. For this very reason, it is stainless, free from longing, and devoid of all desire due to its state of contentment. Having attained—that is, having realized as one's own self—the state known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), if you, O Great-souled One, prevail over the mind—that is, if you become capable of conquering the mind—then that [state is yours].
Then: "Obeisance be to you. To one of what nature? To the one of supreme intellect (*atidhiye*), to the one of exalted wisdom; to the great (*mahate*), to the one endowed with greatness;
to the existent (*sate*), to the one whose essential nature is pure being (*sanmātra*). Thus, may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the fifteenth canto in the "Stability" chapter of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Then, having interrupted the speech of that son of Bhṛgu, the Blessed Lord Kāla spoke these words in a deep-sounding voice.
Having drawn forth—that is, having made the object of his censure—the son of Bhṛgu, Śukra.
Time says:
O Bhārgava, abandon this body, which is now like that of an ascetic woman; enter this [new] body, O virtuous one, as a king enters his city.
"Belonging to the Samaṅga ascetic," meaning related to the Samaṅga ascetic.
O sinless one, at the proper time, having performed penance again with this body born of your former birth, you must assume the position of the lords of the Asuras.
This is clear.
When the end of the great aeon has arrived, you must cast off this Bhārgava body, like a withered flower, so that it is not taken up again.
This is clear.
O high-minded one, having attained the state of liberation while living, remain in this body with its former form, acting as the preceptor to the great lords of the Asuras.
By means of her former form known as Śukrā.
May it be well with you both; we shall go to our desired direction. There is not even the slightest thing that would not be desired by that mind.

[Objection: "But how is it that even for you there is something desired? To this he says: "Nothing at all. That [mind] does not exist as anything whatsoever for which there is no desire. Therefore, the sense is that because I too possess a mind, I likewise have something desired.
Having said this, as the two of them were releasing the flower, he vanished from between them like the sun, the radiant one, disappearing simultaneously with its rays from heaven and earth.
The sun is the one with heated rays; [it shines] upon the two worlds, heaven and earth.
When the Blessed One had departed after speaking of that destiny, Bhārgava reflected upon the course of necessity, which is indivisible and fixed by fate.

Like the spring season entering a beautiful creeper that has been withered by the cause of time but is destined for the auspicious emergence of future flowers, [the Lord] entered the body of that young woman.

"Indivisible" means impossible to break. "Named Time" refers to that cause which is called time; by it she was "dried up. "Mādhava" is the spring season; by metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*), it refers to the springtime aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). She is one whose auspicious rising—like that of flowers—is about to happen.
[She is] her. (MT 4.16.8–9)
That brahmin’s body, pale and bodiless, fell trembling quickly upon the ground like a creeper whose roots have been severed.
The body of a brahmin, the body of a samaṅga, and the body of an ascetic.
When the life-force had entered that body of his son, the great sage performed a restoration of vitality with mantras and the waters from his water-pot.
Nourishment is filling.
Then all her slender veins shone forth, filled [with blood], like rivers in the rainy season whose hollows are filled with floods of water.
This is clear.
Like a lotus pond in the rainy season or a fresh creeper in spring, when she was full, her life-breaths blossomed like sprouts.
This is the body of Bhārgava; "full" means full of vital breath (*prāṇa*). Of that body, the "sprouts" are those that have swollen in the form of *apāna* and the other [vital winds].
Then Śukra arose, his vital breaths flowing forth, like a rain-cloud rising from its roots through the union of moisture and wind.
From the root, beginning from the very root.
He, whose form was purified, first saluted his father, just as a cloud newly risen greets a mountain with its thundering.
This is clear.
Then his father embraced his body from long ago, his conduct moist with affection, just as a rain cloud after a long time embraces a mountain slope.
This is clear.
Bhṛgu beheld with affection his former body as a son; the conviction "this one was born from me" carries away even a person of great intelligence.

"Regarding the phrase 'tānayīm,' which means 'related to her son': [an objection is raised]—'How could such a body, belonging to one endowed with such knowledge, have been looked upon by him with affection? To this, he replies: 'mattaḥ' (from me)."
At that time, the affection arising from the thought "this is my son" even overcame Bhṛgu; for this sense of "otherness" and "self-identity" persists as long as the physical form exists.
Otherness is the state of being other; "mine-ness" is the state of belonging to a self. As long as there is form, so long is there the body. That which is destined to be will inevitably come to pass.
Then the father and son became mutually adorned by one another, like the sun and a lotus-pond rejoicing at the end of the night.
At the end of the night, at dawn; they were joyful.
Right here he tells two other similes:
like a pair of chakravaka birds joined together after a long separation, or like a peacock and a cloud whose affection is deepened by the arrival of the rainy season.
Having stayed there for a moment with that conversation, which was suited to their long-standing and firm longing, those two of great intelligence then rose.
There they reduced that body of the twice-born Samaṅga to ashes; for who indeed, born into this world, does not observe established custom?
Conduct means worldly conduct.
Thus, in that sacred forest, those two—Bhṛgu and Bhārgava—remained, blazing with ascetic power like the moon and the sun in the sky.
This is clear.

The two masters of the world, who had realized what is to be known and were liberated while living, performed their penance with perfect tranquility and great stability amidst the floods of various places, times, and conditions.
Of what nature is that austerity? It is that in which there is excellent tranquility; such is it.
Then, in the course of time, Śukra attained the status of preceptor to the Asuras, while Bhṛgu remained in his own appropriate and untroubled station.
In the state appropriate for oneself, namely the state known as liberation while in the disembodied state (videhamukti).
He summarizes the account of Śukra with a verse at the end of the chapter, beginning with "This Śukra":

"This Śukra was first born from this Supreme Abode (paramapada) in due order, possessing noble fame; later, through his own swift wandering into the paths of memory, he became thus utterly agitated within various states of existence. From this [Supreme Abode], as the Self of all...

From the supreme state (*paramapada*), known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which exists prior [to all], from that highest station; throughout the various stages (*daśāntara*), beginning with *sama* and ending with *aṅgātapa-sattva*, in these particular states—thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the sixteenth canto in the "Stability" chapter of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, the intuitive flash of the son of Bhṛgu arose from direct experience; just as it became fruitful for him, why would it not be so for another?"

O Blessed One, by means of this very account just described, that intuition— the intuitive manifestation consisting of the experience of entering various wombs— of this son of Bhṛgu has become fruitful, endowed with the result known as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*),
due to the cause of direct experience. Otherwise, there would have been no experience concerning the ascetic Samaṅga, whether related to Bhṛgu or related to oneself.

The sense is that it would be logical [to say] "it should be so. Likewise, in that same manner, for another person—that is, a person distinct from Śukra—how could that intuition (*pratibhā*) not be fruitful? It certainly would not; for what appears in a dream as one's own state of being an elephant and so forth is not experienced through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replies:
"At that time, this pure intelligence first arose from the state of Brahmā for Bhārgava; it was not stained by any other previous birth."

This was his first [insight], preceded by that [previous one], because it arose immediately from the foot of the Brahman Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu; for that intellect, which had as its object the creative intuition (*pratibhā*) regarding various wombs, was pure, being untainted by the accumulation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births.
Consequently, that intuition of his, consisting in the transition through various wombs, became fruitful. Others, however, [claim it was] the very first, because it arose [at the beginning].

The meaning is that, being stained by the web of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) arising from various previous births, [beings] do not experience their own innate intuition (*svapratibhāna*) as a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

"Now, what is the nature of this pure state of mind? To this he says: "Upon the complete cessation of all desires... "When there is the total subsiding of all desires—that is, of all longings directed toward the manifold web of various objects of enjoyment—the state of the mind that remains is called *sattva*; it is described as this very stainless consciousness (*cid*). [The commentary explains: "Of all desires" means of all the wishes directed toward the various networks of objects to be enjoyed.

When there is pacification—either through the power of deep sleep and so forth, or through right knowledge and so forth—of the mind (*citta*) or the intellect (*manas*), that state, that abiding, which exists, is called "being" (*sattva*) by the wise. That very same stainless consciousness (*vimalā cit*) is declared to be stainless intelligence (*vimalā mati*). Furthermore, this very pure intelligence is [the nature] of that which has arisen for the first time.

It occurs for one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta) as well; however, the distinction is that for one in whom this has arisen for the first time, it is directed toward external objects, whereas for one liberated while living, it is characterized by the relinquishing of external objects.
Having spoken by way of a specific illustration, he now explains by means of a general principle:
Whatever the mind, whose nature is pure being, contemplates, that very thing quickly comes to be just so, like a whirlpool in the water of the ocean.

The stainless self of being (*nirmalasattvātman*)—that is, the mind whose nature is the stainless being mentioned in the preceding verse—whatever it may be and in whatever manner it is joined, when one contemplates it, bringing it into the range of continuous reflection, that object immediately becomes joined in that very same manner. What is that object like? It is like a whirlpool; just as [a whirlpool] situated in the ocean [is formed] by the water.
The whirlpool immediately becomes joined with another kind; such is the meaning of "tathā" (thus).
By this account, he states that his own intended point is established:
"Just as this delusion of the son of Bhṛgu arose spontaneously, so too is each individual case here illustrated by the son of Bhṛgu.
Just as this aforementioned delusion of the son of Bhṛgu [arose].
The delusion, which consists of forms appearing as various types of births, has arisen and manifested by its own nature.

In this very same way, it arises for each individual person. The meaning is that all beings perceive the world as nothing other than the form appearing to their own minds. To further solidify this point, the example of semen is given once again.
He says: "An example is given here."
He makes this very point easy to understand through various analogies:
"Just as the seed brings forth its own sprouts, leaves, and so forth with a wondrous transformation, even so does the mass of all living beings [arise] from delusion."

Just as the sprout, leaf, and so forth— which are unique to a seed and not shared with other seeds— bring about a wonder, producing a joy in the form of swelling; for (*hi*) is certain, so too does the world-form, which is the unique whirlpool (*bhramaṣaṇḍa*) belonging to all the multitudes of beings (*bhūtasaṅghānām*), bring about a wonder, producing the happiness of various tastes.
The point is that although this cycle of existence appears as something common [to all], it is in fact distinct for each individual.
This entire universe that is perceived is indeed exactly like this: each thing arises falsely, and it sets forth falsely as well.

This entire world, which is saṃsāra, that is seen and experienced by us—indeed, as a certainty—in this very manner, it remains exactly so. This whole universe arises falsely at every moment; the suffix *kta* here denotes the present tense. And it sets falsely as well, because it has always remained exactly thus in its nature as the Supreme Consciousness (*paracit*).
The intended meaning is that it is impossible for [the self] to be the object of the arising and setting of what is real (satyabhūta).
Nothing in this world ever sets or rises for anyone; this is mere delusion, a magical illusion expanding in vain.
This world is illusion; it has the form of illusion.
Just as this forest of saṃsāra exists within our own appearance, so indeed do thousands of such forests exist for them, each perceived by one another.

Just as this forest of saṃsāra exists for us—appearing before us as something transcending the senses, yet manifesting as "this" despite being of the nature of pure consciousness which transcends all senses—so too do thousands of such forests of saṃsāra exist for them.
In response to the question of why these are not seen, he provides the qualification: "not seen by one another."
*Mithaḥ* means mutually; *adṛṣṭāni* means not brought within the range of vision.
He tells the analogy of mutual perception:
"Just as the activities of dreams and imagined cities are not seen separately from one another, so too are these delusions of cyclic existence."
The summary meaning is this: just as one person does not experience the dream of another, so too one person does not experience the saṃsāra of another.

If it is asked, "How then can there be a distinction between creations for each individual? the answer is: no, because even with respect to a single object, we observe that it is to be abandoned by one person while being something to be acquired by another.
He provides this summary:
"In this way, there exist multitudes of cities whose nature consists of mental constructs of space; they are not seen by one another except through the vision of knowledge."

This being so, there exist multitudes—that is, collections—of such cities whose forms are like the mental construction (*saṅkalpa*) of cities and the like in the sky. [Note: The use of an adjective for the word *nagara* (city), which has become a subordinate member (*upasarjana*) in the compound, is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*). By those multitudes of cities, [those very multitudes of cities are perceived] without the vision of knowledge—that is, without the knowledge known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
Without [ordinary] vision, they are not seen—that is, they are not perceived—by one another. However, they are indeed seen by the vision of knowledge (*jñānadṛś*).
Therefore, the intended meaning is: "For this very reason, I see them, whereas you do not see them."
He explains that even all those well-known beings, such as *piśācas* and others, possess this same nature:
"For *piśācas*, *yakṣas*, and *rakṣasas* truly exist in such forms; their bodies consist of mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) and are composed of pleasure and pain. (MU 4.17.12)
This is clear.
He extends this very same nature even to himself:
"In this very way, O descendant of Raghu, we and these others have come into being; our forms consist of our own volitions, conditioned by the state of being both false and real. (MU 4.17.13)
Regarding falsity and truth, they are "cultivated" (bhāvitāḥ), meaning endowed with cultivation, within their own state of truth.
Having thus spoken briefly of the distinction, he speaks again in general terms:
"For such indeed is the course of creation and transmigration for others; it is not real, yet in reality, this state exists within the unreal."
