Of such a nature, it is of the form of a reflection. When others have crossed over into pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), that which is called "creation" (*sarga*) is the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*);

this "creation-cycle" (*sargasaṃsṛti*) is not real, for its nature is unreal. But on the other hand, in reality—that is, from the perspective of the ultimate truth—this creation-cycle abides in the non-substantial void (*śūnya*). For it is impossible for the creation, being a non-substantiality, to have pure consciousness—which exists as a substantial reality—as its substratum.
By means of the reasoning previously stated, he provides the conclusion regarding his own desired thesis:
"In this very way, each individual thing that has arisen is indeed in vain, just as the essence of spring exists in the form of the nine-fold cluster [of flowers]. (MU 4.17.15)
In this way, according to the manner previously described; *vāsantika-rasaḥ* means the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) associated with spring (*vasanta*).
This first, one's own volition, has thus attained great expansion, such that it is perceived in this way through a firm and ultimate transcendence.

This is the first [creation], which arose prior to that [subsequent creation] as Brahmā’s own volition (*svasaṅkalpa*) alone. In that manner, it has reached a state of great renown and extreme prevalence. In this way, by such a method, it is perceived—that is, determined—with firmness, with immovability, and with the nature of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), by people; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Each individual mind, arisen and abiding within the belly of its own intrinsic nature, perishes as it perceives this world as being engaged in such [dualistic] activity.

"Sva" means one's own; "svabhāva" refers to one's essential nature, known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). "In its belly" means as if in its belly, but not in a literal belly. "Situated" means existing. "Each" means in every single one. "Arisen" means produced. "Mind" (*citta*)—[the world] which has such an undertaking, that is, which possesses the undertaking seen [by the mind]. Behold this world; experience it.
"It perishes" means that it falls away from the reflective awareness of its own true nature.
By the power of appearance it exists, yet by the observation of the actual thing it does not exist; the web of the world is a long dream, the tethering post for the elephant of the mind.

By virtue of appearance; for it is not logical that there should be an appearance of what is non-existent—this is the meaning. Because of the observation of reality, because of the observation of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Indeed, the world does not persist by means of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*). Who is the web of the world? It is a long dream.
For the world is indeed the existence of the mind, and the existence of the mind is the world; in the absence of one, both perish, and that occurs through the investigation of reality.
That is the absence of oneness; it arises from the non-investigation of truth, that is, from the investigation of truth.
He recalls the answer to the question posed by Śrī Rāma:
"For the manifestation of a pure mind is indeed true; for the coloring with saffron adheres only to a stainless cloth. (MU 4.17.20)
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "spotless" (*niṣkalaṅka*), meaning free from impurity (*mala*).
The quality of one who has not been brought low by another necessarily increases; the intellect of one who is not assailed by discursive thoughts becomes clear.

"Of that which is not brought [by others] and not overcome. Having stated the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he explains the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "of that which is not overcome. "Inspiration" (*pratibhā*) means a manifestation (*pratibhāsa*). It "arises," meaning it appears as something fruitful.
Just as gold does not remain [pure] when placed upon a soiled cloth, so a single vision does not remain stable when the mind is withered.
"Suvarṇaḥ" means beautiful, such as white and other colors; "mlāne" means when it is withered, defiled by conceptual construction (saṃkalpa).
Just as a gem is purified by polishing, or as copper is purified by the proper application of methods, so too does the purification of the mind arise from long-term, firm, and continuous practice.
In one [practice], such as right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and so forth; that which is firm practice, namely the constant contemplation thereof—on account of that.
Śrī Rāma asks:
How do these sequences of time and action, along with their rising and setting, arise within the mind of Śukra, given that the world is of the nature of a mere appearance?

In a world whose nature is mere appearance, it is not logical for the sequences of temporal activity that manifest within it to possess both rising and setting; and the point is this: how could such a thing have arisen from the mind of Śukra?
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Just as this world was perceived by Śukra through his father and mother, so it remained established in his mind, like a peacock within a peacock's egg."

Whatever this world was seen by the semen produced from father and mother, that very same [world] remained situated within the mind of that semen. How? Like a peacock; the meaning is that it was just as a peacock exists within a peacock's egg.
That which has been tasted from the treasury of its own nature arises through this sequence, just as a sprout, leaf, and so forth, a creeper, flower, and fruit arise from a seed.

Then, by means of this semen (*śukra*), that world which resides within the mind—[emerging] from the sheath of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kośa*), which is the very nature whose form is the mind—from that sheath in its specific form; having arisen in succession, it is tasted, that is, made the object of relish. Regarding this, he states an illustration: "by means of the seed. (MT 4.17.26)
Whatever is the essence of a living being's latent impressions (vāsanā), that very thing it perceives within; here, a dream is the illustration, and this world is but a long dream.

Now, one might ask: "How can a dream serve as an illustration here? To this he replies: "It is indeed a long dream. And its length should be understood here as being due to the persistence of the appearance for a long time.
O Rāma, has the thicket of saṃsāra not indeed arisen individually for each person, manifest within one's own self like the web of dreams of soldiers and men at night?
For at night, the net of dreams arises individually and distinctly as the specific forms of the men in the army.
Śrī Rāma asks:
Does this flood of the thicket of worldly existence merge with itself spontaneously, or not? If so, you ought to explain that to me accurately.

Whether this flood of the thicket of worldly existence meets with others through its own inherent nature, or whether it does not meet them—whether it be mutual or otherwise—you ought to explain this correctly and thoroughly;
that is to say, you should relate it properly.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Indeed, a defiled mind does not deserve union with vigor, just as iron that has not been heated does not adhere to other iron; but when it is purified and heated, it melts together."

The word *hi* indicates certainty. "Defiled" (*malina*) means corrupted by the impurities of passion (*rāga*) and so forth; for this very reason, it is "lacking vigor" (*avīrya*). The mind (*manaḥ*) does not deserve "union" (*śleṣa*), that is, contact, with another [the Self]. With what is it like? It is like iron (*ayaḥ*). Just as iron does not deserve union when it is not heated, such is the meaning. But (*tu*), in the alternative case, when the mind is "pure" (*śuddha*), the mind merges—that is, it unites—and the iron likewise [merges when heated].
When heated, it dissolves into water.
The pure principles of consciousness merge with one another; for just as waters of a single nature attain unity, those that are turbid do not.
This is clear.
He expresses this very point with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"For the purity of the mind is indeed a single state consisting of being free from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the absence of perception of unreal objects; having awakened from that state of deep sleep, it attains union with the Supreme through the yoga of those subtle elements. (MU 4.17.32)

"Hi" signifies certainty. "Abhūtasaṃvedanātma" means having the nature of perceiving unreal objects—that is, the essential character of perceiving things that are not established. "Vivāsanatvam" means the state of being devoid of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) known as the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of objects. "Eka" means solitary or alone. "Cittasya śuddhiḥ bhavati" means the mind becomes pure. "Tat cittaṃ" refers to that mind. "Suṣuptātma" means having the nature of deep sleep. "Yat padaṃ" means that state or place. "Tasmāt" means from that. "Tasyāḥ śuddheḥ hetoḥ" means by reason of that purity. "Prabudhya" means having awakened; "turyākhyam bodhaṃ prāpya" means having attained the awakening called the Fourth (*turya*).

By means of the application of the subtle elements (*tanmātra-yukti*), through union with the subtle elements, he "goes" to—that is, attains—contact with others, which is a merging with them. Furthermore, by the application of the subtle elements, "merging" should be understood as the knowledge that everything shares a single material cause (*ekopādānatva*) together with oneself.
Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the seventeenth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! But how can the mind, through the logic of being composed of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), meet with other things? To this, he says:
"In all the clusters of transmigratory existence, there is no difference in the manifestation of that which consists of the nature of the seed-form of the subtle elements. (MU 4.18.1)

The seed-form is the very nature of the seed; that which is the *kalā* (portion) belongs to that self, meaning to that essential nature—namely, that which has the form of the seed of the gross elements.

Of the manifestation consisting of the five *tanmātras*, that is, of the manifestation in the form of the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*), there is no differentiation within all the clusters of transmigratory existence—that is, within all the clusters in the form of creation—within that manifestation, within that radiance. It is just as there is no differentiation [of the clay] within jars and other objects made from clay.

In the case of vibration (*sphuraṇa*): therefore, by means of that very subtle element (*tanmātra*), the merging of the mind with something else is indeed logical; this is the intended meaning. And those subtle elements (*tanmātrāṇi*) are to be understood as the five—sound and so forth—which serve as the seeds of the gross elements, whose bodies consist solely of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and which have been mentally separated from space and the other gross elements.

With the intention that not only does union with the [gross] creations occur through the application of those subtle elements (*tanmātra*), but union with Brahman as well occurs through them alone, he says: "Whether it be engagement or withdrawal, preceded by the attainment of the subtle elements, immediately after the state of deep sleep for the entire class of living beings. (MU 4.18.2)

Because the entire multitude of living beings, the whole collection of souls, is in a state of deep sleep—due to this condition of deep sleep—thereafter follows either *pravṛtti*, which is the merging with other creations, or *nivṛtti*, which is the merging into Brahman in the form of withdrawal from the creations; this occurs precisely preceded by the attainment of the *tanmātras*, that is, preceded by union with the subtle elements. This takes place in deep sleep.
Because the emanations exist as their seed, there is no possibility of cessation; because the emanations do not exist in a state of manifestation, there is no possibility of activity.

Thus, it is said, "immediately after [the state of] deep sleep. By the mention of "immediately after," the necessary presence of deep sleep here is indicated, since the necessity of deep sleep—which stands as the bridge between Brahman and the emanations—is perfectly clear.

In this context, the distinction between the spheres of activity should be understood as follows: active engagement pertains to those liberated while living (jīvanmukta), whereas cessation pertains to those liberated after death (videhamukta).
As for the activity of others, however, since it is rooted in ignorance, it is not appropriate to discuss it here.
Because it is the subject under discussion, he explains separately that the process of manifestation is preceded by the attainment of the subtle elements (tanmātra):

"Those living beings who possess the state of active engagement have reached the stage of the subtle elements; through their oneness with the subtle elements, they perceive mutually imagined creations. (MU 4.18.3)

Those living beings who, though possessing the nature of those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), remain engaged in worldly activity due to the persistence of residual impressions (*sattvaśeṣa*) and are thus joined with such activity—

they perceive creations that are merely conceptualized as having a conceptualized nature through the logic of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and by being unified with them; they see these mutually, for the minds of those liberated while living meet one another.
Herein lies the supreme secret.
Through the single channel of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the diverse reservoirs of creation mingle with one another and attain density on all sides.
The five subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—that which is their unity—is itself the channel, the path for the flow of water; by that [channel], [it attains] density, the state of being solidified.
Now, do all the floods of creation flow together through the single channel of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), or only some of them? To this he says:
"Some have reached a separate existence and have gone to dissolution separately; others exist as world-systems that have been formed in mutual conjunction. (MU 4.18.5)
Some have impure intellects; some in the latter half [of the verse] have pure intellects. These are produced and constructed, but not innate.
Now, on what basis do such floods of creations abide? To this he says:
"Wherein thousands of world-systems, innumerable within every single atom, exist without touching one another—that is the forest named Brahman. (MU 4.18.6)
Not joined to one another, they are unmixed with each other; in every atom, part by part.
Having attained density, it does not merge with anything else; whatever has grown in whatever place and in whatever manner, that alone it perceives, and nothing other than that.
The creation has reached a state of density, a state of solidification. It does not attain—that is, it does not undergo—mutual union.

For that creation [is so]; by implication, the subject situated therein [is meant]. Whatever is rooted and familiar in a particular place, that very thing one perceives there, and nothing else. In this context, the impurity of the subject's intellect is stated many times as the underlying cause.
Due to the power of present-day mental constructions, the successions of living beings have become mutually conjoined, forming the habitual tendencies of creation.

The present mental kingdom is *saṅkalpa* (volition). By its power, successions of living beings (*jīvaparamparā*) become mutually united. The sense is that because they possess identical mental kingdoms, living beings meet one another. Of what nature are these successions of living beings? They are those whose *bhāvanās* (creative contemplations) consist in the establishment—that is, the reality—of creations (*sarga*). This is the underlying idea.

The creations of those with pure intellects always meet through the channel of identity with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*); however, for those with impure intellects, they meet only occasionally through the state of a single resolve (*ekasaṅkalpa*).

Now, one might ask: how has this existence of the body attained such manifestness, that for those whose intellects are veiled by the impurity called *saṅkalpa* (volitional thought) arising from its power, there is no merging with other creations through the channel of identity with those subtle elements?
To this, he says:

"The existence of the body is deeply rooted, while the absence of the body is forgotten; because it is so thoroughly established as 'body-ness,' the sky of consciousness has forgotten its true Self. (MU 4.18.9)

Because it has attained the state of being a body by means of the space of consciousness (*cidvyoman*); because it has fully developed into the condition of a body through the agency of the space of consciousness;

that is to say, because the state of being a body has been conceived as one's own self (*svātman*). Thus, the existence of the body has become established and has reached full growth. But on the other hand, the absence of the body (*dehābhāva*) is ultimately real—the absolute non-existence throughout the three periods of time relative to the body. By what kind of space of consciousness? By that which has been cultivated as one's own self.
By one who has forgotten the self—that is, whose true nature has been forgotten—"forgotten" means having been brought to a state of forgetfulness.
Now, he explains the merging of one creation with others through another illustration:

"Just as the pure vital breath, by piercing the supreme vital breath, perceives the kingdom of the mind of the one to be pierced, so does that which resides in man perceive the creations. (MU 4.18.10)

Just as one whose vital breath (*prāṇa*) has been purified through *prāṇāyāma* and other means is a "yogi of the vital breath" (*prāṇayogin*), because of the piercing of another's vital breath—that is, because of the piercing, which is to say the pervasion, of another's vital breaths; or, as it is said, "because of entering another's city," he knows the kingdom of the mind of the person to be pierced—that is, the person who is to be pervaded. It is just like that.
Residing in a human body through that very channel, yet entered by another person, he is a man liberated while living (jīvanmukta), or a person who has first arisen from Brahman;
he knows the creations—that is, the creations of persons who have taken recourse to them.
Having thus given a complete answer to the question posed by Śrī Rāma, he now recounts the fragments of instructional statements mentioned here and there previously:
"The Self of all multitudes of living beings rests upon three states known as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep; in this regard, the body is not the cause. (MU 4.18.11)
In this context, regarding the reliance upon the three states.

Thus, within the Self—which consists of three other states—the state of being a living soul shines forth; and within that, corporeality shines forth, just as the state of being a wave appears in heated water.

In this Self, which is delimited by the state of being a living soul (*jīva*), whose nature consists of the three states and which appears as something other—that is, distinct—from itself; [in that such Self]. (MT 4,18.12)

Having reached the state of the power of consciousness (citkalā) and abiding in the state at the end of deep sleep, the enlightened living being returns [to its source], while the deluded one proceeds toward emanation.

The state of the digit of consciousness (*citkalā*) is the state called the Fourth (*turya*). The Awakened One (*buddha*) is one capable of the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of that digit of consciousness; he "turns back," meaning he no longer indulges in attachment to sense objects. When his nature is pure, he "proceeds," meaning he engages in [compassion]; for when that occurs, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) proceeds. It consists precisely in the unity of the two, as is demonstrated by perfect friendship.

Of what nature is loving-kindness (*maitrī*)? It is precisely of the form of the unity of the two. For the very meaning of the word "loving-kindness" is the oneness of the two. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is that which has excellent friendship as its illustration. "Excellent friendship" (*susauhārda*) means a state of being a praiseworthy friend. An "illustration" (*nidarśana*) is an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). That [loving-kindness] is such [an example]. For in the case of excellent friendship, there is indeed the unity of the two.
An ignorant individual soul (jīva), having awakened from deep sleep, partakes in its own creation; yet, because consciousness is all-pervading, another [soul] is led away by the creation of another.
The meaning is that it possesses its own creation; that is, it has exactly the same nature as it had prior to the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*).

The "leading by means of another creation" should be understood as a transformation of its nature. Alternatively, the leading by means of another creation may be applied by using the example of the emission of semen and so forth.

[Objection: "In that particular creation, where does another creation exist by which he is led? To this, [the author] says: "In every creation, there are other creations of distinct forms; within those as well, there are floods of creations, like the layers of a plantain leaf. (MU 4.18.16)

Just as there are other leaves within the leaves of a plantain tree, and yet others within those, so too there are other creations within creations, and yet others within those; this is the summary meaning: "The pavilion of the plantain leaves of Brahman possesses a thick growth of leaves in the form of creations that fill one another; it is naturally cool."

In each single creation, that which fills other creations—that collection of other creations—is itself the leaves. He whose existence (vṛtti) or state is robust (pīvara), being of the nature of expansion through those [leaves], is such that there is no difference in the plantain tree even as there are hundreds of leaves; likewise, there is no difference in the reality of Brahman even as there are hundreds of creations.
This is clear.
Just as a fruit arises from a seed and, through its essence, becomes a seed once again, so too Brahman, having become the mind, becomes Brahman again through awakening.

Just as a fruit, having come into being and manifested from a seed that serves as its material cause, may again become a seed through the causal factor of its sap; so too, Brahman, having become the mind through awakening, may again become Brahman.
The seed, caused by sap, unfolds as the fruit; the individual soul, caused by Brahman, unfolds in the form of the world.
This is clear.
It is not appropriate to say what the cause of taste might be; nor is it appropriate to speak of its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) further, because it is devoid of differentiation.
"How is it not tenable? To this he says: "Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Intrinsic nature is ultimately nothing but that which is devoid of distinction (*nirviśeṣa*).

It is not tenable to bring it within the scope of an effort [to define or refute] it. The intention of the phrase "because it is devoid of distinction" is that if an effort were made regarding intrinsic nature, then because there would be no distinction, such an effort would necessarily apply to all intrinsic natures. Thus, it is because it is devoid of distinction.

Furthermore, non-existence cannot be asserted anywhere regarding that which consists of all things; nor can there be a cause or the like for that which is not a cause, or for the ultimate primal cause.

The intended meaning is that it is impossible for that which is non-existent (*asat*) to consist of everything. Regarding the phrase "not without a cause" (*nākāraṇa*): it refers to that for which no cause exists;

that is, in the Supreme, the Exalted, the Primordial Cause, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). In such a state, there is no "cause and so forth," because its status as a primordial cause would otherwise be lost.
This is the intended meaning.
Just as a seed is seen to become its own fruit without abandoning its own form, so too Brahman remains both the fruit and the seed without abandoning its own form.
The reason for Brahmā’s persistence in the state of being a seed is precisely the non-abandonment of his own body.
Everything possesses the form of a seed, whereas that state (pada) is formless; therefore, it is not possible to equate them, and thus there is no analogy for Śiva.
The entire, complete nature of the seed becomes possessed of form; for that reason, from that cause, there is no analogy for Śiva, the reality of pure consciousness alone.
Space itself is born from space, yet it is not born as something other than that; therefore, know, O Brahman, that this world is neither unborn nor born, like the sky.

From Brahman—which is like the sky due to its absolute purity—space itself is born. To the question, "How is this so? he says: "And not... The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason. Since that which is called the world is space, it does not arise—that is, it is not produced—in the form of something other than Brahman, i.e., in a form perceived as distinct from Brahman. He states the conclusion: "Therefore... Therefore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it was never born.
Know that the world, which has arisen from appearance, is the Brahman-ether, the space of Brahman.
Seeing the visible, one does not perceive one's own self as the seer; for whom, whose consciousness is overcome by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), does the innate state arise?

The seer perceives the visible—the multitude of entities that have become the objects of the act of seeing—but he does not see, nor does he experience, his own self, his innate nature as the seer. For such a person—whose consciousness is assailed by conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and led away from its own inward orientation—how can his innate state, his true essential nature, arise or manifest? It does not.
The meaning is that it belongs to no one at all.
When the delusion of water in a mirage exists, what cleverness is there? But when cleverness exists, what is this mirage?
Therefore, the sense is that cleverness itself should be nurtured through association with the virtuous and similar means.
The seer, as clear as space and all-pervading, does not see itself, even though it has become the act of seeing—like one's own eye; oh, what a delusion!

Like space, it is transparent and utterly pure by virtue of its nature as pure consciousness alone; it is the seer. It does not see itself—the self known as the seer—which has become "seen," having entered into the state of being an object. How so? Like the eye.
Just as the eye does not see its own self, such is the meaning. Oh, what a delusion! This is the state of confusion.
Brahman, which is as pure as space, is not attained even with effort; if that which is visible is seen as something visible, its attainment is very far off indeed.
To the question "Why is it not obtained?", he says here: "The visible. The meaning is that, because it is visible, the very non-perception of the visible is the attainment of Brahman.
Where even something as gross as you is not seen without careful attention, there the visibility of a subtle object for the observer is as if cast far away.

In whatever object, without focused attention, one as gross as you is not perceived; in that very object, the visibility of a subtle seer becomes utterly remote. The phrase "one like you" is said with reference to the body.
The seer remains only the seer and does not touch the state of being seen; and while the object of sight is seen by him, O Rāma, the seer is not seen.

The seer is the agent of the act of seeing; he remains solely the seer. That seer does not touch the state of being seen, the objective nature of the visible. O Rāma! By that seer—that by which the visible is seen—the sense is that the visible possesses the quality of being seen. By that seer, the seer himself, whose very form is the seer, is not seen, because of his extreme subtlety.
Existence.
Only the seer exists as one; for here, the seen does not exist at all. If the seer, who is the self of all, remains as the seen, what indeed is the state of being "seen"?

The meaning is that it is possible because only that [consciousness] is capable of withstanding such analysis. If the observer, who is of the nature of all things, exists as the object—that is, exists in the state of being an object—then what kind of "objectivity" could there possibly be? Furthermore, one must necessarily accept, according to the logic of a dream, that the observer exists in the state of being an object.

Now, raising the objection, "How can the seer abide as the object seen?", he provides an illustration: "Just as whatever is accomplished by an all-powerful king happens quickly in that very manner, so too does He Himself arise in the form of those [objects]. (MU 4.18.33)

Just as whatever object is brought to completion—that is, made the object of the act of accomplishment—by a sovereign (*samrāṭ*) who possesses all powers, by a king endowed with every capacity, that very object quickly becomes so;
when investigated, it is that very king himself who arises and manifests in the form of each respective object. This is [the meaning].

This is the state of being: just as an all-powerful king manifests through the medium of his own non-differentiated knowledge as the reality that constitutes the manifestation (*vivarta*) of that knowledge, so too does the seer manifest through the medium of his own non-differentiated act of seeing as the object being seen, which constitutes the manifestation of that act of seeing.
Just as a grove, radiant with the splendor of sweet honey, remains resplendent even while not abandoning its state of being juice, yet abounds with fruits, flowers, and leaves; ||| MU_4,18.34 |||

Thus, the radiance of consciousness, having become the individual soul (jīva), becomes the embodied being; yet, without ever abandoning that state of pure consciousness, it consists of the vision of the Seer.

This word *darśana* is a noun derived from the verbal root *dṛś* (to see) with the suffix *lyuṭ*. Therefore, its meaning is "consisting of the vision of the visible. This constitutes a pair of verses.
Just as the earthy essence arises from its own self through a flood of thousands of various non-dual parts, so does consciousness arise through the delusions of "I-ness."
*Bhauma* means relating to the earth.
Of the trees of the effulgence of consciousness, which shine by themselves within the Self and are laden with hundreds of branches of visible objects, no end is perceived here.
Consciousness alone is the sap; its efflorescence is that of the trees, which is to say, of the worlds.
Just as a eunuch experiences the aesthetic wonder of a flavor within himself alone, so too does this consciousness perceive the various states of worldly existence individually.
The aesthetic wonder produced by rasa, which takes the form of a swelling [of emotion], is the "aesthetic wonder of rasa" (rasacamatkṛti).
In whatever manner and by whichever vital power its own cycle of manifestation arises, consciousness within itself proceeds accordingly toward that very state—the existence of beings and worlds.

It arises and vibrates; consciousness (*cit*) is the very nature of consciousness. That is the power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*). Within itself, in its own midst, it attains—that is, reaches—each respective state of existence of beings and worlds: the state of beings who are the substrata thereof, and the established arrangement of the worlds.
Certain streams of living beings meet one another; having wandered through saṃsāra on their own, they eventually come to rest after a long time.
Some, endowed with pure intelligence, [attain this] after a long time, immediately upon the falling away of the body.
In this same way, you perceive yourself with this subtle and supreme vision, as well as thousands of world-nets even within the interior of a single atom.

You—your own self, which is called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—behold, that is, you experience, by means of this supreme, most excellent, subtle vision—that is, by means of perfect knowledge whose form is subtle because its object is a subtle reality—in this context.
The word *tathā* (likewise) is used for conjunction; likewise, you behold thousands of world-nets even within other atoms. The word *api* (even) [indicates inclusion].
This indicates the impossibility of perceiving thousands of world-nets within other atoms.
The objects of worldly existence are present in a wall, in space, in stone, in flame, in wind, and in water; they exist in everything, like oil in sesame seeds.
The intended meaning is: by virtue of having as its essence pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is the seed of the world.
When the mind becomes pure, then the individual soul (jīva) becomes consciousness (citi). And that [consciousness] is pure and all-pervading; therefore, there is a mutual merging between them.
That indeed [is so] because of that purity.
The long, great dream of the world, which fulfills the delusion of self-existence for all beings beginning with Brahmā, has arisen spontaneously from within itself.
The meaning is that it fulfills the delusion of its own existence and causes the delusion of its own existence.
Certain successions of beings pass from one dream to another; therefore, their perception of walls and such things remains most firm.

Certain successions of beings (*bhūtaparamparā*), that is, rows of beings, pass from one dream— consisting of a particular cycle of existence— from another dream— a dream consisting of a different cycle of existence. For that reason, for these rows of beings who have gone from one dream to another dream, there exists a very firm perception of walls and so forth, in the form of "this is a wall," and so on.
Knowledge exists.
Whatever one contemplates upon anywhere, that quickly becomes fully manifest there; even that which is seen by her in a dream is indeed real at that very time.
By her, it was piled up.
Within the atom of consciousness exist all atoms of experience, just as within a seed exist the atoms of leaves, creepers, flowers, and fruits.
"Collectively" means having the forms of all things, such as jars and cloths. "Atoms of experience" (anubhavāṇavaḥ) means fragments of experience.
The supreme atom of consciousness contains the entire universe within itself; it holds the latent space within space—abandon the delusion of duality and unity.

The atom of consciousness (*cit-paramāṇuka*) is the atom whose nature is consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). It holds—that is, it maintains—the world-atom, the atom whose nature is the world, within the wall of its own self. He states the result [of this] by saying "merged" (*līna*). Therefore, the space called the world is merged in the space called consciousness. He describes the result of this as "the unity of duality" (*dvaita-ekatva*).
Thus, therefore, abandon and cast off the delusion of duality and unity; for there exists only the pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), which is absolute and cannot even be described as "one."

The consciousness, by means of its own atoms known as space, time, action, and so forth, experiences other atoms within itself, since the existence of another atom [as a separate entity] is impossible.

"By its own [powers]" means by those very powers that constitute its own nature. "Atoms" refers to atoms whose forms are manifold. "Within itself" means within its own self. "Of another atom" refers to an atom that is distinct from consciousness (cit) and consists of space and other such qualities.
Itself manifest as everything, the pure mass of atomic consciousness is experienced through the perception of bodies, from Brahmā down to the smallest insect.

"Experienced through the vision of the body" means brought within the range of experience. "Residing in a worm" means ending with a worm. In the word *anubhāvita*, the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is used in its own sense (without changing the meaning), which is an archaic usage (*ārṣa*).
In reality, there is nothing here whatsoever that has been manifested; yet the atoms of consciousness themselves experience duality as their own self-nature and as objects of enjoyment.
Furthermore, as to the question "What is this that throbs?", he says here: "by itself" (*svayam*). The atoms of consciousness (*cit-paramāṇavaḥ*) are portions of the intellect (*cilleśāḥ*).

Duality (*dvaitam*) is the nature of duality consisting of forms such as pots and cloths. "By itself" (*svatvam*) means its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāvam*). They "taste" (*svādayante*) it, meaning they bring it into the state of being an object of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra-viṣayatām*).
The mass of atoms of consciousness, possessing a vast body, shines forth by itself, emitting the fragrance of pure awareness through the flower-like gateways of the eyes and other senses.
"Of expansive body" means one whose essential nature is vast; "the fragrance of consciousness" refers to the fragrance consisting of the cognition of jars, cloths, and so forth.
Someone perceives other things as external forms, which are in fact a mass of consciousness; for consciousness, being all-pervading and indestructible, is indeed the seed of all that is visible.

A certain person—that is to say, one who has entered the waking state—perceives, in an external form, other objects that appear as distinct from himself; he experiences them as "these are external," [perceiving] the seeds of the visible world called consciousness (*cit*), which, because they are all-pervading and likewise imperishable, are dense with consciousness (*cidghana*) by virtue of being the very nature of consciousness. MT_4,18.53 //
Within himself alone, a certain person perceives the entire world in its completeness; therein, through excessive mental construction, he rises up and sinks down.
"Someone who has entered the state of sleep," that is to say; "only within," meaning only within oneself and not externally.
Seeing one dream after another there again and again, he rolls about in false pits like a stone fallen from a mountain peak.

What is someone doing? The connection with the preceding verse is that they are seeing one dream after another again and again. Of what nature is this person? They are "vainly" (mithyā), meaning fruitlessly. They are "tumbling" (luṭhita) into "pits" (avaṭeṣu), namely the pits called existence and non-existence.
Like what? Like a rock fallen from a mountain peak.

Some are closed in on themselves, while others remain in delusion within their own selves; these multitudes of embodied beings, vibrating from the essence of their own consciousness, are submerged in it.
Some have entered the state of deep sleep; they are closed in, seized by slumber, within the Self enveloped by ignorance—the multitudes of embodied beings, the hosts of individual souls.

He speaks of those who, having entered the fourth state (turyāvasthā), perceive within themselves the delusive agitation of the world and living beings; by some of them, that [world] is seen as such, based upon it as if it were an unreal dream.

Those living beings who are liberated while alive perceive the delusion called the world—the delusion known as the world—only within, in the mind, and not externally. By some of them, that visible world is thus accepted as being internal alone. How so? Like an unreal dream; for those liberated while alive, having entered the fourth state (turya), perceive even the external world as a dream.
They experience it as being internal precisely because they perceive its nature to be that of an illusion.
Because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the self of all, that which is visible is real within the Self; for wherever the All-pervading is present, there indeed everything arises.

That visible object becomes real within the Self, within its own essential nature. Why? Because its own nature, called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), is the self of all, existing in the form of everything. This is the meaning: although the visible object is unreal as "visibility" established in dependence upon a seer, it is real by virtue of having as its core essence that very nature which is synonymous with pure consciousness, abiding as the form of all things.

"It is indeed real in its own essential nature. [The opponent asks: "But how is this so? To this, he says: "Omnipresent" (*sarvaga*). For (*hi*), because that which is omnipresent—that is, pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*), which is synonymous with one's own nature (*svabhāva*) and is all-pervading—exists wherever there is anything, there every visible object arises and manifests. Therefore, like the pure consciousness that constitutes its very nature, the existence of the object is inseparable from it.
The sense is that even the visible world is indeed real.
Within the manifestation of creation that exists inside the living being (jīva), a multitude of living beings arises; and within that [multitude], yet another [multitude] likewise arises.
This is clear.
A living being is born from within a living being, and within that too there is another living being; everywhere, like the core of a plantain leaf, the seed of life continues to live.
"He lives" means he assumes the agency of the preeminent activity of living.

This infinite [reality], which is the revolution of the intellect regarding the visible world, is uniform; like the state of being a bracelet or other ornaments in gold, it perishes through mere thorough understanding.

The infinite is that which appears as devoid of limits; this is the visible world. It perishes—that is, it goes out of sight—by means of thorough knowledge alone, specifically by the realization that "this is indeed nothing but pure consciousness," and not by any other cause. It occurs simultaneously, not gradually. The meaning is that its destruction is established through the experience of it as being of the nature of pure consciousness. What is this [visible world] like?
By the perception of the visible—that is, by the cognition that "this is the visible"—that which has supreme, excellent, and all-encompassing growth [is revealed].

What is this like? It is like the state of being a bracelet and so forth. Just as the state of being a bracelet existing in gold perishes through thorough understanding—the knowledge that "this is only gold"—so it is here; such is the meaning.
For one in whom the inquiry "Who am I? and "What is this? does not arise, there persists this long, feverish delusion of being alive, from which neither beginning nor end is ever liberated.
Unreleased from beginning to end and flowing in an uninterrupted stream, the delusion in the form of a fever that "I am the individual soul" is called the *jīvajvara-bhrama*.
The discernment of that person of right mind should be known as having borne fruit, for whom the greed for enjoyments diminishes day by day.
Regarding the term "to be understood": the word "by the wise" is to be supplied here. "Greed for enjoyments" means the longing for enjoyments.
Just as medicine, when applied to the body, brings about health, so too does discernment, when directed toward the conquest of the senses, become fruitful.

"Applied to the body" means employed within the body. "Bearing fruit" means endowed with the fruit known as liberation; the sense is that the conquest of the senses alone is the direct means toward liberation.
Discernment exists only in words, like a brilliant fire in a painting; for one who possesses such [verbal] discernment, that state of being a discerning person leads only to suffering.
The phrase "of whom" (yasya) is connected with the first half-verse; it is stated that [the body] is "abandoned" with the intention of referring to the mind (*citta*).
Just as the wind makes its presence known through touch and not by speech, so too it is understood that discernment arises only through the attenuation of desire.
This is clear.

Know that which is called "wondrous nectar" to be no nectar at all; know that which is called "wondrous fire" to be no fire at all. A woman in a painting is surely not a woman, and discernment in words is merely a lack of discernment.
Just as nectar and the like depicted in a painting lack the capacity for causal efficiency— such as satisfying thirst— and thus are not truly nectar and so forth,

so too is that which is described by words alone. Therefore, the meaning is that discriminative discernment (*viveka*) which does not accomplish the conquest of the senses lacks the causal efficiency known as liberation, and is therefore nothing but non-discernment (*aviveka*).
Furthermore, what kind of person is a man of discernment? Regarding this, he says in a verse at the end of the chapter:

"First, through discernment, passion becomes attenuated and then enmity is destroyed along with its very root; thereafter, that in which [all these] are utterly exhausted is the purifying state—therein lies discernment. (MU 4.18.68)

In whichever person there is passion and enmity— that is, hatred— if, through discernment (*viveka*) and investigation, it first attains attenuation and subsequently, immediately after that attenuation, is utterly exhausted and perishes,
that person is pure; in that person, there exists the state of being discerning, which is the possession of investigative wisdom.
The meaning is that [the two] do not determine existence and non-existence by mere statement alone. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the eighteenth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Because it is exceedingly difficult to understand, he explains once more the very meaning previously stated:

"The seed of the individual soul is the Supreme Brahman, existing everywhere like space; by means of that, the individual soul exists in manifold ways even within the world contained in the belly of the individual soul. (MU 4.19.1)

The seed of living beings is the locus of their manifestation; the Supreme Brahman is like the sky, like space. It abides as the essential core of its own nature throughout the entire web of the world, which is everywhere regarded as an object of perception. For that reason—from that cause—the "belly" of the living being refers to its central region. Within that resides the world, the world appearing in forms such as dreams and the like; even therein [it abides].
The soul exists in manifold ways, in various forms consisting of both stationary and moving entities.
In response to the inquiry "What follows from that?", he says:

Because the nature of the Self is a single, dense mass of consciousness, the various classes of living beings exist within the individual soul like the layers of a plantain tree or like insects in the belly of a man. (MU 4.19.2)

Therefore, because of that state of being a single, absolute mass of consciousness—wherein the self is a solid mass of consciousness (*cidghana*)—the various classes of living beings exist within the living, like the layers of a plantain tree.
For just as there are other layers within the leaves of a plantain tree, so too are the classes of living beings; they are like insects, such as the insects found within the belly of a man.
They exist; that is the meaning of "tathā."

"Now, from what is the individual soul (jīva) produced? To this he says: "O Rāma, just as in the summer a worm may arise from a film of sweat, so too, by virtue of its consciousness, the void itself spontaneously becomes a living soul, assuming that very name."

O Rāma! In the summer, during the summer season, due to the moisture of impurities (*kalkasvedāt*)—where *kalka* means filth and *sveda* means sweat—from that moisture of impurities, whatever worm arises in whatever form, by virtue of its consciousness (*cittvāt*), it becomes a living being (*jīvībhavati*) spontaneously in that very form. As for the space (*kham*), how is it? It is that which bears the respective name of each [worm].
"Of the worm"—that is, that which has the name "worm. This is the point: first of all, in the summer, various kinds of worms are born from the sweat of putrid matter (*kalka*).

Let their body indeed consist of that putrid sweat; however, as for the living soul (*jīva*), since its status as a living being would otherwise be inexplicable, it must be space (*ākāśa*) itself endowed with consciousness (*cittva*). This is because the production of the mere body from the sweat of putrid matter is already complete, and nothing else is present [to constitute the soul].
And therefore, all living beings are indeed of the nature of space.
In whatever manner those seekers of life strive for the realization of their own self, in that very manner they quickly become [perfected] through various methods of worship.

They consist of space; they are living beings. To the extent that they strive for the realization of their own selves through various methods of worship—through diverse modes of striving consisting of manifold sequences of worship—to that same extent they become [those very objects].
Having stated this in general, he explains it specifically:

"For those who sacrifice to the gods go to the gods; those who sacrifice to the yakṣas go to the yakṣas; those who sacrifice to Brahman go to Brahman. One should therefore take refuge in that which is not insignificant. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9)
He states the result with the words "yat" (that which). The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied. Therefore, a person should rely upon that which is not trivial.
[Objection: "In that case, how did Śukra attain such manifold forms without his own body? To this, he says:
"For that Śukra, the son of Bhṛgu, because of the purity of his own consciousness, was instantly bound by nature through the object seen for the first time. (MU 4.19.6)

He is the son of Bhṛgu, Śukra, as mentioned in the previous section. The word *hi* indicates certainty. Because of the purity of his own consciousness through this initial descent, he was immediately bound by the first perceived object; thus, by his very nature, he was made to turn toward himself without effort.
Therefore, there is no contradiction—this is the intended meaning.
When consciousness first reaches a newborn infant who is noble and unwithered, it assumes that very form; no other [form] whatsoever exists.

She is noble and pure; for that very reason, she is unfading, having not yet reached any turbidity. She is the consciousness of Brahmā, arisen immediately [after his emergence]. At first, at the very beginning, whatever she perceives before her, she becomes of that same form. Another consciousness, which arose earlier than Brahmā, does not exist without effort; it comes into being only through effort.
Thus it is; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of liberation.
At this time, Śrī Rāma asks about the question that had previously flashed in his mind:
"O Blessed One, you should explain the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming; how is it that waking is waking, and how does dreaming become non-waking?"

In response to the inquiry, "What shall I say?", he asks, "How?"—meaning, "How could there be waking while one is awake? How could there be dreaming while not awake? The intention is: "Tell me this very thing. Śrī Vasiṣṭha gives the reply: "That which is endowed with stable conviction is called waking; that which consists of unstable conviction is declared to be a dream. (MU 4.19.9)
That which is joined with a stable cognition— that is, with a recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the form "this is that very same thing"—
is called "waking" by the wise. That which possesses unstable cognition— that is, which lacks the recognition capable of providing stable knowledge— is declared and described as "dream" by the wise.
He explains how the state of dreaming-waking can sometimes occur in both waking and dreaming:

"If that which was seen for a moment in the waking state persists through another period of time as a dream, then that waking state attains the nature of a dream, and the dream reaches the state of waking. (MU 4.19.10)

If that which is characterized as waking— that is, an object that has become the domain of waking cognition— were to be seen for only a moment, it would mean that it perishes immediately thereafter. Likewise, if that which is in a dream— that is,

an object that has become the domain of dream-cognition— were to persist through another time, remaining even at a time other than the time of the dream, then indeed, what is seen in a dream [would persist].

Even an object that is perceived directly at dawn becomes, at that time, a dream because its cognition is unstable; it attains the state of being awake because its cognition is stable. A dream is a cognition that grasps dream-objects; it attains the state of being awake because its cognition is stable.
Now, one might ask: "How can this be so? To this, he says:
"The distinction between the states of waking and dreaming does not exist without stability and instability; for the experience of all things is always equal in both. (MU 4.19.11)

Since the distinction between the states of waking and dreaming does not occur without stability and instability [respectively], it follows that for a momentary waking state to be a dream and for a stable dream to be a waking state is entirely logical; this is the intended meaning. Here, he declares "equal" (*sama*) as the proof for all experience (*anubhava*); that is, the experience residing in all things within these two—the waking and the dreaming states.
The totality of experience is always—at all times—and everywhere—in all places—exactly the same. The phrase "it transcends stability and instability" should also be connected here.
He states the conclusion:
that which attains stability is called "waking"; hear now how dream, characterized by momentary dissolution, comes to be.

Therefore, that which attains stability is called "waking" even though it is a dream by the wise; that which is characterized by momentary destruction is a "dream" even though it is waking. Listen to how this occurs; the meaning is: listen to how there is stability and instability in waking and dreaming.

He explains that very point: "The life-element (jīvadhātu) exists within the body by which one lives; it is called 'vitality' (tejas), 'prowess' (vīrya), 'the life-element,' and so forth—know this, my dear. (MU 4.19.13)

The element called *jīva* is the *jīvadhātu*. It exists within the body; by means of that *jīvadhātu*, the body is made to live—that is, it is caused to perform the activity of sustaining life. The term "is made to live" (*jīvyate*) is a grammatical usage ending in the causative suffix (*ṇic*). O dear one! That *jīvadhātu* is designated by such names as "radiance" (*tejas*), "vitality" (*vīrya*), and "the living-element" (*jīvadhātu*). And here, the word *dhātu* refers to something internal to the body, like the marrow and so forth.
It is employed metaphorically because of its similarity to conduct.
When the body, through mind, action, and speech, engages in worldly activity, then that perfected aggregate of the life-element (jīvadhātu) flows forth.

When— at which time— the body becomes engaged in worldly activity through mental action, through its own inherent function, and through speech; then that element of life (jīvadhātu), being fully developed and complete, "creeps forth," meaning it circulates throughout the entire body.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says:

"For as that [consciousness] spreads through the limbs, awareness arises from touch; because of its fullness, it is called 'mind' (citta), wherein the delusion of the world is internally dissolved. (MU 4.19.15)

When that constituent element of life (*jīvadhātu*), which consists of consciousness, spreads through the limbs, then— by virtue of contact with the limbs, that is, through contact with the constituent element of life— consciousness indeed, being the vibration of the constituent element of life and taking the form of the perception of cold, heat, and so forth, arises and manifests. That consciousness, containing within it the delusion of the world, [manifests] because of its nourishment— that is, because of its nourishment through the spreading of the constituent element of life.
It attains the name "mind" (*citta*). If it is asked, "How can consciousness (*saṃvid*) have the delusion of the world latent within it?"—it is true.

Consciousness arises from the element of the living being (*jīvadhātu*), and at the time of its emergence, the element of the living being arises already endowed with the delusion of the world, because the element of the living being has the delusion of the world latent within it. Therefore, consciousness also has the delusion of the world latent within it.
Success!
Crawling through the apertures such as the eyes and so forth, it perceives within itself a form composed of the external world, rich with various shapes and transformations.

That consciousness, flowing through the apertures such as the eyes and so forth, perceives and contemplates within itself a form that is external in nature—that is, having an external character—rich with various modifications of form such as jars, cloths, and the like; it is as if these jars, cloths, and so on were accomplished by mere mental resolve. Nor should it be asked how this is possible, for it is observed in dreams.
Just as in a dream it is consciousness itself that appears in various forms, so too it is in the external world; thus there is no contradiction.
Because of its stability, one then understands "this is waking" by means of that very state; this is declared to be the sequence of waking. Now hear the sequence beginning with deep sleep.

By that very consciousness alone— and not by any other inert thing such as the body— is one's own nature, which is rich with various forms and transformations, understood— that is, known— as "waking," because it remains exactly so for some time due to its stability. Having thus concluded the procedure concerning the waking state, he makes a formal promise to explain the procedure concerning deep sleep and the others, [beginning] with the words "the sequence of waking."
He describes the very sequence beginning with deep sleep:
"When the body is not agitated by mind, action, or speech, then this pure element of life remains in a state of peace. (MU 4.19.18)

It does not waver because of exhaustion; the meaning is that it does not engage in worldly activity (*vyavahāra*). At that time, the element of life (*jīvadhātu*) is clear, possessing the impurity known as "slumbering movement. For this very reason, it is peaceful, being devoid of agitation. It remains completely still. The word "tu" (but/however) indicates certainty. Although there is no question posed by Śrī Rāma regarding the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), nevertheless, concerning the waking and dreaming states...

The determination of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) is necessarily [required] because of its intermediate state; for it is not logical that a person, having departed from the waking state, should go to the dream state without first reaching deep sleep, since deep sleep exists everywhere as a boundary, like a bridge. Although pure consciousness (*śuddhacit*) indeed exists everywhere in the middle as a bridge, nevertheless, like a flash of lightning or a gem, [it is not perceived].

Because it is not an object of coarse vision, its nature as a bridge is not mentioned; however, for those possessing subtle vision, its mention is not appropriate because it would be of no use to them.
"What will be accomplished then? To this he replies:
"The heart within is no longer disturbed by winds that have attained equilibrium, just as a lamp in a windless chamber produces only light. (MU 4.19.19)

"Equanimity" (*samatā*) means being evenly balanced due to the absence of agitation produced by the mind. By the winds that have arrived—that is, by the vital breaths (*prāṇa*)—this element of life (*jīvadhātu*) within the heart is not agitated; it is not made subject to agitation. By this, it is indicated that through the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*), the restraint of the breath (*prāṇarodha*) will be accomplished, and through the restraint of the breath, the dissolution of the mind will be accomplished. Even in that regard, for some, the dissolution of the mind is held to occur through the restraint of the breath.

For us, however, the restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) occurs precisely through the dissolution of the mind (*manonāśa*) accomplished by means of right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). If that [restraint] is an auxiliary factor therein, there is no fault. Therefore, in every respect, the dissolution of the mind is [achieved] through the restraint of the vital breath. Yet, it is held that the dissolution of the mind [attained here] is not absolute, like the dissolution of the mind induced by liquor and the like. In this matter, only those endowed with intuitive insight (*pratibhā*) are the authority; enough of this prolixity. [This concludes the section on] the element of life (*jīvadhātu*).
Like what? Like a lamp. Just as a lamp, which produces light alone, is not disturbed by winds in a windless dwelling—such is the meaning.

What results from that? To this he says: "From that, consciousness does not move into the limbs; therefore it is not agitated. Nor does it come to the eyes and other [senses], nor does it go out through the apertures. (MU 4.19–20)

Then that element of life (jīvadhātu) does not flow through the limbs; it does not perform movement. By that non-flowing of the element of life, consciousness—which is consciousness in the form of the vibration of the element of life—is neither agitated nor arises. That consciousness does not enter the apertures such as the eyes, nor does it go outside; it does not come forth.
In response to the inquiry as to where that [consciousness] resides, he says:
It vibrates within the living being itself, just as the consciousness of oil is in the sesame seed; the consciousness of cold is in frost, and the consciousness of fluidity is in clarified butter.

This consciousness (*saṃvit*) manifests within the individual soul (*jīva*), that is, precisely in the midst of the soul which is its own substrate. Like what? Like the consciousness of oil—that is, consciousness in the form of oil; "consciousness of oil" means simply "oil. Just as that [consciousness] manifests in the sesame seed, so it is here—the meaning is "in that manner.
This should be applied similarly to the other two examples as well.
Now, one might ask: what does the individual soul (jīva) do at that time? To this, he says:

"The individual soul, remaining for a certain fraction of time in a state of tranquility within itself, enters the state of deep sleep, which is gentle like a mild breeze and devoid of conscious thought. (MU 4.19.22)

Then the individual soul (jīva), remaining for a certain minute fraction of time—so subtle as to be impossible to describe—in its own tranquil nature, which is the self consisting of knowledge, first abides [therein]; thereafter, it enters the state of deep sleep (sauṣuptī-daśā), which is unconscious, composed of ignorance, characterized by gentle breath, and where the vital airs flow evenly. By this, [it is shown] that between the waking and deep-sleep states...

The entry into the central abode (*madhyadhāma*) has been described as something to be known by those with subtle vision; it is with this very intention that it was stated [in the scriptures] that it occurs at the beginning of sleep and the end of waking, and so forth. Enough, then, with revealing this secret.

Now, one might ask: since the individual soul (*jīva*) is indeed free from agitation during deep sleep (*suṣupta*), why does it not possess the fourth state (*turya*)? In response to this expectation, he says:

"Having known [the Self], when the mind has ceased [its activity], whether one is at peace or even engaged in worldly affairs, one who is awakened throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep is said to possess the fourth state. (MU 4.19.23)

Having known—that is, having correctly realized—one's own self as being of the nature of pure consciousness alone; when the mind, which is of the nature of conceptual construction, has ceased—that is, become dissolved—even while engaging in worldly activity, meaning even while performing conduct for the sake of maintaining the body; one remains tranquil, not undergoing the agitation caused by such activity due to extreme proficiency; and likewise in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

The awakened one is one endowed with perfect knowledge as to what these forms are like; he is not, however, a dullard. He is remembered by the wise as "possessing the fourth" (turyavān). But the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*) is not such as this; therefore, the sense is that it does not possess the fourth.
He begins to describe the dream state:
when that vital element—the consciousness—is set in motion by the vital breaths (prāṇas) which have attained a state of gentleness from deep sleep, it then arises as the mind (citta).

*Sauṣuptam* means deep sleep itself; therefore, by means of the winds that have attained a state of gentleness (*somyatā*), when— at the time of the transformation of deep sleep— that element of the individual soul (*jīvadhātu*) is moved, then at that moment, that consciousness— which is consciousness in the form of the vibration of the element of the individual soul— arises, having become manifest through the state of the mind (*cittatayā*).
Having arisen through the state of consciousness, what does it do? To this he replies:

"It perceives, within itself and swiftly, the web of the world residing within its own interior, as an expansive seed [perceives] a tree, through successive revolutions of parts and sub-parts. (MU 4.19.25)

Then that consciousness, whose nature is mind, perceives—that is, experiences—the web of the world, which exists within itself in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and resides within its own self, but not externally. It perceives it quickly through a succession of delusive movements, rather than through those possessed of innate sequence; that is, by means of minute portions, parts in the form of objects, and tiny fragments. How is this? Like a seed, just as it expands.
One perceives within oneself the seed as it is about to sprout and the tree; for otherwise, its emergence would be impossible. Such is the meaning.
He explains that very point in detail:
when the life-element (*jīvadhātu*) is somewhat or intensely agitated by the vital winds (*vāta*), it is carried along like the sky; one then perceives within oneself a movement in the void.
The meaning of the sentence is that it is simply the nature of an abundance of wind that a person perceives movement through the sky in a dream.
When he is flooded by water, then he experiences within himself the agitation of the water and so forth, just as a flower experiences its own fragrance.

This element of living beings (jīvadhātu) is flooded—that is, filled—with water in the form of phlegm; it experiences a commotion such as being swept away by water, a disturbance consisting of being carried off by a flood and so forth.
When it is overcome by bile and other humors, then it experiences within itself a pervasive agitation of the heat of fire and so forth, as if it were entirely external.
But from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no expansion outward; thus, the word "as it were" (iva) is employed.
When one perceives external places and times as red-colored and filled with blood, because that perception is of the nature of direct experience, one sinks right there.

When it becomes filled with blood—that is, saturated with blood—then one perceives external objects and times as being red in color; not only does one perceive them, but one also sinks right there into them.
[Objection: But how does it perceive various worldly activities? To this he says:

Whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*) it cultivates, that it perceives within while asleep, just as [it perceives] through the apertures agitated by the vital air (*pavana*), or externally through the eyes and other senses. (MU 4.19.30)
That is the life-element (*jīvadhātu*). While asleep, it experiences whatever latent impression (*vāsanā*), whether pure or impure; it perceives that within.
How so? In that manner—just as it perceives externally, being stirred by the wind through the apertures such as the eyes, namely the doors of the eyes and so forth.
Having grasped the definition of dream, he explains:
when one whose sensory openings are unassailed remains undisturbed within, that which he experiences through consciousness immediately is called a dream. (MU 4.19.31)

That is the life-principle (*jīvadhātu*). With its sensory apertures unassailed, remaining inwardly undisturbed and free from external agitation, it experiences—that is, undergoes the experience of—the world as its object through consciousness (*saṃvid*), which is the phenomenon known as awareness. This is what is called "dream" by the wise.
He describes the characteristic of the waking state:
"That which, with the openings of the senses fully engaged, being agitated by external cognition, one perceives—that, the most wise say, is waking."

"Those who possess intelligence in an exceeding degree" means the most intelligent (*matimattama*). Since [the states of] waking and dreaming alone were questioned, their characteristics are stated here in summary during the conclusion; not those of deep sleep.
He concludes this with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Thus, by you who have now realized this within yourself, O one of celebrated great intellect, do not maintain a belief in reality here; for in a world that is unreal, there is nothing to be cultivated but the contemplation of the defects of death, destruction, and saṃsāra."

Thus, by you—who have known, who have understood, and for whom great wisdom has therefore become renowned and spread—there should not now, while the world is non-existent, be any "abiding in reality" (satyatāsthā)—that is, an adherence of the form "this is real"—within the mind; it should not be brought within the scope of contemplative cultivation. What is this abiding in reality? It is that which consists of death and seizure.

And "saṃsṛti" means birth, death, and transmigration; these themselves are the defects (*doṣas*). That which brings about or accomplishes them is "such" (*tādṛśī*). For while one abides in the reality of *saṃsāra*, the defects such as death inherent therein cause affliction. But when one abides in their unreality, even those [defects] are themselves unreal; what kind of affliction could they possibly inflict? Indeed, the son of a barren woman [cannot harm anyone].
It subdues [all obstacles]. Thus may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the nineteenth canto in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) of the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! Thus, having determined the nature of the waking state and the others as asked by Śrī Rāma in the middle [of the discourse], he resumes the subject at hand:
"All this has been told to you by me, O Rāghava, for the purpose of defining the form of the mind, and not for any other reason whatsoever. (MU 4.20.1)

O Rāghava, all of this—that whatever one strives for, in whatever manner, one becomes that very thing—has been told by me to you for the purpose of defining the mind, that is, for the sake of ascertaining the nature of the mind. It was not told for any other reason, because such would have been useless.
The mind performs an investigation of itself;
whatever it contemplates repeatedly with firm resolve, that it becomes, just as a lump of iron attains the state of fire through contact with flames.
Abundantly, through repeated practice.
The views of grasping at existence and non-existence, and of rejecting them, are imagined by the mind; they are neither unreal nor real, being merely the cause of the mind's restlessness.

Those things for which mental instability alone is the cause are "caused by mental instability. For a rope-snake or the like, being caused by mental instability, is not real because it lacks causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritva*); yet, it is not unreal either, because it appears [to consciousness].
For the mind is indeed the cause and the agent; it is the cause for the existence of the world. It is the defiled mind that expands this [universe] through its manifold forms.

The word *hi* indicates certainty. The mind (*manas*) is the cause—the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) and the agent (*kartṛ*). The agent is the factor (*kāraka*), which consists of both the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) and the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). It exists because this mind, being defiled—corrupted by the impurity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—spreads out this world as having the form of the universe. The sense is that no other entity here attains the status of an agent.
And here, the status of the dream as an illustrative example is perfectly clear.
For the mind, O Rāma, is the person; it must be directed onto the auspicious path, since all prosperities in the world are achieved solely through its conquest.
That which is to be enjoined is that which is to be impelled onto the auspicious path, which is the very nature of discernment. For indeed, because all prosperities in the world—
sovereign powers consisting of both enjoyment and liberation— are to be accomplished by means of the conquest of that mind, which consists in its being directed toward the auspicious path.
[Objection: "But since the body exists as the person (puruṣa), how can you say that the mind, which is apprehended by the eye, is the person? [Reply: To this he says:
"If the body were indeed the body, how could the great-minded Śuka have gone through various different births arising from many bodies? (MU 4.20.6)

The body is the gross form (*sthūla-śarīra*). By metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇayā*), the body is the person (*puruṣa*). If it were so, then that [person] would be the semen (*śukra*). How could he have attained such various distinctions, arising from many bodies, since the body exists in only a single form? // MT_4,20.6 //
It declares that the fruit [arises] from that; for the mind is indeed the person, and the person is indeed the mind. Whatever this [mind] becomes, that it undoubtedly attains.
"Indeed" (*hi*) signifies certainty. This mind is "composed of that," meaning it consists of the continuous pursuit of its respective objects.
He states the supreme fruition:
"That which is not hollow, effortless, free from conditions, and devoid of delusion—exert yourself in the pursuit of that, and you shall attain its very state."

Therefore, whatever object is substantial— not hollow— and effortless, being devoid of the need for exertion, and is free from limiting conditions (*anupādhi*) as well as delusion— pursue that. Thereby, you will attain the state of reality (*tattā*), which is the nature of an object devoid of qualities such as hollowness and the like.
He expresses this very point even with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"The body falls into the state of the mind, but the mind does not enter into the physical form. Therefore, O fortunate one, let your mind here fall into that which is true, and abandon everything else that is untrue."
This is clear. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twentieth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Here Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, this great doubt of mine revolves within my heart like a restless wave in the ocean."
It turns away and vibrates.
In that which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, all-pervading, eternal, and free from affliction—whence has this withered consciousness called "mind" arisen?

Because it is impossible for that which is not delimited by space, time, and so forth, to effect the delimitation of its own self-delimiter; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of substance and the like is intended. It is *tata*—pervasive; *nitya*—eternal, devoid of prior non-existence, non-existence after destruction, and absolute non-existence; *nirāmaya*—free from the disease known as mental construction (*kalanā*). This consciousness (*saṃvit*) is *mlāna*—stained by the nature of conceptualization and discursive thought—and thus bent toward the mind (*manonamnī*).
The vibration called consciousness—why has it arisen? The sense is that its appearance here is not logical.
Since there exists no other name, neither in the past nor will there be in the future, how, of what kind, and in what manner could its stain exist, and where?

Because there is no other entity distinct from the reality of pure consciousness alone—this being the certainty regarding names—it has not existed, nor will it exist. Its stain, which consists of the form of mental constructs, how could it exist? Of what nature would it be? In what manner would it exist?
Where would it exist? Since its existence is impossible in every respect, the meaning is that it does not exist at all.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Well said, O Rāma! Your mind, which seeks liberation, has been rightly described by you; it is the supreme outflow of wisdom, like a cluster of blossoms from the Nandana grove."
It has the highest outflow and the most excellent current.
This mind of yours, intent upon investigating what comes before and after, shall attain that exalted state which was reached by Śaṅkara and the other great sages.
Regarding that object which consists of the investigation of what precedes and what follows, therein the supreme is the highest state called liberation, the most excellent station.
"In that case, give the answer to my question. To this he replied: "O Rāma, this is not the time for your question now; this question is addressed only when the final conclusion is being stated."
The connection is that this question is stated by me as having been answered and brought to completion.

[Objection: "But if at the time of the final conclusion (siddhānta) this question does not come to your memory, then what is to be done? To this he says: "At the time of the final conclusion, you must ask me about this point; by that, your final conclusion will become as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of your hand. (MU 4.21.7)
Like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, it is free from effort.
"But surely, why do you not speak at this very moment? To this he replies:
"This question of yours is appropriate at the time of establishing the final doctrine; for the cry of the peacock is fitting only in the rainy season, while the song of the swan belongs to autumn."
This is clear.
The innate blue hue shines in the sky at the end of the rainy season, whereas during the rains it arises from masses of clouds as vast as mountains.
