At the end of the rainy season, in autumn—that is, in the other fortnight—the blackness of the monsoon shines forth. Of what nature is it? Like Dānu, the mother of the Dānavas; it has arisen, been produced, from that mass of clouds which is lofty.
Having concluded this, he returns to the subject at hand:
"This supreme determination of the mind, which has been commenced here, is the subject under discussion. Listen, O observer of noble vows, to that by whose power the birth of living beings occurs."
This supreme determination of the mind has been undertaken by us. Of what nature is it? It is "pertinent," meaning it is relevant by virtue of the context;

the sense is: "Listen to this very thing. O you of noble vows (*suvrata*), listen—that is, hear—that by whose power the birth of the multitude (*janatājanma*), the birth of the mass of people, occurs; for it is a constituent part of the determination of the mind—this is the intended meaning.
He explains that very point:
"In this way, O Rāma, it has been determined by all those seeking liberation that this very nature, characterized by the mental activity of thinking, is indeed karma."

O Rāma! This being so—when the certainty stated in the previous chapter stands as the ultimate reality—the mental activity known as reflection (*manana*), which is the function of the mind, has this [Prakṛti] as its substrate; that is, it has this very nature. This very Prakṛti, which is the material cause of the world, is the Root-Nature (*mūlaprakṛti*). It has been determined by all seekers of liberation to be "action" (*karman*); for it is the reflection of the mind.
Such is the action; this is the summarized meaning.

Listen now to how that manifoldness of opinions among eloquent speakers has arisen through the distinction of their defining characteristics, as they speak with various perspectives on the scriptures.
Listen! That action, which consists of the mental deliberation of the mind, has reached a state of manifoldness among eloquent disputants due to differences in their defining characteristics.

The sense is: "I shall explain how that very [action] came to be. Of what kind are these eloquent disputants? They are those who speak—that is, those engaging in debate—by means of various and diverse philosophical perspectives (*śāstradṛṣṭi*), which take the form of treatises (*śāstra*). Otherwise, there would be no difference of opinion.
It would not exist.
He explains that very point:
whatever state the mind, flickering with its own thoughts, takes hold of, it enters that very state, just as the wind, situated in the midst of a thick fragrance, takes on that scent.

By means of the mental faculty (*manas*), which is characterized by the quality called "thinking" (*manana*) and is restless—wandering among various objects—the mind grasps or takes hold of whatever state, whether auspicious or inauspicious, or whatever specific latent impression (*vāsanā*) arisen from the thinking of objects. It "goes toward" each of those; the meaning is that it becomes composed of the continuous succession of those very things. How so? Like the wind. Just as [the wind] situated in the midst of a dense fragrance...
The wind attains fragrance; that is the meaning of "so be it."
Then, having determined that very [object] and conceptualizing it as such, he colors his own sense of ego with that internal passion.
Based on that certainty, one attains flavor in that very [object]; then, through identification with that, it occurs in the body and subsequently even in the faculties of perception.

Then, having determined that very state— that very nature— of that mind, and having reflected upon it, and having ascertained it thus, conceptualizing and repeatedly contemplating that alone and nothing else, he colors his own ego-construction— his innate function of the *ahaṃkāra*— with that passion, which consists of the nature of that state, thereby making it tinged with attachment.

"Reflecting on when this might be mine" means up to that point. "Then, having ascertained that"—namely, the ascertainment of that state, an ascertainment of the form "this is truly wonderful"—"having taken hold of it. "In that very [state]," whether auspicious or inauspicious, "in that very particular latent impression (vāsanā)," he "attains flavor," which is to say, enjoyment or attachment. "Then," from that.

Immediately after that—*tu* being used for emphasis—the state of being identical with that [object] occurs in the body; for otherwise, since it would be impossible for there to be any activity consisting of engagement or avoidance toward an external object which has its own distinct nature, this state of identity occurs not only in the body but also in the sense organs. Otherwise, it would be impossible for them as well to repeatedly perform their respective functions therein.

The organs of action, however, are apprehended by the body alone. For instance: first, a person outside consumes a wood-apple or similar fruit; thereafter, his mind retains the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of that fruit within;

then, he repeatedly performs a mental recollection of that very thing in the form of a latent impression; finally, through that [impression] in the form of a latent impression, he colors his own ego-sense (*ahaṅkṛti*).

Consequently, the sense faculties (*buddhīndriya*) that depend upon it also become directed toward that very object; thereafter, the body which serves as their support performs movement directed toward that same object. This constitutes a pair of verses.

"Now, from where does this come? To this he says: "For the mind consists of that, O Rāma; the body follows it, and by its power, it attains the nature of that [mind], just as the wind within a flower attains the nature of fragrance."
Whatever it consists of, whatever its nature may be—that very state, that state of being composed of that.
When the sense organs are active, the group of action organs then vibrates of its own accord, like particles of earth stirred by a gust of wind.

"It vibrates" means it becomes oriented toward its own activity by itself, without any external impulse. What is it like? It is like the dust of the earth; just as the dust of the earth vibrates by itself when the wind is stirring, so too is the meaning here.
When the group of organs of action is agitated, it fully manifests its own power; thus, extensive action is produced from it, like a mass of dust from the wind.

It manifests—that is, it expands—its own power, which is its inherent capacity toward its own effect; and the action, consisting of the taking up of objects, is accomplished—that is, it is brought to completion.
It declares the fruition:
"For thus the activity of the mind is the seed of action; the mind is known as such. The existence of these two is non-different, just like that of a flower and its fragrance. (MU 4.21.19)

This being the case, the remainder [of the sentence] is: "from the mind, from the vicinity of the mind, action arises. By the wise, that which has action as its very seed—that is what is remembered. The sense is that the mind arises from action. He states the conclusion: "therefore, by the non-difference," etc. Thus, the existence of these two—action and mind—is indeed non-different. Of which two?

Just as [there is no relation] between a flower and its fragrance; for even external action, which depends upon the body, cannot be accomplished without following the mind. And the point is that there is nothing called "mind" apart from being of the nature of mere latent impressions (vāsanā) produced by action.
Whatever state the mind assumes through the power of firm habituation, its vibration—known as action—responds accordingly, and it thereby relinquishes its various branches.
Whatever it may be, whether auspicious or inauspicious; the branches consist of the nature of volitional constructions (*saṅkalpa*).
Likewise, he performs that action which yields its fruit with diligence; then, having quickly experienced that very taste, he is bound.

The phrase "by way of the body" is to be understood as the ellipsis. That very object, when taken as a mental state (*bhāva*), means that one who is permeated by its latent impression (*vāsanā*) becomes more firmly bound.
Furthermore, he says this very thing:
whatever state one takes up, one perceives that as the reality; the certainty arises in him that "this alone is the highest good, and there is nothing else."
The thing is real.
For they always strive for the sake of virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation; indeed, their minds are firm in resolve through their own very practice.
By one's own practice, and not by the instigation of another.
He states the very purpose for which this treatise was composed:
"Having fully accepted the respective positions of the followers of Kapila as determined by their own minds, they have fashioned these philosophical perspectives based on scripture. (MU 4.21.24)

Of the followers of Kapila, that is to say, of the Sāṅkhyas who follow Kapila— with their minds, having accepted their own position, that is, their own conviction— the views of the treatises, which expound upon primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa), have been constructed.

They distinguish themselves as followers of Kapila alone, thinking, "In liberation there is no other way to attain it"; thus, with minds so conditioned, they remain intent on elaborating their own view, deluded by their own restrictive rules.

Those whose minds are cultivated and disciplined through meditation—by means of the errors regarding restrictive rules they themselves have created—the point is that even for these [others], there exists a difference of opinion solely due to the power of the mind.
The proponents of Vedānta, having determined and conceptualized through their intellect—aided by reasoning and endowed with tranquility and self-control—that "this is Brahman," [attain liberation].

But regarding liberation, they maintain that there is no other way to attain it; thus, with their minds conditioned in this way, they remain fixed in the delusions of their own restrictive rules while expounding their own views.
The method (*upāya*) consisting of hearing and so forth, which is the means of reasoning (*yukti*).

The proponents of consciousness (vijñānavādins), through their intellect which flashes in the form of its own delusion, reveal their own view by means of their very own arbitrary delusions regarding restrictive rules.

The Vijñānavādins, the Buddhists who maintain the non-duality of consciousness, clearly explain—that is, they reveal—their own view, which takes the form of the proposition that "this [world] is indeed consciousness alone."
By the Arhats and others, as well as by various [others], diverse scriptural perspectives have been fashioned according to their own preferred inclinations and through diverse modes of conduct.
And by the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the Cārvākas and others is intended.
For these various styles of expression, though mature, arise from their own certainties like a multitude of gentle water bubbles rising from a causeless source.
The meaning is: "as if by those [waves] which arise suddenly, like a mass of gentle water bubbles arising without cause; thus, the *rītis* are the styles of the scriptures."
O mighty-armed one, the mind alone is the single source of all these modes of being, just as the ocean is the source of jewels.
It is the source, that is, the place of origin, for all those [treatises] composed by the Sāṃkhyas and others.
The neem tree and the sugarcane are not simultaneously bitter and sweet; the moon and fire are not cold and hot. Whatever is practiced by the mind is perceived exactly as it has been so cultivated.

Pungent and sweet, bitter and sweet—otherwise, due to the differences in the fluctuations of the mind, there would be no distinction between what is to be abandoned and what is to be accepted; for that very thing which stands as something to be abandoned for one person may be something to be accepted by another.
One should not indeed strive for that unartificial bliss which he describes as the fruit; rather, the mind must be led to become one with that [reality], and by that means it is attained.

The word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is to be supplied [from the context]. Since there is no sweetness by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in any external object whatsoever, therefore, that which is unartificial—because it exists independently of objects such as enjoyments—is the bliss that is one's own essential nature (*svātmarūpa*). A person should, for that purpose, indeed (*vai*)—the word "indeed" (*vai*) signifying certainty—strive. But by what effort is this [attained]?

"It is attained"—to this he replies: "By the mind. By the person, the mind—which is of the nature of volition (*saṅkalpa*)—must be led to that state of being identical with it, which is the form of bliss that has become one's own self. The meaning is that, by means of the path taught in the inner science (*adhyātma-śāstra*), one must make the mind solely intent upon the contemplation of that [bliss]. By the mere act of leading the mind to that state of identity through such effort, this uncreated bliss [is realized].
is attained.
[Objection: But how can the mind, which is under the sway of pleasure and pain, be brought to a state of identity with that [Reality]? To this, he says:
"By completely abandoning the trivial objects of perception residing within the child of saṃsāra, the mind is no longer helplessly dragged away by the pleasure and pain born from them. (MU 4.21.34)

*Saṃsāra* itself is the *ḍimba*, meaning a child; that which "stays therein" is such [a child]. The *dṛśya* (the visible) is the collection of objects that are the domain of the act of seeing. *Jahat* means leading [them] to a state where they are no longer the object of one's own orientation. *Manaḥ* (the mind) is not forcibly dragged away—nor made subject to external power—by the *sukha-duḥkha* (pleasure and pain) born from that [visible world], i.e., produced by the visible. The word *avaśaḥ* (not under control) takes the gender of the subject it qualifies.
"Is there not some fault in the visible world? To this he replies:
"O sinless one, do not contemplate the visible world—which is impure, unreal in nature, delusive, a cause of fear, a mere appearance, expansive, and a cause of bondage."
O sinless one! Do not contemplate the visible object, which is unworthy of being contemplated; do not make it an object of the mind’s continuous reflection.

In response to the inquiry, "For what reason should I not contemplate it?", he states the qualifying attributes beginning with "impure. It is "impure" because it generates sins such as passion and the like, and is thus devoid of purity. It is "of the nature of non-existence" because it cannot withstand investigation into its true form, and is therefore devoid of ultimate reality.

Delusion (*mohana*) is that which produces the delusion consisting in the notion of "self" with respect to what is not-self. It is the cause of fear, being the basis for the fear arising from death and so forth. It is an appearance (*ābhāsa*), whose nature is mere appearance and does not exist as a reality. It is expansive (*ābhogin*), being endowed with extension. It is bondage (*bandha*), because it acts as an obstruction to the knowledge of the self and thus has the nature of bondage.
This is indeed illusion, this is ignorance, this is a mental construction that brings fear; the wise know that state of being absorbed in consciousness is what constitutes karma.

This is the cultivation of the visible; it is self-established. It becomes illusion; it becomes ignorance; it becomes a cultivation or a latent impression that brings about fear. [The opponent asks: "In that case, what is the nature of karma? To this, he says: "Of consciousness. That is, of consciousness in the form of the mind. "Consisting of that" means consisting of the visible. This is what occurs, according to the wise.
They know that to be action; the sense is that action is also this very same thing.
"Now, what is the nature of this mind by which the cultivation of the visible world is produced and designated by names such as 'illusion' (māyā) and so forth? To this he replies:

"Know that the mind, which is the state of the seer being one-pointedly absorbed in the visible, is delusive; it exists only for the sake of error, being false like the work of a spider on the ground. (MU 4.21.37)

Know that for the seer—the agent of the act of seeing—the mind’s one-pointedness toward the object of sight, its being directed toward it, is delusive; it causes delusion. That [mind] exists for the sake of wandering, for the production of error; it becomes false. The meaning is that, by being a mere appearance, it does not exist as a real entity. How so? Just as on the ground—that is, on clay—the work of a makrola, which is a coating of lime.

It is just like that: for example, a plastering of lime applied to clay does not exist in reality, because the clay remains as it is and the lime exists only as a coating. Likewise, the mind appearing within pure consciousness (cinmātra) does not exist in reality, because pure consciousness alone remains as it is; this is the meaning.
Now, one might ask: how can the mind, which consists of the continuous flow of the seer and the seen, exist in a false form? To this, he says:
"This experience of being absorbed in the nature of the seen—this is the wine of saṃsāra, called ignorance by the wise. (MU 4.21.38)
By us, that which is the state of being identical with the object—the state of being focused solely on the object—of the nature of the seer, which is the very nature [itself], is perceived.
Because it produces delusion, this is called ignorance (*avidyā*), having the form of the intoxicant of *saṃsāra*.
Therefore, the meaning is that the mind is indeed of the nature of ignorance and is devoid of substantial reality.
"What harm is caused by this ignorance? To this he replies:
"The world, afflicted by this, does not attain what is auspicious, just as one whose eyes are blinded by a cataract does not perceive the brilliant light of the sun."

By means of this ignorance, which consists in the identity of the seer with the seen, [the obscuration of] the auspicious—which is the nature of resting within one's own self—is [veiled]. A *paṭala* is a specific type of eye disease.
"Now, from what does that arise? To this he says:
"And that arises by itself from volitional construction (saṅkalpa), like a tree in the sky; by the mere absence of volitional construction, it perishes by itself. (MU 4.21.40)
It arises and manifests. One might ask: "How then does it perish? To this he says: "By mere non-conceptualization" (*asaṅkalpanamātra*).

That is, by the mere absence of conceptualization (*saṅkalpākaraṇamātra*). For this very reason he says "by itself" (*svayam*); for non-conceptualization is not an effort, but rather the cessation of conceptualization itself.
"Now, what is accomplished by the destruction of ignorance? To this he says:
"O Mahāmati, when mental cultivation has been exhausted through mere non-ideation, by its own clarity and by playful discernment..."
When all objects have attained stability within the state of non-attachment, when the vision of truth has become clear, and the unreal has come to its end; MU 4.21.42.
That Self, which is non-conceptual consciousness and a pure essence, is fully attained; it is that whose neither non-existence nor existence, nor happiness nor suffering, exists.

In meditation, within ignorance; by means of inquiry—that is, by the investigation of one's own self—of what nature? By its own clarity, meaning "arisen from the clarity of one's own self," is the ellipsis. Again, of what nature? By that which is playful, endowed with expansion. In non-attachment, in freedom from clinging. "Truth-vision" (satyadṛṣṭi) is vision whose object is truth; when that [vision] is serene—that is, when it is perfected—in the unreal, in that which has become untrue.

The meaning is "in the visible. Of what nature is the Self? It is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), having the form of that consciousness (*cit*) which has emerged from conceptualization regarding the objects of the visible. It is "clear" (*accha*), meaning its very essence is such; the sense is that it does not have the nature of the body and so forth, which are insentient (*acid-rūpa*). Therefore, the implication is that the destruction of ignorance is not fruitless. In response to the inquiry, "Of what kind is this Self? [the following is said:]

He says, "not non-existence. For that Self, there is no non-existence, because it manifests as the self-nature of all; indeed, no one says, "I am not. And one who says so would surely be an object of ridicule. Likewise, its existence is not [absolute], because it is not an object of either external or internal organs, like the horn of a hare. Bliss (*sukha*) is, by implication, the state of being blissful (*sukhitā*). It is not...

[The state of] happiness and so forth exists because it has the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as its locus; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of their manifestation even during deep sleep and similar states.
[The state of] being pained is the state of having suffering as its locus; this does not exist [in that case] for the reason already stated.

Furthermore, what is there in that state? To this he says: "Therein is found the state of absolute oneness (kevalībhāva), which is not attained through unworthy contemplation, nor by means of the mind, the senses, or [wrong] views. (MU 4.21.44)

By a person endowed with right knowledge, within his own self—that is, upon his own inner wall—is attained the state of being absolute (*kevalībhāva*), which is the total absence of everything except pure consciousness (*śuddhacinmātratā*). It is said that "it is attained" only in a figurative sense, because for that which has already attained its singular form, there is no possibility of further attainment. In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), however, there is no dependence on anything to be attained; even the status of being an "attainer" is not tenable therein.
Enough with speech that leads to conceptual construction; it is not attained through that deceptive and unwholesome cultivation, nor is it attained by means of the mind, the faculties, or views.
He who is devoid of even those infinite latent impressions that are non-different from himself, just as the sky is free from rows of forest trees.

That which is the Self is devoid of even those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are non-different from itself, even though they are its own essential nature; this is because its nature is pure consciousness alone (*śuddhacinmātra*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the status of latent impressions as being the "Self" is established solely by their being objects of that [consciousness]—for a latent impression does not become a latent impression unless it is made an object of pure consciousness. And this making into an object occurs through a relation with itself.

Thus it is logically established. Furthermore, when the relationship is examined, it rests upon oneness; for if there were duality, the relationship would be untenable precisely because of that duality, since its existence is established through contradiction. Indeed, a relationship between two contradictory things, such as darkness and light, is not possible.
Enough of this elaboration. What is it like? It is like space (*vyoma*). Just as space is devoid of rows of forests, so too is it [devoid of relation].
It exists; that is the meaning of "tathā."
Now, if that alone is the Self, then from where has this bondage in the form of the visible world come? To this, he says:

"Just as the state of being a snake is imagined in a rope when it is perceived doubtfully, even so is bondage imagined by the unbound Self through the nature of the space of consciousness. (MU 4.21.46)

Just as a person imagines a snake in a rope that is perceived with doubt— certainly not when there is certainty— in exactly the same way, by means of the self which is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), by means of the self whose nature is the space of consciousness, while being entirely unbound, the so-called bondage of the visible world is imagined,
brought about through mental construction (*kalpanā*).
[Objection: But how can this imagined bondage be destroyed? To this, he says:
An imagined object is [destroyed] by another imagination; it assumes that very state of being "other," just as the sky [appears different] during day and night.

Every imagined object is an imagined thing. By another conceptualization—distinct from itself—that very [object], while remaining existent, assumes otherness. Like what? Like space (*kha*). Just as space, while remaining the same throughout day and night, assumes otherness; such is the meaning. Therefore, the destruction of the imagined occurs precisely through another conceptualization.
Existence.

Now, since that which is distinguished by qualities such as non-triviality does not exist as a conceptual construction, how can it be so constructed that the conceptualization of *saṃsāra*—distinguished by qualities such as triviality—is destroyed? Furthermore, without conceptual construction, the destruction of conceptual construction cannot be accomplished, just as iron cannot be [worked] without fire.
To this, he says:
Whatever is non-empty, effortless, free from limiting conditions, and devoid of delusion—that very thing, when conceived as such, conduces solely to happiness.

That entity which is non-trivial—meaning devoid of trivial qualities; effortless—meaning free from being accomplished through exertion; unconditioned—meaning it is devoid of conditions because even that which is considered a condition does not deviate from its true nature; and free from delusion—meaning untouched by error because its essential nature is pure, true consciousness—that is that very entity. It exists through the conceptualization of it, by means of conceiving its non-triviality and other such attributes.

Thus, that which has such a nature as being non-trivial and so forth comes to be. This is because within the pure essential nature (*svarūpa*), there is no room for words that depend upon distinctions such as triviality or non-triviality.

[Objection: "In that case, even that must be abandoned. To this, he says: "That is for the sake of bliss alone. That reality, characterized by qualities such as non-triviality—even though it is conceptually constructed—is solely for the sake of bliss; that is, for the sake of resting in the pure essential nature which is free from both triviality and non-triviality.
Thus, the meaning is that it is possible to destroy the conceptualization of qualities such as emptiness by means of a counter-conceptualization possessing qualities such as non-emptiness.

[Objection: But how can the destruction of bondage—which is a real, visible form—be accomplished by mere imagination? To this, he says: "Just as there is fear that a lion exists inside an empty granary, so too is there the fear 'I am bound' within the empty body. (MU 4.21.49)

A *kusūla* is a chamber in the form of a mechanical device for the purpose of trapping a lion; it is a visible bond, and though it may be real, nevertheless, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it does not act as a binder for you, whose nature is pure consciousness (*śuddhacidrūpa*). For the meaning is that space is not bound by ropes.
Just as a lion is not found when one looks inside an empty granary, so too, when examined, that which is fit to be bound by saṃsāra is not found.
This is clear.
[Objection: "In that case, how does this cognition in the form of the bound and the binder—'this world' and 'I am this'—exist? To this, he says:
"This notion, 'this world' and 'I am this,' has arisen as an error for the ignorant, like a fleeting shadow in the dark of night. (MU 4.21.51)
In the dark time of night, the cognition in the form of "this world" and "I am this" arises as nothing but an error; such is the summarized meaning.
[Objection: But how does such an illusion arise? To this he says:

"By the power of conceptual construction, for a living being, entities—whether existent or non-existent, auspicious or inauspicious—reach non-existence in an instant, and existence again and again. (MU 4.21.52)
"By the power of conceptual construction" means by the power of one's own discursive thought.
He explains this very point in detail:
"The mother herself, having assumed the state of a housewife and hanging from his neck, performs the duties of a wife, bestowing the bliss of sexual union."
The word "by delusion" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Like a beloved taken up as a mother, hanging from one's neck, she causes the intoxicating state of passion to be utterly forgotten at a distance.

Here too, "by delusion" is the ellipsis to be supplied. This state should be understood to apply to those who are middling sinners and the like; however, for great sinners, even here only delight arises.
He states the conclusion:
"And having observed the multitude of entities which yield results according to their nature, no single form is declared here by the wise regarding these entities."

Having observed that the flood of objects— which yields fruits corresponding to one's disposition— is [perceived] by a wise person who knows the true nature of things, no single form among these objects is proclaimed or described here in this world.
Through firm cultivation, whatever the mind intensely contemplates in a certain way, it perceives for that duration a corresponding result in that very form.

O mind, whatever object one contemplates and investigates through firm cultivation, that result— being the fruit of such cultivation— is perceived in that very form at that time and for that duration; and in this context, a dream should be understood as the illustrative example.
He states the established conclusion:
there is nothing that is not true, and there is nothing that is not false; in whatever manner and by whatever means something is determined, it is characterized as such by that very means.
This has been determined and reflected upon; otherwise, the point is that a single object would not be a source of joy for one person and a source of suffering for another.
The mind, having cultivated the elephant of space, pursues the female elephant of the forest of space who dwells within that very sky, perceiving it as the elephant of the void.

The mind, having cultivated the elephant of space—that is, having become the elephant of space, as it were—pursues the female elephant of the forest of space. Of what nature is she? She is such that she stands in the sky, which serves as the foundation for the forest.
He states the ultimate result:
"Therefore, O Rāghava, abandon volition itself, which consists of the nature of all things; being well-composed, abide in the Self by means of your own self."

That which consists of all existence and has the nature of all objects is the Self (*ātman*). It is indeed volition (*saṅkalpa*) itself that manifests externally in various forms. "Abandon [it]" means do not bring it forth; even if it has already manifested, the meaning is that you should simply practice equanimity (*upekṣā*).
For abandonment in every respect is not possible to perform until the state of disembodied liberation (*videhamukti*) is reached.
"But how can I abandon a thought that is already arising? To this he replies:
"For a gem is indeed incapable of performing the act of negating reflections because of its insentient nature, but such is not the case for one like you, O Rāma."

By "inertness" (*jaḍabhāvena*) is meant by way of being insentient. One such as you is sentient (*cetana*). For the renunciation of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*) is achievable through conscious awareness (*saṃvedana*), and that indeed exists in you; such is the meaning.
He speaks the means of renunciation:
O Rāma, whatever is reflected here in the jewel of your mind, having determined that it is not a real substance, do not allow yourself to be colored by it.
Passion (*rañjanā*) is the state of being colored (*uparaktatva*).
He states another means:
"Or else, considering that very [world] to be true and non-different from the Supreme Self, contemplate the Self, which is without beginning or end, by means of the self."
For, by cultivating the realization of non-difference from the Supreme Self, one indeed achieves the cultivation of the Self that is without beginning or end.
O Rāghava, may those objects that reflect in your mind not color you—yourself being attached to another—just as a crystal [is colored by the objects reflected in it].

O Raghava! Of what nature [is he]? He is one whose self—that is, whose mind—is attached to another Supreme Self, whose essential nature is distinct from all other states of being. The implication is that otherwise, the absence of coloring by reflected objects would not be logical. To whom are you like? You are like a crystal; just as a crystal joined with another color undergoes coloring produced by that other color.
It does not cause attachment; such is the meaning.
"But surely, how can the absence of passion toward the body be possible? To this, he replies with the final verse of the chapter:
"Just as various fresh stains enter a stainless crystal clearly, so too let the desires for worldly existence enter you clearly through the practice of non-attachment. (MU 4.21.64)

The absence of conceit (*vimananam*) means being devoid of the mental state called conceit (*manana*), which is the nature of the mind. Just as various colors enter a stainless crystal, so too may the "colors" consisting of the conceptualization of objects enter You, even though You are pure due to the absence of "reflection"—which is a synonym for conceit. This is the summary meaning: if a color that does not produce a stain should come [to You], there is no loss whatsoever.
Such is the intended meaning. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-first canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrī Mokṣopāya-Ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Since the very same matter previously stated is established as being expressed in this section on "Stability," he states it once more:

"For the living being who has performed inquiry, whose mind’s fluctuations have dissolved, who abandons discursive thought through the knowledge of the knower, and whose self is somewhat realized—" *Muktika Upaniṣad* 4.22.1.

For one who has abandoned the visible as something to be discarded, who has attained that which is to be accepted, and who perceives the Seer while no longer perceiving the visible as a seer; // MU 4.22.2 //
While remaining awake within the supreme reality, yet living as if asleep upon the path of worldly existence which consists of dense delusion.

Because they are ultimately and utterly devoid of flavor, even those pleasures that are flavorful are tasteless; thus, he is without relish for enjoyments that are delightful when indulged, being himself devoid of passion and free from desire.
When the dullness in the mind has fully worn away and attachment has dissolved, the self attains oneness with the waters, just as a mass of snow melts completely in the heat of the sun.
And when their cravings have subsided like rivers at the end of the rainy season—their inner depths once agitated by a mass of surging waves—then [the mind becomes tranquil].
When the net of worldly tendencies has been torn asunder—like a bird-net by a mouse—with the swift force of disillusionment that loosens the bonds of weak attachments;
Just as water becomes clear upon reaching the *kataka* fruit, so too does one's own nature become perfectly serene through the power of higher knowledge (*vijñāna*).

For a living being, that is, for a person; by the power of consciousness—that is, by the power of the knowledge of the pure self—his own nature, his true form, becomes thus clarified, meaning it becomes stainless. How does it become so? Just as water becomes clear upon coming into contact with the *kataka* fruit. In response to the expectation of under what conditions it becomes clear, he says: "The self proceeds," and so forth. When attachment has departed...

When the defect known as attachment has perished; when dullness has decayed and been cast out; and therefore, when the mind is dissolving and on the verge of melting away, it attains oneness with the water of the Self—that is, with the water called the Supreme Self—just as a mass of snow, when exposed to the heat of the sun, does so. Furthermore, under what conditions? Immediately thereafter, when all cravings have ceased.

While they were subsiding—of what nature?—while they were surging with waves, possessing an internal agitation through masses of waves consisting of the nature of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*). Of what kind [were they]? Such as those. Like what? Like rivers.
Just as they subside at the end of the rainy season, in autumn; such is the meaning. Furthermore, when what occurs? When the net of worldly tendencies (*saṃsāra-vāsanā*) [subsides].
When the net of birds has been torn asunder by a rat with the speed of its aversion—of what nature is that net?

It is one whose "knots"—meaning the bonds consisting of desire and so forth—are "not firm," being such that their connection or attachment has been loosened. Of what nature is the living being [who acts thus]?

He is one by whom "investigation" has been made—that is, one who possesses discernment in the form of [asking], "Who am I? Whose is this saṃsāra?"—such a person is one whose mind has its mental fluctuations dissolved (*vigaladvṛtticetaḥ*).

Of such a one—of the knower alone, for it is only the knower who possesses the capacity to abandon mental construction (manana); thus it is said "by virtue of being a knower. This means [he perceives] something as being indirect (*parokṣatayā*), but not as being direct (*aparokṣatayā*). By implication, that which is to be accepted is the form of the pure seer (*śuddhadraṣṭṛrūpa*). The object seen (*dṛśya*) and the seer (*draṣṭṛ*) are the form of the seer. For one who sees [them], there is the non-seer (*adraṣṭṛ*), distinct from the seer; for one who does not see [it], [there is the state] regarding tastes (*raseṣu*).
The phrase "even while sleeping" is to be supplied [to each verse]. "Free from longing" means devoid of hope. This is a *kulaka* (a group of verses forming a single syntactic unit).
"What else will be his attainment? To this he says:
"Free from passion, free from attachment, free from dualities, and free from dependence, the mind emerges from delusion like a bird from a cage. (MU 4.22.9)
"Free from attachment" means devoid of clinging; "without support" means independent. This is due to delusion—that is, from non-investigation consisting in the conceit of a self in what is not-self.
With its wickedness and doubts stilled, and with its restless distractions gone, the mind, its inner space completely full, shines like the full moon.
In this context, "wonder" (kautuka) should be understood as pertaining to the object; it is that which is complete, filled with innate bliss, and whose interior is such [as described].
Having produced supreme beauty, and with its depressions and elevations cast far away, it rises everywhere as level as a windless ocean.

She by whom supreme beauty was produced; for through equanimity a person always possesses a serene countenance. "Dūrodasta" refers to the state of being devoid of depression and elation—a description emphasizing the underlying state—meaning that in her, there was no such fluctuation between low and high spirits.
Consisting of darkness, deluded, and with its interior shattered by dullness, the night at dawn shrinks away like the latent tendencies of worldly existence.
The word *iva* is connected with the word *kṣapā*.
The lotus-pond of wisdom, with its shoots of merit, blossoms when the sun of insight has been seen; it shines with stainless light like the sky at dawn in embodied form.
This is clear.
Wisdoms that captivate the heart and are capable of gladdening the world proceed forth as the fortunes of sentient beings, like the rays of the full moon.
The fortunes of sentient beings are the perfections of the quality of purity.
He provides a summary: "What is the use of saying more here? The one of great intelligence, who has known what is to be known, neither rises nor sets, like the unmanifest expanse of space."

The meaning is that it neither rises nor sets; it does not deviate from its own essential nature, which is called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). It is like the sheath of space that has never come into being, situated within the supreme space.
For one whose own nature has been fully understood through investigation and whose self has arisen [in its true state], even these—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, and Śaṅkara—become objects of compassion.

One by whom the nature, that is, one's own true form, has been fully known through investigation—toward such a person [compassion arises]. The meaning is that compassion arises in him even toward those who are objects of pity, because he perceives the agitation caused by the creation and dissolution of the world; [he is] one whose inner mind is free from egoism, even though his outward form is manifest. Conceptual constructions do not reach him, just as deer cannot reach the water of a mirage.
They do not attain self-mastery, nor do they exercise it; moreover, the absence of egoism in one whose form is manifest is indeed a marvelous feat.
Like waves, these worlds come and go on all sides; do not embrace birth and death, which arise from the self, as if they were real.
They embrace and bring under their control; because there is no conceit of a body, there is an absence of conceit regarding birth and death situated therein.
Manifestation and disappearance constitute the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra), and no other sequence exists; one who beholds them through these two perspectives rejoices and does not suffer.

Thus, by means of these two—namely, manifestation and disappearance—he rejoices when there is illumination, that is, when the true nature of reality is revealed, and he does not suffer. For one who has known the true nature of things rejoices in objects and does not suffer;
for it is observed that only one whose true nature is unknown suffers from the fear of snakes and the like regarding [what is actually] a rope and so forth.
Just as the space within a jar is neither born nor dies when the jar is decorated or defiled, so too is the self here, even when the body is adorned or corrupted.
The meaning is that it is because of the absence of identification with the body.
When the cool dawn of discernment has arisen, the latent impression born from the weight of false delusion withers away, like a mirage in the desert when the clouds have vanished.
That which is a mass of delusion is of a false nature; it is by that [delusion] that she is raised up. For in a desert with clouds, a mirage indeed subsides, since its very arising is from heat.
As long as one has not investigated "Who am I? and "How is this?", the grand spectacle of saṃsāra remains like darkness.
The inquiry, "What is the nature of this darkness? remains for exactly that long.
He truly sees who perceives this body—which arises from a mass of false delusions and is the locus of calamities—not as a self.
He who does not perceive this body as a self—that is to say, he who does not view it through the notion of "I"—he sees; he sees correctly. This is the summarized meaning.
He who perceives the pleasures and pains of the body as arising from the influence of place and time, and as being "not mine," is free from delusion; he truly sees.
Of me, who am pure consciousness alone; of me.
He truly sees who perceives both himself and everything else through a vision that is eternally undivided, seeing all as nothing but the light of consciousness.
The light of consciousness is the nature of the radiance of pure awareness.
He who sees everywhere that "I alone" am endowed with activity throughout the infinite reaches of space, direction, time, and so forth—he truly sees.

Space, direction, and time—of which the world is the beginning—that world, beginning with space, direction, and time, is without limit or end, being devoid of any boundary. I alone am that world whose nature consists of space, direction, and time;
for the reality of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), whose essence is the sense of "I," exists as the very substance of all things. Otherwise, the sense of "I" would not manifest everywhere.

Because even in the case of insentient things, there is no difference in their possessing existence (*sattā*) as something endowed with consciousness, despite their not being perceived; and because it is possible to infer the manifestation of that [consciousness] even therein, the claim that "it is not everywhere" is untenable. Of what nature is that? It is "endowed with activity. The separate mention of activity—even though it is already implied by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)—is for the purpose of indicating its preeminence. Thus, in this way, "everywhere" means in all [things].
The meaning is that he who perceives [this] in various places and times truly perceives; no one else does.
He who perceives that "I am subtle" and all-pervading—though [the self] is conceptually imagined as being ten million times the size of a hundred-thousandth part of the tip of a hair—he truly sees.
The pervasiveness of that which is subtle is wondrous; and here, subtlety should be understood as being beyond both the external and internal organs.
He who perceives within that which is all-powerful, infinite in nature, abiding within all beings, non-dual, and consciousness—he truly sees.
He is consciousness, the conscious self. Of what nature is he? He is omnipotent; otherwise, the world in its manifold forms would not manifest.

He is the infinite self, for even the end is swallowed up within him alone, and thus he is devoid of it; indeed, that which is already swallowed cannot conceal the form of the swallower. He stands within all beings, abiding in the interior of every state of existence.
Otherwise, the thought "I am" would not manifest. Being non-dual means that even that which is considered as a second has not lost its nature as being that [Self], and is thus devoid of a second.
In this way, he who sees within—that is, in the mind, and not with the eye—he truly sees. MT_4,22.28.
The wise one who perceives that "I am not this body, which is subject to birth, old age, and death, and is agitated by the fear of mental and physical ailments"—he truly sees.
The wise one possesses the certainty that the self is the reality of pure consciousness alone.
"My greatness pervades horizontally, upwards, and downwards; he who sees that there is no second to me—he truly sees."
"Of me," [meaning] of me whose nature is pure consciousness alone, and not of one whose nature is the body and so forth.
All this is strung upon me like clusters of gems on a thread; he who sees that "I alone am the mind's driver" truly sees.

"How is everything woven upon you? To this he says: "The mind is the thread. For pearls are woven upon a thread; and the "thread-ness" of the consciousness (citi) is to be understood through its pervasiveness and its subtlety.
"I am not, nor is there anything else here; Brahman alone exists, and even that does not exist. He who sees thus the middle between being and non-being—he truly sees. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.6)

In this world, I am not that which has the form of a limited body and so forth; nor does there exist a universe standing as something other than me, distinct from me, because it is not perceived in deep sleep. Brahman alone—the all-pervading reality of pure consciousness—exists in the ultimate sense, for it is impossible to speak of its total non-existence, since it has never been negated.
No delusion is possible therein; that is Brahman. And yet it does not exist, because it transcends both the external and internal organs.
It is thus: the reality called pure consciousness alone, which is the middle between existence and non-existence and serves as their junction. He who sees this truly sees.
Whatever exists in the three worlds, that is but a single limb of mine; he who perceives this within himself as a wave in the ocean—he truly sees.
For me, whose nature is pure consciousness alone, the entire world—composed of parts of that very consciousness—is experienced within the dream state.
"She is to be pitied and protected by me alone; she is my younger sister. He who looks upon the three worlds as fragile in this way—he truly sees.
If a younger sister is likewise delicate and fearful of destruction, she is just like this.
When the states of "I-ness" and "otherness," as well as "thou-ness" and "mine-ness," have ceased through the realization of the Great Self, that one with clear vision surely perceives reality.
The meaning is: because of the existence of the mind; that is to say, because of the perception of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) everywhere.
He who perceives the body consisting of the Bhairava of Consciousness—free from the pursuit of objects of thought and filling the entire web of the universe—he truly sees.

Free from the pursuit of objects of thought, that Bhairava of consciousness—called "consciousness" (cid) because he devours all—is Bhairava; his body is his essential nature (*svarūpa*), which consists of that.

Whether one perceives pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, or whatever notions of discrimination there may be, thinking "I do not know" or indeed perceiving [them as such], one certainly does not fall away.

Whether perceiving "I am pleasure, pain, existence, non-existence, and the conceptualization of discrimination," or perceiving "I am not this," one does not fall away, nor does one incur loss; for in both cases, there is the attainment of the nature of pure consciousness alone. Indeed, apart from pure consciousness alone, there is nothing that is either all-pervasive or transcendent.

When the world is filled with the supreme reality of one's own self and devoid of anything else, the man who perceives thus sees: "What is there for me to abandon? What is there to be accepted? (MU 4.22.38)

Of one's own self, which is of the nature of pure consciousness alone—by that existence which is the nature of manifestation, [the world] is filled because it abides as its very essence; otherwise, the manifestation "I" would be impossible. Likewise, in a universe devoid of anything else other than pure consciousness, what could there be to be abandoned? Since it is impossible for one's own self to be abandoned, the meaning is that there is nothing at all.

What is there to be acquired? Since one's own self is always already attained, the meaning is that there is nothing at all. Seeing and experiencing in this manner, a person becomes "possessed of sight"—that is to say, others are blind.
I bow to Him for whom all notions of what is to be rejected or accepted have ceased—He who is beyond reasoning, devoid of appearance, and is pure Being alone.

This world is beyond reasoning (*apratarkya*), meaning it is impossible to conceptualize; it is without appearance (*anābhāsa*) because it abides in its own peaceful nature, free from manifestation; it exists as pure Being (*sanmātra*) alone. With this certainty, for that person whose notions of what is to be rejected and what is to be accepted have perished—I bow to that person. The sense is that he alone is superior to all.
He who, like space, is the single Self even while pervading all things, yet does not undergo the coloring of existence—he is the Great-Souled One, Maheśvara.

That person who, though being the one Self like space— the all-pervading Self— and though existing within all states of being, remains engaged in worldly activity regarding all objects necessary for the maintenance of the body, yet does not undergo "staining of states"— that is, staining in the form of joy or resentment within the state of the mind— he is a great-souled one, a great person, and becomes a Maheśvara.
Because it is endowed with great power.

I bow to him who has reached that state—the one who is free from the conceptualization of darkness and light, who has become the very nature of time, who is gentle, perfectly equanimous, and established in his own self.

He who is liberated from that conceptualization of darkness and light—that is, of insentience and sentience; who has attained the nature of time, which consists of the manifold variety of activity, by bestowing existence upon it as its very essence; who is gentle, cool, and established in his own true nature—he who has reached that state, him I revere. Herein, the Sun is described as something unprecedented.
He expresses this very same point with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"Salutation to that Śiva, who possesses supreme awakening, whose infinite activity is entirely equal toward all things throughout the world—things that possess diverse and beautiful manifestations within the manifold processes of their arising and passing away;

[salutation] to Him who is the sole refuge of all and the one who has gone beyond all. [The commentary explains: "Beautiful manifestations" (*cāruvibhavāsu*) means endowed with praiseworthy power; "diverse" (*cittrāsu*) [refers to the various modes].

In the various arts pertaining to the world—consisting of the combinations and collisions occurring at the times of rising and setting—the mental activity becomes exactly the same, infinite and thus free from destruction. Here, "infinitude" is stated with reference to its firmness.
To that one who possesses supreme awakening, who is endowed with the realization of the supreme reality of the Self—to that auspicious person who has become Śiva.
Let there be homage! And may it be auspicious, for Śiva is of equanimous conduct, the sole refuge of all, and the embodiment of supreme awakening. MT_4,22.42 //
Thus ends the twenty-second canto in the Section on Stability within the *Mokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! Furthermore, he describes the majesty of the discerning one alone:
"He who rests upon the supreme state, established like the whirling of a wheel, is not defiled even while exercising sovereignty over the city of the body. (MU 4.23.1)

The "supreme state" (*uttama-pada*) is the most excellent station known as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). One who "takes hold" of this is called an "upholder of the supreme state. Being "established like the whirling of a wheel" means being situated everywhere; that is to say, remaining in activity without any mental connection (*niranusandhāna*). Such a person is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Even while exercising sovereignty in the city of the body, he is not defiled; he is not seized by the pleasures and pains arising from that [body]. Thus it is said.
The meaning is this: even a king, relying on the highest station, wanders everywhere throughout the city while exercising his sovereignty.
For one who knows that, this great city of his own body—resembling a pleasure grove—is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; it leads only to happiness, not to suffering.
It is for happiness alone, because it is the means for attaining the bliss that is ultimate liberation; it is not for suffering, because there is no taint of suffering [in it].
In this regard, Śrī Rāma asks:
"O great sage, how indeed does the cityhood of the body come to be? And how is it that a yogi dwelling within this [body] becomes solely a partaker of the happiness of sovereignty?"
This is clear.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha spoke this reply:
"O Rāma, this city of the body is delightful and endowed with all virtues; for the wise man, it is rich in infinite diversions and illuminated by the sun of self-perception."
One's own light is the self-luminous; that itself is the sun. By it—through the medium of reflective awareness—that [object] is illuminated, brought into manifestation toward oneself.

He describes her possession of all excellent qualities: "The interior of whose world is illuminated by the light from the windows of her eyes; whose shanks are reached by the expansion of the main street of her hands."

The windows are the eyes; the radiance or light of those two makes the interiors of the worlds visible—that city in which the spaces between the worlds are thus revealed. Even in a city, the interiors of the worlds become visible through windows constructed at the city gates. The two gate-towers are the hands; by means of them, the feet are reached, which are like the lower legs (*upajaṅghala*).
That [city] which has regions near the forest is called *upajaṅgala*; such cities have a main street (*pratolī*) extending as far as that [forest].
Her line of body hair was like a creeping vine, her skin was garlanded with watchtowers, and the circles of her calves and thighs were as sturdy pillars resting upon her ankles like guggulu resin.
The skin itself is the watchtower and the rampart; by it she is adorned. Guggulu is the stone that serves as the foundation for the pillars.
Its feet are divided by lines like formidable stones first fashioned [by a craftsman]; it is delightful, with its boundaries defined by the skin, vital points, sinews, marrow, and joints.
Those two parts divided by the two lines are the two feet, which are indeed formidable stones (*ugraśile*). Of these two, she was fashioned first;

for at the time of the first creation, stones that have been partitioned are established. She is one whose joints and boundaries (*sandhisīmā*)—that is, the limits of the joints—are composed solely of a mass of skin, vital points, and veins (*carmamarmasirāsāra*).
With the opening of her vulva fashioned from the panels at the front of her two thighs, she was covered by a veil of shimmering tresses like a covering of lotus petals.
The two thighs themselves are the door-panels; from their tips she was fashioned, provided with the construction of the door-panels.

The private parts themselves are the exit, the location of the doorway, which she possesses. She is covered by that very shimmering mass of hair, which serves as a covering made of glass-like material. //MT_4,23.8//
Adorned by a garden-like face with its beautiful shadows of eyebrows, forehead, and mouth, her expansive cheeks were strewn with the blue lotuses of her glances.
That face, which possesses a beautiful luster through its eyebrows, forehead, and mouth, is itself the garden; she is adorned by it.
The lake of her chest has the bud-like breasts fixed within it, and the mountain for her playful sport is her shoulders covered by the dense line of body hair.
And she was covered with thick rows of hair, and her shoulders were like playful mountain peaks.
With her bowl of desired food cast into the cavity of her belly, she makes a sound through the agitation of wind expelled from the hollow of her long throat.

In the cavity of the belly, that is, in the pit of the stomach; by those excellent foods, meaning fine meals, used as a pretext. She is one who possesses bowls of desired delicacies—that is, broken vessels containing desired food. Even in royal cities, there are vessels for desired delicacies. In that long throat-passage, it is emitted and moves about.
Whatever wind there is, by its agitation, it is made to sound—that is, endowed with sound; even in a city, the sound of wind occurs within the cavities.
Adorned with whatever objects are obtained as determined by the marketplace of the heart, the city of the vital breath flows incessantly through its nine gates.

The heart itself is the marketplace, and [the city] is seated upon it as its stall. It is adorned by those objects which have been determined—that is, resolved—to be worthy of acceptance, and which are objects encountered according to their natural course, arriving through the flow of one's own experience. For even in the marketplaces of a city, objects are determined [to be of value].
Her mouth is a gaping chasm filled with fragments of bone from visible teeth; her tongue, flickering like a firebrand, wanders within that cavernous mouth as she devours her food.
Even in the city, fragments of bone are cast away by meat-eaters into the pits; *cilla* is a particular kind of bird.
The hollows of her ear-cavities were covered by a mass of hairy grass; the edges of her buttocks were bound with chains, and her back was a vast wilderness.
Her buttocks were like chains; with them, her sides were curved and beautiful. She was one whose back was like a vast wilderness (*jaṅgala*).
Even in cities, chains are placed at the junctions of the wilderness for the purpose of restraining thieves and the like.
The mud of endless [defilements] has been drawn out from within the waterwheel of the anus; the noble lady of self-reflection now sports in the garden-ground of the mind.

"With the water-wheel severed" means with the mechanism of the water-wheel broken. By that [action], "from within"—that is, from the interior region—"the endless mud was extracted," meaning the mud in the form of excrement was removed from her. They even remove the mud from a city. Regarding the phrase "the garden of the mind": for in the mind of the wise, only self-reflection vibrates day and night.
The restless monkey of the sense-faculties is firmly bound by the rope of wisdom; she is delightful with the blossoming flowers of laughter in the garden of her face.
For the wise man binds his flickering senses with the rope of discernment; and it is indeed fitting that flowers bloom in a garden.
For the knower, his own body-city is the most beautiful of all auspicious things; it leads only to happiness and not to suffering, and to the highest benefit.
The city of one's own body possesses all the qualities of the cities previously described; it is one's own bodily city for the sake of the supreme benefit, which means for the sake of liberation.
Is this [pleasure] a giver of happiness for the ignorant, or not? To this he replies:
For the ignorant, this is a collection of coffers containing endless sufferings; but for the wise, it is a collection of coffers containing endless happinesses.

*Kośamālikā* means a garland of storehouses; the meaning is that it produces endless suffering. The sense is that for one who does not know the pure reality (*śuddhatattva*), this [body] causes them to experience torment day and night. Now, one might object: "In that case, would such a thing not be the same even for a knower? To this he says: "But for the knower" (*jñasya tu*). The word *tu* indicates a distinction. This refers to one who has known the reality of the pure self (*śuddhātmatattva*).
This is because he does not partake in suffering for that purpose; the point is that one person does not become a partaker of suffering on account of another's purpose.
"Is it not then the case that this [ignorance] will cause suffering to the knower at the time of its destruction? To this he replies:

"O subduer of enemies, when this has been destroyed, nothing of the knower is destroyed; when it remains, everything remains established for him. Therefore, this [ignorance] brings happiness to the knower. (MU 4.23.19)

The intended meaning is that its essential nature consists solely of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), distinct from this [phenomenal world]. Now, one might object: "In that case, even during the period of worldly existence (*sthiti*), there would be no purpose for her [the *vidyā*]. To this he says: "While she remains" (*sthitāyām*). The meaning is that everything is well-established, because she accomplishes all tasks conducive to liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*).
He provides the conclusion: "Therefore, by her... (*teneyam*) [MT 4.23.19].
"Now, has it not been stated by some that this [body] is also a chariot? To this he replies:

"Because the Knower, having mounted it, traverses the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) sufficiently for the sake of all enjoyments and liberation, therefore this is remembered as the 'chariot of the Knower'."
This city of the body.
Since sound, form, taste, touch, smell, kinsmen, and prosperity are indeed obtained through this very [wisdom], it is therefore the bestower of gain for the wise man.

If it is asked, "What gain does the knower have through the acquisition of sound and other objects?"—it is not so; for there exists the acquisition consisting of the knowledge that gathers the powers of the reality of the Supreme Self by means of sound and the rest.
O Rāma, when this [intellect] itself bears the web of the activities of pleasure and pain, then it is capable of supporting the weight of all things everywhere.
This is the city of the body; for the knower perceives pleasure and so forth as belonging to the body alone, not to himself.
For in that city of the body, the Knower, free from delusion and devoid of agitation, dwells while exercising sovereignty, just as Indra does in his own city.
Free from delusion regarding this, I am devoid of egoistic conceit; free from agitation, I am undisturbed.
He does not let the wild horse of the mind gallop toward the hollows of arrogance; he does not surrender the daughter of wisdom to the twin forms of greed.

In the hollow of the swelling pit that is the form of sense-objects, amidst the grand display of the abyss, there exists that which is called greed, whose nature is dualistic. To that [greed], he does not give his daughter Prajñā (Wisdom). He does not allow Wisdom to be swallowed by greed;
thus, he perceives no vulnerability in the enemy kingdom of ignorance. He cuts away the very roots of the fear of the enemy that is saṃsāra.

Ignorance itself is the foreign kingdom; by metaphorical extension, it is the king who has become an enemy. He does not perceive it—not to mention the possibility of entering it. This king of ignorance does not perceive his own vulnerability (*randhra*), for he is utterly defeated. (The particle *tu* has the sense of *eva*). He does not perceive it because he has been conquered.
In this world, which is a cycle driven by the essence of craving and seized by the turbulence of desire, they do not sink into the gambling match of the senses where pleasure and pain are overturned.

In that [place] where there is a reversal and turning back of the essence of craving; which is difficult to grasp due to the agitation of desire; wherein the two dice of pleasure and pain—pleasure and pain themselves being the dice—are cast and impelled; therein they do not sink. For indeed, for a king, sinking in gambling is a fault.
Even gambling with dice is surely enveloped by craving and desire.

Moving according to the course of his desires, he incessantly performs ablutions at the confluences of rivers and sacred bathing places, both externally and internally, moment by moment, in due succession.

"Externally" means in the external world; "internally" means in the mind. Because the mind itself is under one's own control, it is the chariot. He whose movement is by means of that [chariot] is [the one described]. Internal bathing, however, should be understood as nothing other than immersion in the cavity of consciousness (ciddhrada).
Unseen by all the people of the city and turning his back on the spectacles of the town, he dwells perpetually in happiness within the inner apartments under the name of meditation.

The king, invisible to all people, remains wandering within the city—both the body and the town—while turning his back on the sight of the city; and here, "meditation" (dhyāna) should be understood as the reflective awareness of the reality that is one's own self, consisting of pure consciousness alone.
This divine city, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation, brings constant happiness to those whose souls are ever-joyful, just like Amarāvatī belongs to Śakra.
The word "of the knower" (jñasya) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
Everything remains stable through that which is stable; nothing is destroyed by that which is destroyed. How could that city of the king not bring happiness?
This is clear.
When the city of the body has perished, nothing at all is lost for the wise man, just as when a jar is destroyed, the space contained within it suffers no loss.
This is clear.
Just as the wind touches an existing jar but not one that is no longer present, so too does the embodied soul touch this city of its own body.
That which is not abiding is destroyed. One who knows that is a knower of reality, perceiving the self as distinct from the body.
Abiding here, this Blessed Lord, the Self, although omnipresent, having experienced the state of being a person created by its own conceptual constructions, has attained the vision of the Self.
Even while acting, he does not act, for though fully intent upon all activities, he sometimes presides over all the matters at hand as if they were not his own.

"Abiding here" means abiding in the body. The word "api" (even/also) indicates the contradiction between [the Self] being omnipresent and [the body] experiencing masculinity. "One who has attained the vision of the Self" refers to the knower of that [Self], not a fool, because such a state is impossible for a fool. "Acting" means acting through the medium of the body and so forth. "Not acting" is due to the conviction, "I am not the doer. "Objects of action" refers to purposes that ought to be performed. He "presides over" them.
He determines them as things to be performed; that is, those that are relevant and have come forth in the natural flow [of the ritual], and not those imagined through one's own deliberation.
Now, one might ask: "If he performs this at some time, what does he do at other times? To this he replies:
"At times, his pure mind, desiring to wander, ascends a lovely, unobstructed, and swaying celestial chariot as if in sport. (MU 4.23.35)

Sometimes that knower of reality, by means of his own playful power (*līlā*), ascends a mental celestial chariot—a vehicle in the form of the mind. For what purpose? To sport—that is, to engage in internal recreation. Of what nature is this mental celestial chariot? It is "unwavering," meaning free from flickering instability. Furthermore, of what nature is it? It is one whose "movement" is "unstruck," meaning unimpeded in any direction. [The word *tam* (it) refers back to] that [chariot], in relation to the term "celestial chariot."
Masculinity; stainless, meaning free from the impurities of passion and so forth; for this very reason, it is lovely.
Now, one might ask: "What does he do there? To this, it is said:
"Abiding there, he constantly delights with Lokasundarī, whose limbs are ever cool, through loving-kindness (maitrī) which is eternally established in his heart. (MU 4.23.36)

He, the knower of that [reality], remaining there in his mental vehicle, sports with Lokasundarī, who is beloved by the world, who eternally dwells within his heart, and who is a woman named Maitrī whose limbs are perpetually cool. The sense is that at times, being inward-turned,
he becomes composed entirely of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

Not only does loving-kindness alone serve as his beloved, but he has two others as well; thus it is said: "Two beloveds stand at his sides—Truth and Solitude—like the two stars Viśākhā beside the moon, gladdening his heart. (MU 4.23.37)
This is clear.
The knower beholds all these worlds, torn asunder by the saw of suffering, like one seated on a pedestal looking at anthills, or like the sun looking down from behind.
In what state were the worlds? They were torn apart and tormented by the saw that is suffering itself. "Ant-hills" refers to ants; the meaning is that they had climbed from one ant-hill to another.
Having long fulfilled all hopes and being beautiful with every excellence, he shines like the full-orbed moon, never again to suffer eclipse.
He is beautiful through every prosperity and every perfection.
Even when indulging in a flood of enjoyments, no weariness arises in him; rather, the *kālakūṭa* poison shines upon the neck of one who has conquered the afflictions.
The meaning is that it leads to exhaustion by way of destruction.
But how is it that this [enjoyment] does not lead to distress for him? To this he replies:
"For when enjoyment is consumed after full understanding, it leads to contentment; and a thief, once recognized and reassured, becomes a friend rather than an enemy. (MU 4.23.41)

The meaning is: having fully understood, correctly ascertained, and known [enjoyment] as being of the nature of the self (*ātmarūpatva*). For when enjoyment is known as being of the nature of the self, it does not cause distress even when lost, because it remains as the very nature of one's own self. Furthermore, the destruction of the self is not logical, because even in the event of destruction, it remains as the witness (*sākṣin*) to that destruction.
In the midst of the tumultuous fray of the throngs of men and women acting as dancers, the wise man beholds the beautiful splendor of enjoyment as if it were a theatrical performance moving far away.
Even another skilled person, during a quarrel among a multitude of actors, goes far away; he neither witnesses the procession nor the drama that has begun.
Just as travelers on a road observe a village festival that has arrived unexpectedly, so too do the ignorant observe the activity consisting of worldly transactions.
The meaning is that he gazes without any further mental engagement (*niranusandhāna*).
Just as the eye falls effortlessly upon objects within its range before it, so too does the intellect of the wise man fall toward its objects with complete detachment.

Just as the eye, free from passion—that is, devoid of attachment—falls upon objects in the various directions that present themselves without effort, so too does the intellect of the steadfast one—the cognition of the knower of reality—fall upon its tasks. The sense is that he performs his duties entirely free from passion.
The senses never take away an object that has been attained, nor do they give it away once attained; thus, the complete knower remains established [in his state].
For this indeed is perfection: the grasping of what has been attained and the non-desiring of what has not been attained.
Those who have not attained [the goal] do not conceive of the right thought, nor do those who have already attained it maintain equanimity; they are as fickle as peacock feathers striking a mountain.
They do not conceptualize, nor do they cause agitation.
With all doubt completely stilled and all curiosity dissolved, the wise one, whose web of conceptual constructions has been utterly exhausted, shines like a sovereign emperor.
This is clear.
Not contained within itself, it expands by its own self within itself; like the ocean of milk, the Self-possessed one is full to its furthest limits and boundless.

He does not measure [anything], for, being filled with bliss, he expands within himself by means of his own self; the sense is that he perceives no other whatsoever within. He is both complete and without limit—complete and limitless—and thus, with a mind that is not deranged and being tranquil, he laughs at miserable creatures who are wretched in their desire for enjoyment and whose senses are debased, as if they were madmen.
The intended meaning is: "What need is there to speak of attachment to that?"
Just as one who desires another’s wife is ridiculed by others, so too is the one who desires sense-objects ridiculed by the wise.

Just as another person laughs— that is, performs a derisive joke— at a man who desires a wife belonging to someone else, meaning one who desires a wife for the sake of another; in that very same way, the wise laugh at the ignorant person who desires the enjoyment of the sense faculties.
One should bring under control with discernment the mind that abandons its own equanimity and happiness and flees toward sense objects, just as one subdues a great elephant with a goad.
Equanimity is one's own happiness, known as equanimity, which is the bliss of the Self; [it is attained] through reflection in the form: "What essence is there in these enjoyments?"
That mental tendency toward which an inclination for enjoyments is granted must be destroyed at the very outset, just like the sprouting of a poison's seed.
That is the mental activity; "at first" means prior to its being set forth. The intention of the word "api" (also/even) is to suggest: "What need is there to speak of that which is not even given?"
"Is there not a result in bestowing favor after one has first been struck? To this he replies:
"For even the honor shown later to one who has been beaten is infinite; even a meager watering acts like nectar for a rice plant scorched by the summer heat."
"Honor" means respect; that is to say, the act of bestowing [it] abundantly.
Now, one might ask: "How is this so? To this he replies:
"For honor and great respect are not perceived by one who is not in need; the flood of the rainy season shines but slightly upon rivers that are already full. (MU 4.23.54)

For because [of this], respect—that is, high esteem—is not perceived or known by one who is unafflicted, meaning one who has not experienced suffering. He supports this point with an illustration: "of the full ones. The flood of the rains over rivers that are already full is but a small trickle;
it does not shine forth, meaning it lacks the quality of gladdening the minds of people. For it is the minds of people that [are gladdened] by rivers that are diminished.
One becomes joyful upon seeing the rising flood of the rainy season.
Even when full and having been benefited, one still desires more; even though it has filled the world, the single ocean takes up all the water.
He is joined with the filling of the world—"he" (saḥ) is the understood subject.

When the mind has been restrained, that subsequent embellishment of its state is highly esteemed because it marks the attainment of what was previously unattained and the expansion of what was already gained.

*Ābhāgamaṇḍanā* means filling with a small portion. *Tām eva* means that very same *ābhāgamaṇḍanā*. *Alabdhavistāraś cāsau labdhaś ca* means "that which was not previously obtained has now been obtained" (*alabdhavistāralabdha*). Its state is its essence (*tattva*); therefore [it is so called]. For one who has not yet attained expansion (*alabdhavistāraḥ*), even what is obtained is considered much. (MT 4.23.56)
A king who is bound and liberated is satisfied with even a single village; but one who is neither bound by others nor oppressed is not satisfied even with a kingdom.
First bound and later liberated is "bound-and-liberated. The sense is that the mind, once thus restrained, finds satisfaction even with a mere fragment of enjoyment.
Since the restraint of the mind is to be accomplished through the restraint of the senses, he speaks specifically of that restraint of the senses:
"Having crushed hand with hand and having ground tooth against tooth, as if trampling limb with limb, conquer your own enemies, the senses. (MU 4.23.58)
The meaning is that the senses, which have turned toward sense-objects, must be withdrawn by means of the power of right knowledge.
