By men who are eager for victory and desirous of rising above others, the sense-faculties must first be thoroughly understood as enemies of the heart.

"Another" refers to one in the form of a king and so forth. "By those desiring to manifest," that is, by those wishing to rise to power; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "they should be known as enemies. Furthermore, the enmity of the sense faculties toward the heart should be understood as their tendency to draw one toward sensory enjoyments.
He offers praise to those who have conquered their minds:
"On this vast earth, rare indeed are those fortunate men of virtuous intent who are counted among the talk of men for having not been conquered by their own minds."
This is clear.
He expresses this very same point with the final verse of the chapter:

"I salute that Arindama, by whom the serpent of the mind—having made its lair in the cavity of the heart and possessing the virulent poison of conceptual constructions—has been brought to a state of total pacification."
The meaning is that he alone is the most excellent. Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the twenty-third canto in the Section on Stability (*sthitiprakaraṇa*) within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

"Now, what is the difficulty in conquering the senses? To this he replies: "The enemies that are the senses are indeed difficult to conquer; they are like the rutting elephants of the sovereign of the great hells, and they are bristling with the arrows and shafts of desire."
Those for whom only their own misdeeds serve as elephants, and whose very hopes serve as the shafts of arrows—such are they; even emperors are possessed of both elephants and arrows.
Those who destroy their own body, which is their first support, are ungrateful; they are the enemies of their own senses, difficult to conquer, and the great storehouse of evil deeds.
They destroy impossible enjoyments and cause one to exert effort toward them.
Having reached this abode of the body, the vultures of the senses—birds fierce in their judgment of what ought and ought not to be done—flit about out of greed for the bait of sense-objects.
Those for whom the two fierce wings are precisely what is to be done and what is not to be done; such are they.
Those rogues who have been caught in the net of the threads of discernment do not harm his limbs, just as one does not swallow a mouthful of stone.
They are vultures for their senses; for vultures do not seize a mouthful of stone.
Those who take delight in sense objects that are charming only at first sight fall into hells whose ends are utterly devoid of flavor.
This is an adjective qualifying "in the objects" (viṣayeṣu), meaning "those in which there is an absolute lack of flavor within."
In this city of the wretched body, one who possesses the wealth of discernment is not helplessly overcome by the enemies that are the senses dwelling within.
While this contemptible body is being experienced, for one who possesses strength is not overcome by enemies against his will.
Those who dwell in the formidable city made of clay are not as happy as those whose minds are self-dependent and who are masters of their own body-cities.
The kings of the outer cities who dwell in formidable earthen fortresses possess self-subdued minds; this is the reason expressed by way of the qualifying attribute.
For one who has brought his senses under control as servants and well subdued the enemy that is the mind, the insights of a Buddha flourish like blossoming flower-clusters in spring.
The intellects of the Buddhas, the knowers; the intellects of the Buddhas—thus, "buddhabuddhayaḥ."
For one whose mental pride has been destroyed and who has subdued the enemies that are the senses, the latent impressions of enjoyment wither away like lotus ponds in winter.
The latent impressions of enjoyment are the residual traces of enjoyment.
As long as the mind has not been conquered through firm practice on the single reality, so long do latent tendencies dance about in the heart like Vetālas at night.
The sense is that when the mind has been conquered, they do not leap about. "The single reality" refers to the reality of pure consciousness alone, which is all-pervading.

I consider the mind of the discerning person to be a servant, because it performs what is desired; a minister, because it accomplishes what is beneficial; and a vassal, because its own senses are under its control. (MU 4.24.11)
The vassal was appointed to the conquest of Śatruñjaya.
I consider the mind of the wise to be a tender woman because of its fondness for caressing, a purifying father because of its protection, and a supreme friend because of its trustworthiness.
From *lālanāt* means from the state of being one who caresses; *snigdhalalanā* refers to a woman (*lalanā*) who is both affectionate (*sneha-yuktā*) and beautiful.

Having personally observed it through the vision of the scriptures, well-pondered, and earnestly entreated for it, the father of the mind bestows supreme accomplishment, having surrendered his own self.
"Properly entreated" means requested. "Having sacrificed oneself" means having destroyed oneself; for the mind accomplishes what is beneficial only by destroying its own self.
Even a father brings about the welfare of his son by sacrificing his own life; thus, he serves as a point of comparison.
Well-polished, well-wiped, well-held, and well-awakened, this jewel of the mind, endowed with excellent qualities and dear to the heart, shines within the heart.
In the case of a jewel, it is one that has been personally recognized and thoroughly examined; it is strung together on all sides with excellent, praiseworthy qualities—both virtues and threads.
This director of the mind ordains for the doer of auspicious deeds those actions which serve as axes for the tree of rebirth and which result in future prosperity.
The *udarka* is that which results in a subsequent fruit; those [actions] for which there is such an *udaya* (arising) belong to a person of virtuous karma, one who performs virtuous deeds.
He states the result:
"O Rāma, having thus washed the jewel of the mind, which is stained by much mud, with the water of discernment for the sake of perfection, become possessed of light."

"For the sake of accomplishment" means for the sake of accomplishment known as the attainment of the reality of the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness. "Possessing light" means possessing illumination; even a washer of jewels possesses light while in the dark, because the radiance of the gem is present.
Even though you are expanded by discernment, do not fall helplessly like an ordinary person into the terrifying stages of existence, which are filled with calamities.

"In the terrifying and fear-inducing [states], do not fall, do not go. The word "even" (*api*) is used to indicate that one should not go even if one possesses discernment (*viveka*), based on the conviction: "Even if I go, what will be achieved for me? The term "ordinary person" (*prākṛta*) means one devoid of discernment.
The implication is that in the event of falling, you too would no longer possess discernment.
Do not disregard this mist of great delusion—this illusory cycle of existence that has arisen, crowded with hundreds of calamities.
Do not disregard me; do not make me an object of contempt by thinking, "What can she possibly do?"
Resorting to supreme solitude and perceiving the truth with your intellect, having thoroughly conquered the enemies that are the senses, cross over the ocean of worldly existence.
It should be understood that even with respect to the two qualifiers, they function as the reason.
There, Indra was conquered by infinite Daityas made of jeweled machines; there, garden pavilions were constructed from the flames of fire that was as cold as snow.
He by whom Vāsava was conquered by those infinite Daityas who were composed of jeweled machines, manifested through illusion, and possessed the very nature of jeweled machines.

He surpassed the sandalwood trees of the Nandana grove with his gardens blooming in all seasons; he surpassed the sandalwood of the Malaya mountains, whose serpents had been carried off by illusory snakes.
He is the one for whom the sandalwood trees of the Malaya mountain have their predatory snakes removed by illusory serpents and whose natural snakes have been driven far away.

The splendor of his inner apartments was eclipsed by the loveliness of women made of gold; there, the Lord, having struck down the wielders of the discus and mace for the sake of playful competition, sported.

He whose inner apartments were eclipsed—that is, surpassed—in beauty by the world of golden women manifested through his illusory power (*māyā*); he by whom the wielder of the discus and mace, Viṣṇu, was struck down by Īśāna (Mahārudra) during a rivalry for the sake of sport; he who was that [Lord]. *Note:* *Māyodbhāvitena* means "manifested by illusion"; *lāvaṇyena jihmitāḥ* means "eclipsed by beauty"; *krīḍārthaspardhā* means "rivalry for the purpose of play"; *īśānena* refers to Mahārudra; *hataḥ* means "struck down. The compound *cakragadādharaḥ* refers to Viṣṇu. The final *saḥ* identifies the subject. The commentary (*MT*) provides the specific context of the rivalry with Śiva.
The sky of his own city was enriched by stars that were masses of jewels flying up incessantly, while its courtyards were knee-deep with an abundance of various flowers.
This is clear.
During the nights, he was like a hundred moons for the entire expanse of Pātāla, while the excellence of his virtues was sung in songs by the gazes of the *sālabhañjikā* statues.
This is clear.
The lordly elephant of the gods was put to flight by the illusory Airāvaṇa, and the interior of his harem was filled with the excellence of the splendors of the three worlds.
This is clear.
Possessed of all prosperity and endowed with all sovereignty, his supreme commands were honored by all the Daitya vassals.
This is clear.
The assembly of asuras rested in the shade of his great forest-like arms; he was adorned with earrings made of the finest jewels from the depths of all the oceans.
All the oceans are indeed caves; the essences of those [oceans] are the jewels; their earrings are [those jewels]; he is adorned by them.
That Asura, who had destroyed the gods and possessed a harsh and terrifying form, came to have a vast army that brought about the destruction of the deities.
Of him by whom the gods have been eradicated—that is, brought to exhaustion.
While that Māyābala was asleep and had likewise departed for another land, the gods, having found a vulnerability, entered his army.
Having found an opening—a gap or an opportunity—in the midst of that army of Śambara; the sense is that otherwise they would not have possessed such power.
Then, for the sake of protection, the Daitya Śambara appointed Dudrika, Havadruma, and others as his own vassals within his armies.
"Appointed" means impelled.
Having reached them as well, the leaders of the gods struck them down, like hawks moving through the sky attacking agitated sparrows.
Having found an opening and gained an opportunity, they also struck those others, such as Dudrika, Hradadruma, and the rest; that is, they killed them.
Furthermore, the best of the asuras appointed other generals, who were impetuous and possessed of a fierce roar, like the waves of the ocean.
This is clear.
The gods quickly struck them down as well; therefore, filled with wrath, he went to the celestial realm (*triviṣṭapa*) in its entirety in order to destroy the immortals.
Fully complete and accompanied by a great army.
There, terrified by his illusory power, those gods vanished, like deer into the groves of Meru’s forest at the sight of the teacher of Gaurī.
The word "in the groves" (kuñjeṣu) should be extracted and connected with the phrase "of the teacher of Gaurī" (gaurīguroḥ).
He beheld heaven empty, like a world exhausted at the end of an eon, with the hosts of minor gods wailing and the faces of the goddesses drenched in tears.
He is Śambara.
Having stayed there in anger, Śambara took what he had obtained, burned the cities of the world-protectors, and went to his own abode.
The collection of jewels has been obtained and placed in his hand.
When hatred had thus become more intense between the Dānavas and the gods, the gods abandoned heaven and vanished from sight in all directions.
In hatred and enmity.
Then, whatever army commanders were appointed with great effort by the Daitya Śambara, those very ones the gods, intent on their own exertion, slew.
This is clear.
Then Śambara, overcome with agitation and filled with intense rage, blazed like a straw fire fanned by the wind, gasping for breath.
Who was it that blazed forth? Like a fire produced from grass (*tārṇa*), meaning just as such a fire blazes toward the wind, so did he. This is the sense.
Then, even after searching throughout the three worlds, he did not find the gods, despite his supreme effort, just as an evildoer cannot find his own good deeds.
This is clear.
By means of his illusory power (*māyā*), he created three terrible and exceedingly powerful Asuras, who arose for the sake of protecting his strength like Time itself embodied in form.
The times and the restraints.
Created by magic, those terrifying beings with arms like wish-fulfilling trees arose, possessing massive bodies like mountains shaken by their own wings.
They rose up; they emerged.
Marked by the names Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, they are each the sole agent of whatever occurs to them, possessing the nature of mere consciousness.
The meaning is that they act as independent agents according to what has been obtained for them, being devoid of any underlying intentionality.
He specifies those very [beings] as follows:

"Because of the absence of karmas, they are devoid of the latent impressions (vāsanā) of previous [lives]; their sole activity is the vibration of pure consciousness alone, free from conceptual construction."

And those three were of what nature? They were "without latent impressions" (*avāsanā*), meaning devoid of *vāsanās*, because their previous karmas had ceased due to their having arisen immediately [in that state]. Furthermore, of what nature were they? They possessed a single action (*karma*) whose form was the vibration (*parispanda*) of that pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) which is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), i.e., free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*); thus they were characterized by non-conceptual activity.
This is the meaning.
Bearing within them a slender portion of the seed of karma called "thinking"—unfertilized and artificial—they have come into manifestation.

Furthermore, of what nature were they? They possessed a subtle, minute, and artificial (kṛtrimā) mental faculty (kalā) called "reflection" (manana), which had become the seed of karma. Having taken up that mental faculty called reflection, they attained manifestation (udaya). The sense is that otherwise, there would be no emergence of Brahmā.
For there, those soldiers, having cast off their latent dispositions (*vāsanā*), follow the activity at hand by tradition, like the coincidence of the crow and the palm fruit.
Successively, by way of mutual dependence; but not by having reflected upon the purpose.

Just as children who are half-asleep move only their own limbs, so too are those [liberated ones], for they are indeed devoid of both latent impressions (vāsanā) and the conceit of selfhood (ātmābhimāna).
Latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*); by means of these two.
They know neither retreat nor flight, neither life nor death, neither battle, victory, nor defeat.
*Abhipāta* is a falling toward [something]; *āpāta* is the act of rushing toward it.
Seeing only the soldiers before them intent on striking, those who had crushed mountains with their blows struck down their enemies in battle.
Those who have become enemies.
Śambara, his mind fully satisfied, thought within the city: "My army, well protected by the illusory asuras, will surely be victorious."

"What was he thinking? To this he replied: "He thought, 'They will be victorious. The *māyāsurās* are those asuras produced through illusion; by them my army is well protected. Indeed (*hi*), it will be victorious—it shall attain victory.
For these [beings] are utterly abandoned by desirable and undesirable latent impressions (*vāsanās*); therefore, they do not fear in battle, nor do they flee, for they are not [bound by] stability."
The meaning is that one who is indeed possessed of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the desirable and the undesirable fears and flees upon perceiving an enemy to be powerful.
Since these do not flee even when struck by the gods, this army of mine is now established as exceedingly powerful.
"Established in distinction" means firmly established.
He concludes Śambara’s reflection with a verse at the end of the canto:

"My army, protected by the tree-like arms of the exceedingly powerful Asuras, will attain great stability, just as the golden ground of the mountain of the immortals remains firm even when struck by the tusks of the elephants of the gods."
Of Sumeru, the mountain of the immortals; the golden earth is the land of gold. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having thus resolved,
the lord of the Daityas concluded his deliberations and dispatched an army, accompanied by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, to the surface of the earth to destroy the gods.
This is clear.
The Daityas rose up from the groves of the ocean, from the mountain caves, and from the divine mountain, with terrifying roars, like winged mountains in flight.
They rose up; they were winged, that is, possessed of wings. Those which were mountains—by their playful movement.
Urged on by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, the Dānavas filled the hollow of the two worlds, which had the sun struck down by the blows of their hands.
Impelled by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; impelled by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Then, from the groves and the caves of the divine mountain, the hosts of celestial dwellers arose, agitated like at the end of a cosmic dissolution, as if terrified.
They were agitated on all sides, thoroughly shaken, [by] the gods dwelling in heaven.
Then that battle between those two, who bore the banners of the gods and the asuras, took place within the world, terrifying like an untimely and violent dissolution of the eon.
That is well-known.
Their heads fell from the sky like mountains with the sun and moon overturned at the time of universal dissolution; their earrings emitted such brilliance that they swallowed the darkness below.

At the time of dissolution, those mountains together with the moon and sun, which had been cast down and driven by the wind, fell likewise from the sky—that is, from the atmosphere—down to the earth. Of what nature were these heads? They were such that the darkness was swallowed by the brilliance vomited forth or emitted by their earrings. Such were they.
Resounding with the lion-roars emitted by the warriors, they reeled like mountains filled with the winds of cosmic dissolution, as if laughing aloud.
Even those possessed by the Aṭṭahāsa [demon] reel about.
The slopes of the great boundary mountains shone, their movements pained by the falling of weapons that were like blows from a thunderbolt, while the circles of lions wandered about in fear.

The slopes of the principal mountain ranges shone. Of what nature were they? They were like the rocks belonging to themselves (the mountains). Those [rocks] were like the weapons; by their falling, the livelihood—the very existence—of those [beasts] was afflicted and miserable.
Furthermore, of what nature were they? They were such that their herds of lions were terrified and consequently bewildered.
They.
From the weapons struck down by their mutual blows, wandering sparks of fire arose like stars scattered at the end of a kalpa.
This is clear.
Upon the shores of that single ocean filled with floods of blood and flesh, there were Vetālas as tall as *kalpa*-tree trunks, striking their cymbals with loud claps.
They sported; they were gleaming. Vetālas are a specific class of spirits. Tāratālinaḥ refers to those accompanied by loud musical instruments.
In the sky, where the clouds of dust were stilled by showers of gushing blood, the tips of the earrings from heads shattered and crushed by weapons lay scattered.
Of the warriors struck down by weapons, those crest-jewels and earrings which were crushed and fell—ten millions of them shone in the sky; this is how they are connected with the preceding verse.

The quarters of space became devoid of any gaps, filled by the Daityas—who possessed arms like the wish-fulfilling trees of a kalpa and forms resembling the sun—as they crushed the great lords of mountains with their blows.
Without gaps, they are dense.
With their walls brought down by the impact of the mass of blazing missiles, the mountains turned into a shower of fragments, as if enveloped by the fire at the end of an aeon.
Enveloped by the fire of the eon, they are whirled about by the fire of the eon.
The gods gathered their splendor, like fires kindled by the horse-sacrifice; they pursued those Asuras, just as winds chase the clouds.
This is clear.
Then, having attacked them, the gods seized those [demons] like cats seizing old mice; the gods and asuras shone in heaven like mountains with blossoming forests swaying in the wind.
The connection is: "The gods seized those asuras. *Otavaḥ* means cats.
They filled one another and the ten directions with showers of weapons, just as the winds fill the forests of Mount Sumeru with clusters of blossoms.
This is clear.
A terrible battle took place between the armies of the gods and the dānavas, like that of two great swarms of gnats within the hollow of the universe, which is like the interior of an udumbara fruit.

"In the very fissure of the earth" means in the fissure between heaven and earth; "within the udumbara fruit" means in the middle of the udumbara fruit. There, within two great swarms of mosquitoes—that is, within two great multitudes of mosquitoes—[they dwell], for indeed mosquitoes exist within the udumbara fruit.
Then, with the circles of world-protectors leaping up in exultation, the terrible roar of battle arose, filling the sky like the clouds at the end of an aeon.
With uplifted hands in gestures of joy, like clouds at the end of an aeon, he rose up.
He describes the roar of the battle in detail by way of a summary:
it was like a paved courtyard on the surface of the earth [spread] across the sky; graspable with the fist, it was as thick and heavy as the belly of a massive, slow-moving cloud.

In what manner was the roar of battle? It was graspable by the fist through its massification in the sky. Like what? Like a paved floor (*kuṭṭima*). Just as a paved floor on the surface of the earth becomes graspable by the fist through its massification, so it was;
such is the meaning.

The slopes resounded with the clashing of weapons and rocks crushed at the initial impact; it was filled with the gurgling of harsh lamentations from those whose hearts were shattered and their spirits destroyed.

It is that mountain whose banks resound with the cries of those who, at the very first impact, were crushed by the rocks that had become weapons; it is grating, being filled with the harsh wailing of those lifeless ones who, devoid of fortitude, have their hearts bursting.
It is nourished by the roar of the clouds of the cosmic dissolution rising as a single perception; it resembles molten gold produced by the friction of the twelve suns.

At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), during the period of universal destruction, there is a roaring sound like that of the clouds at the end of an aeon (*kalpa*); he whose swelling is like that [sound] is [described]. His resemblance is to the gold that flows from the collision—the mutual clashing—at the end of an aeon of the twelve suns; the meaning is that he is equal to it by virtue of being an uninterrupted stream.
Having rebound from the impact against the wall of the cosmic egg and returned to the earth, the flood of the great stream fell into a pit like water struck by a dam.
Furthermore, of what nature was he? Having rebounded from the impact against the wall of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), he went to the earth. Like what? Like the flood of water from a great stream.
Just as that [flood], being struck by a dam, returns to its source—that is, its place of origin—so too did he; such is the meaning.
It possessed the forceful roar of the wind from the wings of the moving lord of mountains; it shattered the necks of the mountain lords as they flew up when their hard filling was breached.

He is one by whom the necks of the lords of mountains were clearly made to fly up through the filling [of the air] with hard, solid weapons— that sound of strength, a powerful noise produced by the wind from the wings of those great mountains that were moving along with their wings, and which was of that very nature.
Its waters resembled the agitation of the Milk Ocean when churned by Mount Mandara; its roar of echoes was like a thundering crash, and it provided a dwelling place for the creatures of the islands.

It is that which has portions or parts resembling the agitation of the Milk Ocean when stirred by Mount Mandara; it is that by which the continents and the lands of living beings are joined together and unified through the resonance of a humming sound in the form of an echo.
Between the two enraged armies there occurred a battle in which the Dānavas were uplifted, and in which cities, villages, mountains, forests, and men were crushed to pieces.
A battle took place between those two armies. In response to the expectation of how it was, he describes the battle in detail with the words beginning "exultant" (*uddhata*).

The quarters were filled with the mountain-like Dānavas cut down by hundreds of great weapons, while the interior of the sky was filled with the dust of mountains of weapons struck against one another.
That [palace] whose quarters were filled with those mountain-like Dānavas who had been shattered by hundreds of great weapons.
The hundreds of peaks of Mount Meru were shattered by the striking of his *bhuśuṇḍī* discus; the lotuses that were the Daityas, Devas, and Asuras were swept away by the wind of his arrows.
*Āsphoṭaḥ* means striking. Regarding *śarā*: lotuses are cut down by the wind.
The old grass of gods and demons was whirled about by hundreds of revolutions of the whirlpools, while the sky was enveloped by the surging waves of the flowing current of the army.

Of the *cakras*, which are specific types of weapons; their *āvartas* are their revolutions, and the hundreds of those [revolutions]—in them they were whirled, joined with the spinning of the wheels. Where the gods and demons themselves were like withered grass—that [place]. Of the surges of the flowing armies, the surges in the form of military arrays (*vyūha*); their *valanas* are their leaping movements. By those [movements], the sky was enveloped and filled.
Of which; that.
The multitude of celestial beings fell, crushed by the falling mountain of Hetya; the cities in the sky were flooded by the mass of ocean waters brought down by his hands.
It is said to be "overflowing" (plāvita).
We were carrying across hundreds of rivers of great missiles—swords, spears, and pikes—while the entire circle of the universe was rendered motionless by the violent crashing of mountain wings.

Those which have great weapons as their very wheels and whirlpools are "those possessing weapon-whirlpools. [The compound refers to] that [place] in which hundreds of rivers consisting of swords, spears, and javelins carry those weapon-whirlpools. *Āsphoṭa* is a striking accompanied by sound; by that, it is "numbed," meaning deprived of the capacity to hear sound.
The city of the world-protectors was being overwhelmed by the flood of blows from the heels of the Daityas, while the golden palace shrieked with the tumultuous cries of women.
"Halahalet" is an onomatopoeic imitation of sound.

The sky was washed with blood by the mountain-like bodies of demons rolling about, which resembled the waters of the intoxicated ocean tossed by mountains; meanwhile, the herds of cattle fled at the roar emitted by the warriors.

[The army] was fleeing, running away from that [battlefield] whose sky was stained with blood— that sky being washed by the mountain-like great waves of the intoxicated oceans tossed up by those very Daityas who were like mountains—
and from the herd of warriors who were rushing forward with a great roar, like the roar of lions, which had been let out by the soldiers.
That is to say, it is where there are multitudes of the wretched.

It was filled with the sun, though repeatedly shrouded by the clouds that are the many eyes of the world-protectors; and it was crowded with hosts of armies visible through the radiance of the gods and asuras.

Of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), that is, the lords of the world (*lokeśa*); those who are many-footed elephants—they themselves are the clouds (*ambhoda*). By them, "completely covered" (*channacchanna*) means excessively obscured. That which is Aryaman, the sun; by him it was accompanied. If so, then how were they seen there by one another? To this he says: "Furthermore" (*punar*). "Furthermore" (*punaḥ*) means in another sense: those splendors (*uddyota*) of the gods and asuras, which are the radiance of their bodies.
Having been made by them, that multitude of troops—that mass of soldiers—was agitated and overwhelmed by it.
It was terrifying with the loud clamor of the *paca-paca* sound of its wings as it flew back and forth over the mountain-like Dānava peaks that served as its points of comparison.
"Pacapaca" is an imitation of sound, as is "bhākkara."
The entire earth, oceans, and mountains were reddened with blood from the torrents flowing from the mountain-like fierce Daityas shattered by the mountain of weapons.
This is clear.
With its forests, villages, and mountain caves—the cities and kingdoms of which had been destroyed—it bore countless asuras, elephants, horses, men, chariots, and mountains.

Those kingdoms, cities, forests, and villages that were ruined and destroyed—their deep caverns, hollows, and central regions held within them countless asura-elephants, horses, men, chariots, and mountains;
[he] whose [chariot it was].
In the arena where iron arrows were scattered by the twanging of bowstrings, the elephant Airāvaṇa was crushed, its temples ground by the blows of fists.

Those iron arrows (*nārāca*) which are as swift as the sound of a lute (*sutālava*); by their row—that is, by being free from them—[the body] is devoid of them; [this refers to the body] of him who has *cāraṇas*, a particular class of gods. //MT_4,26.37//
It shattered mountains with torrents of rain like the clouds at the end of an aeon, and it pulverized the great boundary mountains, which were blown up by the impact of massive thunderbolts.
In this context, the "downpour" (āsāra) should be understood as consisting of stones.
The Danava was set ablaze by the masses of flames leaping from his provoked fire, yet he extinguished that fire by pouring out the ocean brought forth in a single hollowed palm.
It has been eradicated; it has been extinguished.
The great mass of water was solidified by the accumulation of lunar coldness and other elements; the mountain ranges were melted by the flames of the fire whose fuel was the dense forest thickets.
For by the cold, water becomes like stone; the meaning is that even mountains used to melt away in the forest.

It was a night of the end of the aeon, with darkness as difficult to dispel as that created by weapons; yet it was a vast canvas of darkness swallowed up by the radiance of a multitude of illusory suns.
This is clear.
It was raining down a shower of illusory fires like the falling rain at the end of an eon, with the friction and drawing forth of sparks, fire, wind, and masses of weapons.

That [place] where there is a raining down like the multitude of fires at the end of an eon with a rain of illusory fire; where there are fire and wind accompanied by the sound of *śīkāra*; where there is such a clashing of weapons; and where there is a dragging away of gods and asuras by means of that [clashing].

It arises from the weapon of the rain of vajras that shakes off the rain of mountains; it is rich in the battle of the weapons of sleep and awakening, and possesses the weapon of the restraint of rain.

That [battle] wherein there was the manifestation of weapons in the form of showers of stones, which were utterly dispersed by a shower of vajras; that battle enriched by "sleep-inducing" weapons (nidrābodhāstra)— namely, weapons that cause awakening from sleep— and accompanied by "rain-stopping" weapons (varṣāvagrahāstra), that is to say, weapons that bring about the cessation of rain.

It bore trees as weapons with moving saws, was filled with water and fire missiles and weapons, was as perilous as a battle with the Brahma-missile, and was variegated by the weapons of darkness and light.
Variegated means made multicolored.
The entire sky was densely packed with countless weapons disgorged by the stars, enveloped by showers of stones and missiles, and radiant with showers of fire-missiles.

"For the sake of missiles" means for the sake of the Brahmā-missile and others. "Udgīrṇāni" means cast forth or abandoned. "Yāni āyudhāni" refers to various weapons; "taiḥ" means by those. "Nīrandhraṃ sakalāmbaraṃ yat" means that which is the entire sky, made dense or without gaps by them. //MT_4,26.45//
In a mere moment, the chariots—with their banners brushing against the moon and their wheels thundering with a roar—leaped over both the mountain of sunrise and the mountain of sunset.
By those [clouds] by which the hare—meaning the hare in the moon—is polished with banners.
The great asura who dies without ceasing from the blow of the vajra; the other asura who is born through the great vidyā of the immortal semen.
The *Amara-mahāvidyā* is the *Sañjīvinī-vidyā*. Since there is no death for the gods themselves due to their immortality, their "death" should be understood as mere affliction (*vyathā*).
With its neck uplifted by battles against the floods of portents and auspicious signs arising here and there, which were protected by the great comet Śubhagraha; MU_4,26.48.
The auspicious planets protect the blessings; Ketu is an indicator of the malefic planets, for it is the malefic planets that bring about portents.
Due to his irresistible enmity, he made the earth, the oceans, and the heavens resemble a world of blooming *kiṃśuka* forests by means of the waters of blood.

Furthermore, of what nature was it? Making the world—along with its mountains, earth, oceans, heavens, mountains, sky, lands, seas, and celestial realms—a forest of blossoming *kiṃśuka* trees by means of the waters of blood from those whose enmity was difficult to restrain.
Of what nature was the world? It was accompanied by the mountains, the earth, the oceans, the heavens, the mountains, the sky, the lands, the seas, and the celestial realms.
A great ocean filled with corpses as numerous as mountains, where massive, swaying carcasses hung from the branches and shoulders of entire trees.
In this context, the great oceans are to be understood as consisting of blood.
The surface of the sky was filled with forests of arrow-thickets, as tall as palm trees, being carried along by their own winds, adorned with flowers and fruits upon their wings.
"By the wind" means struck or impelled. "Winged flowers" refers to those [trees] with shimmering fruits; here, "fruit" (phala) should be understood as the thorn (śalya).
With the forest-arms of headless trunks as numerous as mountains, they were dancing, while fallen clouds, celestial chariots, and the stars of the gods lay scattered about.
That [mountain], from which have fallen the celestial chariots of the clouds and the divine stars.
Mountains were pierced through by arrows, spears, clubs, darts, and axes; the sky was covered with fragments of walls fallen from the seven worlds.
The meaning is that the walls of the seven worlds fell down.
The firm drum, like a cloud intoxicated with incessant sound, resounded so loudly upon its back that it caused the elephants at the bottom of the netherworld to cry out.
Where the elephants of the netherworld (pātālatalavāraṇāḥ) were roaring because of the hearing—that is, the act of listening—to the sound of the *pṛṣṭha* [hymn]. //MT_4,26.54//
The long mountain of Dānavas was drawn forth by the hand of Vināyaka, while the hosts of Siddhas, Sādhyas, and Maruts were rendered motionless on the slopes of every quarter.
This is clear.
The Gandharvas, Kinnaras, gods, and Cāraṇas fled away; the leaders of the Gandharvas lay dead, mangled, emaciated, and falling down.
This is clear.
The host of Daityas and Dānavas had for the most part achieved victory, while the army of the gods was suffering, and Indra was utterly despondent.
This is clear.
It possessed the great radiance of red weapons blazing in the northern quarter, and at every moment it was intense with the light of a burning glow that dispelled the darkness.
That place where the great radiance of weapons is reddened by the fire that meets [it] from the northern direction (uttarāśayā)
— by which the fire arising from the burning of the temple is to be understood; where, at every moment (pratikṣaṇam),
there is a blazing conflagration of houses, and which is intense with both light and darkness produced thereby — here, "darkness" refers to that caused by smoke.
It should be known.
With a verse at the end of the chapter, he describes the movement of the wind:

"Winds that signaled the time of universal dissolution blew from the quarters of the sky; their bodies were thickened by the falling of thunderbolts, they scattered fragments of shattered rocks, and they were terrifying with their immense, gurgling roar."

The winds blew—that is, they were blowing—from the mouths of the directions. Of what nature were they? They were such that their limbs were massed together by the falling of thunderbolts; the meaning is that they had gathered in one place due to the descent of the thunderbolts.
For this very reason, they were such that they shattered fragments of rock. Furthermore, there was a most intense *gharghara* sound—a gurgling noise.
Therefore, "voracious" means those that swallow other sounds; thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the twenty-sixth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
What happened after that? To this he says:
"While that terrible tumult of battle was then occurring, as the bodies of gods and asuras fell like fragments of mountains... (MU 4.27.1).
As streams of clouds flowed from the sky like the floods of the Gaṅgā, and as the multitude of gods were enveloped in the cord amidst the thick roar of their released lion-roars;
Upon a tiger that had crushed all the abodes of the gods by the drawing back of its own claws, and which had covered the immortals in battle with its fierce and violent fury;
When Airāvaṇa, his rut exhausted, was intent on flight, and the army of the Dānavas had swelled like the sun at midday.
With their limbs and weapons fallen, and with blood flowing like water from breached dikes, the divine armies fled.

"Overthrown" means they were cast down upon the earth by the *asuras*. "Those whose limbs and weapons were halved" means, in short, those whose limbs were severed and whose weapons were broken. For that very reason, "from which blood was flowing"—such were the divine armies that fled, driven by fear. Like what? Like waters whose embankments have burst. Wherein? [In the midst of the battle.]

"When he was there," and so forth. When that great asura named Dāman—who had covered the immortals (amaras) in a battle characterized by fierce fury—was present, [the gods fled]. This is a *kulaka* [of verses].
Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa followed those [demons], even though they had long since vanished, with loud laughter, just as fires follow their fuel.
Those divine armies followed after them, running behind; the word "api" (also/even) indicates that following those who have vanished is not appropriate.
Although they searched with great effort, the asuras could not find the gods, just as lions cannot find deer that have flown away into a forest thick with nets of clouds.
This is clear.
When the hosts of immortals had not been captured, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa then went with joyful hearts to their lord residing in the treasury of Pātāla.
The lord Śambara.
Then the gods, being despondent, recovered for a moment and went to the immeasurably powerful Brahmā in order to find a means of victory.
Dejected and fainted; having recovered their breath and regained consciousness.
To them, whose faces possessed the splendor of deep redness, Brahmā appeared, like the moon appearing to the oceans that have been turned crimson at evening.

"With blood" means with *rudhira*; those whose faces (*ānana*) are red—of such [beings]. "In the evening" (*sāyam*) means at the time of the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsandhyā*). Alternatively, the moon should be understood as the agent in the act of making [the sky] red, because it is red at the time of its rising;
thus, "then" means at the time of evening.
Having prostrated before him, those gods fully related to him that matter uttered by Śambara, concerning the sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.

Those gods, having bowed down to that purpose—which was set in motion by Śambara, manifested by Śambara, and which consisted of the sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and Krama, known as the sequence beginning with Dāma—properly related it to him. Having heard all of that and having reflected upon it, Brahmā, the discerning one, spoke these words of consolation to the host of gods: *te surāḥ śambareritaṃ śambaraprādurbhāvitaṃ taṃ dāmavyālakaṭakramam arthaṃ dāmādikramākhyaṃ vastu praṇamya tasmai samyak prakathayan | tam ākarṇyākhilaṃ brahmā vicārya ca vicāravid uvācedaṃ surānīkam āśvāsanakaraṃ vacaḥ ||* MU_4,27.12 ||*
That army of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa; the host of gods, the celestial army.
Brahmā said:
"Alas! At the end of a thousand years, Śambara must die by the hand of Hari; therefore, let the Lord of the Immortals wait for that time."

Alas, what a tragedy! By Śambara, acting as the agent, at the end of a thousand years, [he must] die in a battle with the Lord of the Immortals, Hari Viṣṇu, in due course. The meaning is that he will not die for that long;
you all should wait for that duration of time.

"Now, what shall we do with Dāma and the others who continue to cause us harm for so long? To this he replied: "O best of immortals, today you must fight these Dānavas—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—and put them to flight by means of illusory warfare."
O best of the immortals, you, while engaging these Dānavas—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—in battle through illusory warfare and causing them to fight, must flee.
[Objection: "But what will be achieved for them by our flight? To this he says:
"By the force of their habitual practice of fighting, the marvel of egoism will enter into the hearts of these [demons] like a reflection in a mirror. (MU 4.27.15)

Of these, Dāma and the others, the "wonder of ego" (ahaṅkāracamatkāra)—that is, the savoring of the sense of "I" in the form "we are victors in battle"—will enter as a reflection into the *āśaya*, that is, the mind.
"But what will be achieved by that? To this he replies:
"However, these gods Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa have their latent impressions (vāsanā) grasped; they will be easy for you to conquer, like birds caught in a net."
Because, according to the method that will be explained, it is the latent impression (vāsanā) itself that acts with necessity.
"But surely, how is it that they cannot be conquered today? To this he replies:

"But today these [Arjuna and his brothers] are free from latent tendencies (*avāsanā*), devoid of pleasure and pain; by striking down their enemies with fortitude, they have attained invincibility even for the gods."

But on the other hand, today they have become free from latent impressions (*avāsanā*), that is, devoid of the impression of "I" (*ahaṃvāsanā*). For this very reason, they are exempt from pleasure and pain;
for this very reason, they strike down their enemies with fortitude—meaning they are invincible even to the gods, let alone to you.
They have reached [this state]. For one who is devoid of pleasure and the like becomes difficult to conquer because he is free from fear.
"But how will these people become submissive through latent impressions (*vāsanā*)? To this he replies:
"Those who are bound by the threads of latent impressions and brought under control by the snares of hope, they fall into subjection in this world like birds tied with ropes. (MU 4.27.18)

Those who are bound by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), being bound by the threads of the latent impression of "I" (*ahaṃvāsanā*), become subject to the snares of desire (*āśāpāśa*) and thus come under the control of the world. Like what? Like birds bound by ropes. This is the meaning: a person is possessed by a disposition (*āśaya*) consisting of the internal latent impression of "I," such as "may this be mine" or "may this not be."
It comes to be; and by means of that, one falls into a state of wretchedness; and because of that, one becomes subject to another.
[Objection: But how can those who are devoid of latent impressions (vāsanā) be difficult to conquer? To this he says:

"For those wise ones who are free from latent impressions, whose intellects are unattached everywhere, who neither rejoice nor feel anger—they are the great-minded ones who are difficult to conquer. (MU 4.27.19)

Those whose intellects are unattached—that is, devoid of attachment in the form of passion and aversion—regarding everything, whether it be to be rejected or accepted. For it is through attachment to what is to be accepted and aversion toward what is to be rejected that a person becomes subject to defeat. Otherwise, kings who understand the proper method would not strive to conquer their enemies by means of bestowing wealth; yet in the absence of such [attachment], one is free from passion even toward one's own body.

The sense is that a person cannot be conquered by anything. Hatred should be understood as a form of attachment because it generates attachment; for, having turned away from things to be abandoned through hatred, a person becomes possessed of a more firm attachment—otherwise known as passion—toward things to be accepted.
He whose internal knots are bound by the rope of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), though he be great and possessed of vast knowledge, is overcome even by a child.
Otherwise, even among the ignorant who are wealthy, those advanced in learning and age would not offer salutation; such is the meaning.
One who constructs conceptualizations such as "this is he," "I am he," or "this is mine," becomes a vessel for calamities, just as the ocean is for waters.

"Ākalitā" means held or grasped from all sides (*ā samantāt*). "Kalpanā" refers to conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), by which [one is possessed]. "Of calamities" (*āpadām*) refers to those of such a nature as "may this happen to me" or "may this not happen."
O worthy one, he by whom the self has been cultivated as limited to only this much, though he be omniscient, has everywhere fallen into a state of supreme wretchedness.

O worthy one, O Indra! By whom the self—its own true nature—which is delimited by this much, and which consists merely of the body and so forth, and is therefore limited—has been meditated upon, made the object of contemplation;
that person, though omniscient, has nonetheless fallen into a state of supreme, unsurpassed wretchedness and misery everywhere.
The meaning is that he goes. For one who is attached to the body, desiring what is beneficial for the body, inevitably falls into a state of wretchedness.
He who has conceived a limit for the infinite and immeasurable reality of the Self has, by that very act, brought himself under his own control.

Because it abides as the witness of the end of the infinite, it is devoid of that [end]. Because the immeasurable abides solely in the form of the knower, it does not touch the state of being an object of knowledge. Of this reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*): by whom—by the ignorant person through whose conceptualization the limitation (*iyattā*), known as being delimited by the body, has been imagined and brought into being; by that very self, the Self has been brought under its own control.
For one who is delimited by a body, subjection to experience is indeed inevitable.
"Now, how can this be so? To this he replies:
"Whatever exists in the three worlds that is distinct from the self, with respect to that, cultivation becomes bound by way of being an object of grasping. (MU 4.27.24)

Regarding the self that has been conceived as finite: whatever else is distinct from it [is what is meant by] "conceived"—this is the ellipsis. That which is conceived exists; because of the conceit of non-attainment toward it, a state of being "to-be-grasped" (upādeyatā) arises, and through this quality of being graspable, one becomes bound by that conception.
The sense is that the very bondage of such conception is what is called "subjection" (vaivaśyam).
It explains that the state of being subject to the bondage of mental cultivation is the cause of suffering due to its lack of propriety:
"The wise know that mere attachment is the cause of endless sufferings; they know that mere non-attachment is the cause of all happiness. (MU 4.27.25)
It is merely a mental resolve, merely a bond of cultivation.
Having established this in general, he now recalls the specific case:
"As long as you maintain a lack of attachment toward the persistence of existence, even Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa cannot truly conquer you, any more than the winds can overcome gnats."
"Without reliance" means devoid of any basis; "in the state of existence" means in the established condition of entities such as the body and so forth.
A living being is conquered by internal latent impressions that lead to wretchedness; otherwise, even a mosquito would be like the mountain of the immortals.
Or otherwise, in the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Wherever there is latent impression (vāsanā), there too comes dejection; for it is observed that being permeated by qualities and defects belongs to what exists, not to what does not exist.

And where latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exist, there wretchedness arises. The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of completing the meter. For (*hi*), because: being permeated by qualities and defects—which consists in being bound to the beneficial and the harmful—is what brings about wretchedness. This is seen in the case of the existent (*sataḥ*), who possesses the reality of a body imparted by latent impressions;

it is not seen in the case of the non-existent (*asataḥ*), who, due to the absence of latent impressions, is like a mere semblance of existence by virtue of having the nature of pure consciousness alone.
He states the result:
"O Śakra, act in such a way that they cultivate within themselves their own latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) in this manner: 'This is he,' 'I am he,' and 'This is mine,'" just as Dāma and the others did.

The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. O Śakra! Just as Dāma and the others cultivate—that is, conceptualize—within their minds such a self-impression (*svavāsanā*), namely the impression of egoism (*ahaṅkāravāsanā*) in the form of "I am this" and "this is mine," so should you act. The sense is that by doing so, they will become conquerable.
[Objection: But how is it that they will not be conquerable by me? To this he says:
Whatever misfortunes there are for people, and whatever states of existence and non-existence, those are the buds—both bitter and tender—of the *karañja* creeper of craving. (MU 4.27.30)
Craving itself is like a thorny creeper because it causes suffering; [the phrase "of that" (tasyāḥ) refers to it].

Bound by the threads of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), this world revolves; when those [impressions] have fully increased, they lead to extreme suffering, and when they have been eradicated, they lead to happiness.
It undergoes transformation; it assumes the opposite state. That is the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*). Annihilation means destruction.
Though one be steadfast, though one be extremely learned, though one be of noble birth, and though one be great—even such a person is bound by craving, just as a lion is bound by a chain.
He is bound and rendered helpless; for one who is seized by craving is indeed manifestly rendered helpless.
For this bird of the mind, which dwells within the tree of the body and rests in the abode of the heart, a snare has been prepared by craving.
This is clear.
Dejected by latent impressions, the world is dragged away by the end-maker (Death), like a helpless bird incessantly gasping, pulled by a rope by a child.
By Kṛtānta, who is Yama in the form of possessiveness (mamatā); for Śrī Vyāsa himself has designated possessiveness as being Kṛtānta.
Enough with the burden of weapons and with wandering about in battle; by means of reasoning alone, you should eliminate the enemy’s latent tendencies along with their misconceptions.

The sense is that nothing at all will succeed for you through weapons and the like against the enemy, who consists of the triad beginning with *dāma* (the bond), and who is possessed of error and associated with perversions.
O leaders of the immortals, while the enemy’s inner fortitude remains undisturbed, neither your weapons, nor your treatises, nor your missiles can conquer you.
When it is unshaken, being free from agitation due to the absence of latent impressions (vāsanā).
But these—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—by virtue of their practice in combat, will take hold within you of an impression consisting of egoism.
"Consisting of egoism"—meaning of the nature "we shall fight."
If those mechanical men created by Śambara do not rely upon latent impressions (vāsanā), they will attain invincibility.
"Mechanical men" means, that is to say, those who are devoid of conscious investigation.
O gods, let them first awaken those [beings] through the battle of reasoning, until they come to possess latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) by the power of practice.
Awaken those possessed of latent tendencies; bring them to transformation.
Then those whose minds are fixed on worldly existence will become objects to be slain by you; for in this world, no one whose heart is pierced by craving remains unshaken.
Now, one might ask: "If they will not be killed even by that [means], then what should be done? To this, he says: "Thirst" (*tṛṣṇā*).
Those whose intentions are pierced by thirst, whose minds are permeated by craving, are "tender" (*pelava*), meaning wretched. All those who are seized by thirst become tender;
therefore, the sense is that even they will certainly be [killed].
He concludes Brahma’s speech with a verse at the end of the chapter:

"This entire world, both even and uneven, has attained stability through its own latent impressions (*vāsanā*); yet it moves like the mass of waves in the ocean. Therefore, let that very [cause] which has set in here be treated."

This entire world, which is experienced as consisting of both the even and the uneven, and of pleasure and pain, has attained stability through its own latent impressions—that is, through the latent impression of the ego. Yet those very impressions, in this world, move and quiver; like what? Like a mass of waves. Just as a mass of waves moves upon the ocean, so too [does this world].
This is the meaning. Therefore, that very latent impression (*vāsanā*) becomes fit for treatment—that is, it attains the state of being suitable for healing. May there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Having said, "He tells of the disappearance of Brahmā," the Blessed Lord vanished right there, like a wave of water that has made its sound upon the shore of the ocean's edge.
In that very place, in that same spot; but not by going elsewhere. "Antardhi" means concealment or obstruction.
But the gods, having heard those words, departed toward their own respective quarters, carrying with them the fragrance of the lotuses, like winds bearing a forest garland.
This is clear.
For some days, they rested in their own beloved palaces, which possessed steady splendor, just as bees rest within lotuses.
This is clear.

Having attained for a short time that auspicious state which brings about their own exaltation, they made a sound like the roar of kettledrums, resembling the thunder of the clouds at the dissolution of the world.
This is clear.
Then, a terrible battle that caused a long delay took place again in the sky between them and the Daityas who had risen from the depths of Pātāla.

The meaning is that [the battle] was merely a waste of time and did not bring about the slaying of Śambara, because his death was declared by Brahmā to occur at the end of a thousand years; "of the gods" is the ellipsis. A multitude of swords, arrows, spears, and mallets arose;
heaps of clubs, maces, axes, and fierce discuses; thunderbolts, mountain rocks, fires, and trees; and weapons with the faces of serpents, Garuḍas, and so forth.

In response to the expectation of what kind of battle took place, he says "vavuḥ" (they blew). They blew, that is, they were blowing; the ellipsis to be supplied is "released by the gods and the Daityas."

The river, with its thick torrents of great waters formed by magically created weapons, swiftly rushed forth in every direction; it possessed a deep roar like a flood of agitated water, and it suddenly swept away hundreds of thousands of rocks, mountains, riverbanks, and trees.

Created by the Rākṣasas through their illusory power (*māyā*), it was produced by magic; it possessed a thick torrent of great water consisting of weapons. Thus, directed repeatedly and swiftly toward the rocky mountain, that mass of weapon-laden water was agitated and prone to surging against the hundreds of thousands of trees on the riverbanks.
That river, which possessed a dense roar, was composed of weapons; it quickly and swiftly issued forth, having gone out in every direction.
In response to the inquiry as to by what means he went forth in every direction, he speaks with specific detail:

"By means of a [torrent] consisting of flaming brands, spears, rocks, darts, swords, lances, arrows, javelins, and mallets flowing in a central current; by means of a celestial palace surrounded by waters like the Ganges; and by means of the drawing in of a rain of thunderbolts in all directions."

"Aśanivarṣaṇa" means a shower of thunderbolts; by that "karṣaṇa," which is the dragging toward the various directions, he went forth—this is the connection with what precedes. For by the rain, the rivers pervade the directions. By what kind of dragging caused by the shower of thunderbolts? They flow in their midst through a current carrying flaming brands, spears, rocks, darts, swords, lances, arrows, javelins, and mallets.

Wherein? Therein. By what kind [of being]? Furthermore, by what kind? That by which the abodes of the immortals have been surrounded by water equal to the Ganges in all directions; therein, by such [a being].

The army of gods, asuras, and siddhas, which consists of bodies as harsh as earth and other elements, and which is like a body of rays in the sky when it comes to dealing blows or receiving them—whichever such host subsides, that very same one, created by illusion, arises again through its own essence.

She who—though her body is as harsh as the earth and other elements in its capacity for receiving and inflicting blows, and though it is composed of that very substance such that it is capable of both delivering and enduring strikes—is, in the ultimate sense, like a ray of light from the sky because she is illusory in nature;
that is to say, she whose form is emptiness (*śūnya*). Being exactly such as she is, she becomes stilled; she dies.

That army of gods, asuras, and siddhas rises up once again; in what manner? By means of *rasa*, that is, by desire; it is "created by illusion" (*māyākṛtā*), meaning fashioned through magical power (*māyā*)—specifically, by Indra and Śambara.

Then the faces of the quarters became like great oceans filled with floods of blood from mountains shattered by weapons resembling mountains; they were filled with forests of palm trees that were actually spears grown upon the divine mountains—the Sumerus—that were themselves the lords of the gods and asuras. Upon those [mountains] grew spears which were the very palm forests belonging to them.

Then there fell a rain of iron lions, still alive, from whose mouths were disgorged spears, arrows, pikes, clubs, swords, and discuses; who had playfully swallowed the mountains hurled by gods and demons; and who possessed fierce rows of teeth and claws that produced a harsh, sawing sound.

Then there was a rain of iron lions—a shower of lions made of iron—that fell. Of what nature was it? It was one from which spears, arrows, pikes, clubs, swords, and discuses were vomited forth and fell together. Furthermore, of what nature was it? It was one by which mountains—released as weapons by the gods and *dānavas* and swallowed or seized with ease—were [consumed]. In that [rain]...
On a stone slab; "resounding," meaning making a sound by virtue of being rubbed; that which is a saw—like that are the teeth and nails;
she who has a fierce garland of them is such [a woman]. Likewise, "endowed with life" means possessed of vitality.

The line of venomous serpents leaped up like a drunken ocean; it was like an army of suns at the end of an eon, manifesting a world-conflagration through the heat of the poisonous flames issuing from their blazing eyes, while the vast earth and mountains were tossed upward.
A row—a line—of venom-bearing serpents; like a mad ocean, it surged forth. Of what nature was it?

Blazing, with flames rising up; that which is the fire-poison of their eyes, its heat arising therefrom; by that, the conflagration of the quarters was displayed, showing the suns of the end of the eon, the suns at the dissolution of the world-cycle.

The army was a long line; by which [line], it was that [army] which was flying up—having the nature of soaring—and which had exceedingly long mountain ranges belonging to the earth as its support. It was she (the army) whose [supporting mountains were thus].

The entire world became crowded with bodies by the swirling currents of rivers of various weapons, which were like the waves of the ocean of the atmosphere; that atmosphere was filled with the sound known as *karkara* produced by the mass (*utkara*) of roaring thunderbolts (*vajra*) acting as sea-monsters (*makara*), and it was surrounded by the lords of mountains. [Note: *Unnāda-vajra-makara-utkara-karkara-antarikṣa-abdhi-vīci-valaya-valita-acala-indraiḥ*: "By those [weapons] whose atmosphere-ocean was characterized by the *karkara* sound from the mass of roaring thunderbolt-makaras, and which were surrounded by the lords of mountains by the circles of waves of the atmospheric ocean..."]

The entire world became exceedingly crowded in its very nature, with the mountain lords encircled by waves—that is, by forms consisting of circular ripples—and likewise enveloped by such [waves]; furthermore, it was filled with river-currents whose weapons were of various kinds, accompanied by whirlpools and possessed of diverse missiles. Thus, the whole universe was completely full.

The sky was for a moment filled with mountains, missiles, weapons, Garuḍas, mountains, and garlands; for a moment with hosts of female nāgas and celestial women; for a moment it was full of oceans, for a moment of floods of fire, for a moment of suns, and for a moment of darkness.

By the phrase "moment by moment," the illusory nature of the oceans and other elements is expressed. Of what nature is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)? It is that which is garlanded—that is, supported—by those Garuḍa-mountains, which are ruby peaks situated amidst mountain-shaped missiles and weapons (*śailāstraśastra*). Furthermore, it is that in which high-ranking Naga women and the women of the Asura hosts reside, as well as the celestial maidens (*surāṅganā*).
However, their [the mountains'] non-mention is because they actually remain in the sky. In the word "Garuḍa," the absence of the long vowel in the letter *ga* is an archaic (ārṣa) usage.
But the mountains manifested by the mantra are in the form of missiles (*astra*), while those dispatched directly are in the form of weapons (*śastra*).

With floods of mountain-like fires from weapons spread through the sky, agitated by the *guḍaguḍā* roar of Garuḍas, the world became like the interior of the celestial realm and the earth blazing at the unbearable time of cosmic dissolution.

The sky was agitated by the *guḍaguḍa*—the rumbling roar—of the Garuḍas; and by means of the floods of mountains that were like fires of weapons spreading therein, the world became such that it resembled the unbearable period of cosmic dissolution (*kalpakāla*).
Thus, the interiors between the celestial abodes and the earth became ablaze right there. Such it became.

The gods sprang up from the surface of the earth like birds from a mountain slope into the sky; yet by an overwhelming force, they fell to the ground like the rocks of mountains shaken during the dissolution of the world.
The phrase "atibalāt" (due to excessive force) is connected with the first half-verse.

Then the gods and asuras, scorched by the great conflagration clinging to the forest-like rows of trees formed by the lofty weapons fixed upon their bodies, took on the appearance of mountains shaken by the winds at the end of an eon within the expanse of the sky.

Then the gods and demons in the midst of the sky, within the firmament, attained the splendor of those mountains shaken by the winds at the end of an aeon. Of what nature were they? They were clinging to the rows of trees and forests that were the very tall weapons fixed upon their bodies. They were such that they were scorched by the great fire arising from the friction of those [weapons]. //MT_4,28.17//

With streams of blood released from the bodies of the lords of the gods and asuras, swirling on all sides, the ocean of the sky bore a full form, like the rising celestial Ganges reddened by twilight.

The gods and asuras themselves were the great mountains; from their bodies, streams of blood were released and flowed all around. By means of these, the ocean of the sky—known as the firmament—fully bore a body that was entirely red like the twilight, appearing as if it possessed a hundred rising Gaṅgās. //MT_4,28.18//
There was a rain of mountains, a rain of water, and likewise a rain of various fierce weapons; there was a rain of terrible thunderbolts, and then a mutual rain of fire from one another.
Those experts in the path of right conduct, who had shattered the walls of all the great mountains, simultaneously released a rain of flowers upon every limb of the quarters of the sky.

Then, in this science of the pacification of weapons, those gods and asuras who were experts—that is, skillful—brought these showers to a complete cessation on all sides. What were these? The shower of mountains and so forth. Not only did they bring them to a cessation, but they also released [showers] upon the limbs of the quarters. Like what? Like a shower of flowers. Of what nature were they? Those by whom the lords of all mountains were shattered.
Those by whom the walls [were made]; they were such. A couplet.

The gods and asuras, distressed by the agitation of their tumultuous battle, with weapons in their hands and limbs mangled by one another, scattering the blood from their broad seats upon the ground, roamed through the sky like fires consuming a forest,
hurling insults at each other.

The gods and asuras wandered through the sky. In what state were they? They were distressed and agitated by the intensity—the exertion—of that battle (*saṅgara*), which was full of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*). Their hands were busily engaged in striking one another’s limbs; such were they. They were like the fires at the end of an eon (*dāma-indra*) for Dāma and Indra, because they caused torment to the mind.
They possessed flickering fires. Even therein, there was a division: the gods were on the side of Dāman, and the asuras were on the side of Indra. They had broad pedestals and broad statures.

Those "pedestals" refer to the shoulders and other such parts; with these, they were strewn with blood, their blood being scattered. Likewise, they were "seizing one another," performing mutual throws against each other.

At that time, with severed heads, hands, arms, and thighs—wandering like locusts through the expanse of the sky, inauspicious, and fierce as masses of clouds—the interior of the world remained shrouded from the sun, with the network of mountains at the horizons obscured by those severed limbs. For this very reason they were wandering; for this very reason they resembled locusts in the sky; they were inauspicious, causing ill fortune; and they consisted of the multitude of heads, hands, arms, and thighs. Thus, the belly of the world remained covered until the sun.
It was such that the horizons and the networks of mountains were covered; by what [was it so]? As if by masses of clouds, as if by the highest clouds.

The universe became as terrifying as the end of an untimely aeon: its fires were intoxicated, its waters agitated by the wind, its sun blazed, its forests withered, the hosts of gods and asuras were shattered, and the walls and corners of the cosmic egg were broken apart.
That whose wall-corners are broken on all sides; such [a place].

It was utterly bewildered, its horizons whirled about by mountain peaks that resounded as they were struck by dense weapons equal to their own size; it was filled with the cries of distress from the winds in the multitude of caves at the summits, as if moaning in pain, and with the abundant roars of lions that had fallen upon it.
[The world] was known to have been violently whirled by the mountain peaks acting as agents; that is, it was understood to be possessed of rotation. How was it whirled?
It was whirled—that is, made to possess rotation—wherein the horizons were set spinning. By what kind of mountain peaks?
By those struck by thick missiles whose size was equal to the mountain peaks themselves. Precisely because of this, they were resounding. Furthermore...

Of what nature were they? They were the winds at the forefront of the floods of mountain caves (*guhaughāgrāṇām vātāḥ*); that is to say, by way of those [winds]. It was as if they were warbling with distress; for one joined with distress indeed warbles. Again, of what nature were they? They were the roars of the lions that had fallen [upon them]; that is to say, by way of those [roars]. With what kind of roars were they crying out?
With abundant and intense [efforts].

The interior of space was whirled about like forest leaves scattered by the wind—by illusions, rivers, oceans, clouds, and conflagrations; by trees, the corpses of gods and asuras, mountains, and floods of rocks; and by showers of helmets, arrows, spears, clubs, and missiles.

The "end of the sky" (*ambarānta*) refers to the middle of the atmosphere. It was "scattered" (*avakīrṇa*), meaning stirred up by the wind; it was like the leaves of a forest. It was "whirling," that is, possessed of a circular motion. To the question, "By what was it whirled?"—for indeed, a whirling motion is not possible for the middle of the sky itself—the text says "the river of illusion" (*māyānadī*) and so forth. The whirling belongs only to the rivers of illusion and other such things moving within the end of the sky; thus, the "end of the sky" is superimposed as the locus of the whirling.

By the forceful blows from the palms of hands that were as difficult to restrain in their constant coming and going as the wings of the king of mountains, there suddenly arose a flood of the ocean of the celestial city—filled with the falling bodies of warriors shattered by the impact of those mountain-kings.

[Grammatical analysis: Those which are the size of the wings of the king of mountains (*adrīndrapakṣaparimāṇa*) and which are uniquely difficult to restrain in their coming and going (*gamāgamaikadurvāra*); such are the hands (*hastāḥ*). Their palms (*talāni*); by means of the blows (*tāḍanāni*) made by them; *drāk* means quickly. The bodies of the warriors (*bhaṭaśarīrāṇi*) which were falling...

Thus were the lords of mountains; their peaks [were shattered], and by those [peaks] the celestial cities were cast down. That flood of the ocean, filled with the waters of those [cities], became—the seven oceans—came into being; such is the meaning.
Then that cave-like expanse of the world became filled with a dense, humming roar; its interior of mountains was washed by blood, and it was crowded with those moving about in pools of gore.
The expanse of the world—that is, the vastness of the universe—is itself the cave. At that time, it became agitated.
In what way? It was such that its atmosphere was filled with a thick, humming roar—the clamor of battle—and its interior spaces between the mountains were washed all over with blood.

That state which is in the form of a pool of blood is the "abode" (*sthāna*); she is "of such a kind" because she exists therein. This usage is like the expression "possessing stability" (*sthitimat*) with respect to "stability" (*sthiti*).
Furthermore, the cave has its interior filled with the humming of mosquitoes, its inner space between the mountains washed by rain, and it is situated within a lake.
With a verse at the end of the canto, he describes the similarity between this battle and the cycle of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*):

"Then that activity of battle, which caused transformations extending through infinite directions, which bestowed pleasure and pain oriented toward rise and fall, and which was crowded with hosts of gods and demons, was indeed similar to this worldly existence. (MU 4.28)

Indeed, in certainty, that activity of conflict here became like the cycle of existence (*saṃsṛti*). Of what nature was it? It was such that it produced a transformation called violence through its expansion across infinite directions; it was such that it bestowed pleasure and pain directed toward decline and rise; and it was crowded and congested by the hosts of *asuras* and *surās*. Such was the cycle of existence.

Furthermore, through its expansion, it produces the modification known as bondage; it becomes the giver of pleasure and pain and is crowded with various objects. May there be auspiciousness! MT_4,28.28 //
Thus ends the twenty-eighth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Thus he concludes the battle:
"By the life-taking Asuras, who engaged in such tumultuous undertakings, impelled by great audacity, battles were commenced in which death was the only goal."
By means of illusion, as well as by dispute, by alliance and by war, by flight, by fortitude, by stratagem, and by bribery.
Through acts of wretchedness, combat with missiles, and frequent disappearances, that battle was conducted by the gods for thirty-five years.
For thirty-five years, that battle was waged by the gods and for thirty-five years with the asuras.
When the question arises as to by what means and in what manner it was waged, [the answer is] "by means of *māyā*," and so forth: by *upāyana*, meaning approaching;
by *kārpaṇya*, meaning through wretchedness; and by *svāntardhānaiḥ*, meaning by means of self-concealments manifested through *māyā*. By what kind of asuras?
By those whose undertakings were for the most part of such a nature; by those life-takers, snatchers of life;

by those who were impetuous, possessed of fury, in their great daring; and furthermore, by what kind of beings? By those for whom death had been undertaken through battles—by such as these [was made] the tilaka.
For eight, ten, five, and seven years, as well as for days and months, rain fell from trees, fire-arms, water, thunderbolts, and mountains.
Showers of trees, fire, weapons, water, thunderbolts, and mountains fell as rain. For how long?
For ten years, eight months, and twelve days—meaning five, seven, and twelve respectively. It should be understood that during other times, it was merely twilight and so forth.
After such a length of time, through the firm habituation of ego-construction, Dāma and the others—whose minds were consumed by it—grasped at the notion "I am."
"Of those whose minds are swallowed by egoism"—that is, of those whose consciousness is seized by such an egoism as "we shall fight. Such are they.
Just as a mirror becomes like the reflected object due to the excellence of its proximity, so too have they attained the state of egoism through the excellence of their practice.
Due to the excellence of proximity and the abundance of presence, it is endowed with a reflection like an original object (*bimba*).
Just as an object that is too distant does not reflect in a mirror, so too the latent impression of an object does not arise due to a lack of practice.
"Farther than far" means: among objects such as the state of battle and so forth, it is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the thought, "This was done by me. (MT 4.29.7)
When Dāma and the others were born, their latent tendencies toward egoism arose; then they fell into a state of wretchedness, thinking, "This is my life, this is my purpose."

When Dāma and the others—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—were born, that is, when they had arisen, those in whom the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) was present; being thus born and fully developed, they then fell into, or reached, such a state of wretchedness and dejection as "this is my life," "this is my purpose. For in the absence of egoism, there would certainly be no wretchedness in the form of possessiveness (*mamatā*), which is devoid of a foundation; yet, when that [egoism] exists...
The sense is that, since it has attained the status of a substratum, that [consequence] is indeed difficult to avoid.
Seized by the latent impression of fear, struck down by the latent impression of delusion, and bound by the snares of hope, they have consequently fallen into a state of wretchedness.
