Then, immediately after approaching in a state of wretchedness, those [servants] such as Dāma and the others were seized—that is, brought under control—by the latent impression (*vāsanā*), which is the mental residue produced by fear arising from the apprehension of the destruction of their bodies; likewise, they were struck down—that is, afflicted—by the latent impression of delusion (*moha*), which is the ignorance consisting in the conception of the self in that which is not the self, such as the body; and by the snares of hope for the sake of the body and other objects that have been made the objects of the conceit of "I" and "mine."
Bound by the snares of hope consisting of objects such as wealth, they have been brought under their own control; they have reached a state of wretchedness, the ultimate limit of misery.
"Surely, what has come of that for them? To this he replies:
"For indeed, by those who are free from egoism, the sense of 'mine' has been imagined in vain, just as the state of being a serpent was [imagined] in a rope by Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa. (MU 4.29.10)

"Hi" signifies certainty. "By those free from egoism" means by those devoid of the sense of "I. "Dāmavyālakaṭaiḥ" refers to Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa. "Then," meaning immediately after falling into a state of wretchedness through the power of egoism; "mamatva" means possessiveness. "Mudhā" means indeed in vain. "Upakalpitaṃ" means firmly established through conceptual construction. What is it like? It is like the state of being a serpent in a rope; the meaning is that it is absolutely false.
He speaks of the very sense of "mine-ness":
"Let this body-stalk, from head to foot, remain firm; 'it is mine'—thus did you, wretched with craving, fall into a state of misery."
This is clear.
"May my body remain firm; may my wealth lead to my happiness"—the fortitude of those whose minds were fixed on such thoughts vanished.
This is clear.

Because their bodies were devoid of latent impressions (*avāsanatva*) and because the enemies of the gods were free from attachment (*anāsthatva*), that intentness upon striking them was instantly wiped away as if polished clean.

Because the enemies of the gods—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—were devoid of latent impressions (*avāsanatvāt*), that is, due to their lack of *vāsanā*; and likewise because they were free from attachment to their bodies (*anāsthatvāt*), meaning they lacked any clinging to their physical forms; that former state of being intent on striking, which had previously existed, was quickly wiped away and destroyed.
The meaning is that this occurred because, through the power of [their] egolessness (*ahaṅkāra*), the fear of the destruction of the body and so forth had arisen.
Thinking, "How may we become stable in this world? they fell into a state of dejection, like lotuses deprived of water.
Pierced means pervaded.
But for those who possessed the conceit of "mine" regarding food and drink, there arose a terrifying delight rooted in worldly existence, which led them to share in the cycle of rebirth.

Those who possess the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) directed toward the body have their own self-conceit; such are they. Their delight (*rati*) is attachment (*āsakti*), which is to say passion (*rāga*). It resides in the states of existence (*bhava*), having worldly objects as its domain; it partakes of existence (*bhavabhāginī*), bestowing the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*).
Then, in that battle, out of fear they became full of hesitation, like young deer in the forest agitated by a herd of rutting elephants.

"Dependence" (*sāpekṣatva*) means being accompanied by such a dependence as "may we not die. "Out of fear" (*bhītyā*) means out of the fear of death. Of what nature were the young deer? They were "agitated"—that is, made to be filled with agitation—by the "herd" (*gaṇa*) of intoxicated elephants.
He clarifies this very state of dependence:
"We shall die! We shall die!"—with their hearts struck by such thoughts, they indeed wandered very slowly in the battle against the enraged Airāvaṇa.
They wandered; they were roaming about.
For those who seek only the body and are terrified of death, their foot has been placed upon the head by way of their own meager courage, bringing about their downfall.

"Only a single body"—this refers to those who desire [only that]. Likewise, for those who are terrified of death, [the enemy] has placed his foot upon their heads; "in the manner previously described" means by way of the aforementioned method. By the agent, which is characterized by a lack of strength (*alpasattvatā*), a "footstep" (*pada*) has been made. The sense is that they have become weak-willed beings. Of what nature is this footstep? It is "one that brings calamity," meaning one that bestows misfortune.
Then, their courage failing, they were unable to slay the soldier standing before them, just as fires whose fuel is exhausted cannot consume the oblation.
Their vital strength faded and their fortitude destroyed, they became unable—that is, they were rendered powerless. Those whose fuel has been exhausted are "those with exhausted fuel."
As the gods struck, those who were easily subdued approached them; with all their limbs mangled and wounded, the soldiers stood like common men.
Of the *vibudhas*, the gods; their state of being easily subdued and easily restrained.
What need is there for much speaking here? With their minds terrified of death, the Daityas fled from the field of battle as the gods surged forward.
This is clear.
While all those renowned mountain-like Dānavas named Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa were fleeing in every direction from the abode of the Asuras, [the Lord acted].
That army of Daityas fell from the sky, fleeing here and there like the host of stars shaken on all sides by the winds at the end of an eon.
This is clear.
In response to the expectation of where it fell, he says:
"In the groves of the Immortal Mountain (Amarācala), upon the rocks of its peaks, on the shores of the oceans, and amidst the masses of clouds."
This is clear.
In the whirlpools and chasms of the ocean, in ravines and rivers, in wildernesses and at the ends of the quarters, and in forests ablaze;
This is clear.
In villages and cities whose treasuries were destroyed by that war, in forests infested with fierce yakṣas, and in deserts where forest fires were breaking out;
Of those Asuras, their treasury—their middle—was destroyed and shattered by battle; [the word refers] to those [beings] who possessed such treasuries.
On the mountains at the edge of the Lokāloka range, in the lakes, and in the cities of Andhra, Dramiḍa, Kaśmīra, and Pārasīka;
This is clear.
In the waves of various oceans, in the masses of Ganges water, in distant other continents, and in the Jambu-tree thickets and creepers;
In those that are far away, existing at a distance.
Having fallen from all sides like mountains, those [demons] in the abode of the Asuras had their limbs and feet shattered and their hands and arms torn apart.
This is clear.
With their entrails like strings caught in the branches, with gouts of blood flowing from their severed limbs, their hooves and heads scattered, and their eyes protruding in rage; ||| MU_4,29.30 |||
Those whose eyes have emerged from their sockets, fallen to the ground, and are rolling in rage.
With their own weapons, they had their armor and missiles shattered by the force of the whirlwind; their various garments fell scattered, tossed about by the wind’s long-reaching reach.
Those whose silken garments fall because they have been overturned—that is, rendered upside down—by that sudden onset from afar; such are they.
Terrified by the harsh clatter of helmets striking against their necks, they hang with the parts of their bodies pierced by sword-blades sharpened on stone.
Those helmets which were clung to their throats produced a specific sound, a clattering noise; those [demons] who possessed a fierce fear arising from that were of such a kind.
The spikes of their armor were pierced by falling onto the tips of *śālmali* thorns, and their heads were shattered into a hundred pieces by the impact against well-hewn stone slabs.

On the tips of *śālmalī* trees—that is, on the tops of specific types of trees—there is something firm; from all sides, it falls. By that [falling], they are impaled; those whose *kaṅkaṭa-śaṅkus*—that is, the stakes of their armor—are thus [pierced] are such [as described].
He brings the section to a conclusion with this final verse:
"At the mere moment of their falling, all those lords of the asuras, together with their weapons, met their destruction in every direction like dust particles entering the waters of the ocean."
This is clear.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth canto, titled "The Chapter on Stability," in the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ. At that time, what became of Dāma and the others? To this he says:
"When the gods were thus gratified and the Dānavas had been slain, Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the rest became dejected and overwhelmed with fear. (MU 4.30.1)
This is clear.
"Now, what did Śambara do? To this he says:
"The wrathful Śambara, his army having been subdued, blazed up in anger against Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa like the fire at the end of an aeon."
The summary meaning is that Śambara became enraged toward Dāma and the others.
Then, out of fear of Śambara, Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa abandoned the assembly of Dānavas and went to the seventh netherworld (pātāla), where they remained.
This is clear.
There, Yama’s servants known as Kukuhās stand, capable of terrifying with vetālas, acting as guardians of that ocean of hell.
This is clear.
Together with them, Dāma and the others brought that period there to an end after ten thousand years, having taken hold of infinite evil latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Together with those *kukuhās*, they—Dāma and the others—led [them] to the limit of ten thousand years, that is, for a duration extending to the number of ten thousand years. How were they?

They were "possessed" (*āttāḥ*), meaning they held fast to "bad tendencies" (*kuvāsanāḥ*), namely the censured formative predispositions (*saṃskārāḥ*) whose objects are wealth and the like. Such were they.
"This woman is my delightful wife; she is mine and I am her master"—for those bound by such hollow affection, time passed away.
It turned back and became transformed.
Then, on one occasion, Dharmarāja arrived at that place by chance for the purpose of investigating the affairs of the great hells.
This is clear.
Not recognizing him as the King of Dharma, the three Asuras did not bow down to him, treating him like a common servant for their own destruction.
"Not fully understood" is the reason expressed by way of a qualification.
Then, by the command of Vaivasvata, these were cast into the grounds of blazing chasms, where their eyebrows were made to twitch.
This is clear.
There, they—along with their friends, wives, and kinsmen—were consumed by piteous cries like trees with their leaves and branches scorched by forest fires.
This is clear.
Born through their own latent impressions, they are again by that very same cruel disposition [reborn] as Kirātas and royal servants who perform the work of executioners.
Those who perform acts of killing are "killers" (*vadhakarmakara*). Those whose form (*ākāra*) is like that are "of such a kind" (*tādṛśa*); the meaning is that they are extreme destroyers.
Then, having abandoned that birth, they were born as crows among the Suhmas; at the end of that, they attained the state of vultures, and from there they became cranes.
That birth is a birth as a servant of a king, among the Suhyas, which are specific regions.
Those of perverted intellect turned him into a Śavara among the Trigartas, a sheep among the Barbaras, and then an insect among the Magadhas.
The phrase "those whose intellects consist of speech" is the reason expressed by way of a qualification.
Having experienced various successions of births here, O Rāma, today these fish remain in a small pond in the forest of Kaśmīra.
"Here" refers to the aforementioned regions; "the other womb" refers to one distinct from being a corpse-eater (*śavara*) and so forth.
In what state do they remain there? To this he says:
"Consuming the thin, watery mud boiled by the forest fire, they neither die nor live, being worn out by the old silt. (MU 4.30.15)
Kalka means impurity.

Having summarized the aforementioned suffering of the womb, he describes the agitation of diverse births: "Having come into being again and again, they are destroyed over and over, like waves in the ocean."
The intended meaning is "according to the principle previously stated."
With this verse at the end of the chapter, he concludes the narrative of Dāma and the others:

"O Rāma, those who have entered the ocean of existence, driven by the winds of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), have long been carried like straw upon the waves in the form of bodies; yet they have not even now attained peace. Consider, therefore, the infinite and terrible power of latent impressions."

"Ūḍhāḥ" means carried away; "upaśamam" means the absence of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). He describes the fruition [of this state] with the word "anantam" (infinite); the word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be understood as the ellipsis. O Rāma! Since such torments were obtained by Dāma and the others solely through the power of latent impressions, therefore you [should seek] the infinite—that which is without end—the terrible, the harsh, the greatness of latent impression, which consists in the notions of "I" and "mine."
Examine and ascertain this; may there be auspiciousness.
Thus ends the thirtieth canto in the Section on Stability within the *Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! To awaken you, O high-minded Rāma, I speak this to remind you of what was previously said; it is not for mere sport, lest the analogy of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa should fail you.

"For the sake of awakening"—that is, for the sake of supreme understanding consisting in the thought that "impressions must necessarily be abandoned. "Not in jest" means not by way of sport; that is to say, not for the purpose of mockery. "I do not speak [thus]," because [the teaching] is non-deceptive—this is the intended meaning.
Relying on the accounts of Dāma and others, he introduces various kinds of instruction:
"Through the pursuit of non-discrimination, the mind easily embraces such a calamity for the sake of endless suffering. (MU 4.31.2)

Due to the lack of discernment— that is, due to the non-investigation consisting of the ego-identification with the body and so forth, which are not the Self— the mind, acting as the agent, through its manifestation, takes hold of— that is, experiences— such a calamity, similar to the misfortunes experienced by Dāma and others, as its object, for the sake of endless suffering, effortlessly, that is, without exertion. Therefore, [it is called] "lack of discernment" (aviveka).
The sense is that it must be abandoned in this way.
To incite [the listener] toward the abandonment of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), he recounts the misfortune experienced by Dāma and others:

"Where, on one hand, was the leadership of Śambara’s army—the destroyer of the immortals? And where, on the other, was the state of being a fish, withered and exhausted in the mud of water heated by the sun's glare? (MU 4.31.3)
The phrase "in the northern half" implies "in Kaśmīra."
Where is that great fortitude capable of putting to flight the hosts of the immortals, and where is this state of being a lowly servant to the Kirāta king?
This is clear.
Where indeed is the noble fortitude of the pure consciousness that is free from egoism, and where is the wicked imagination of the ego arising from the influence of false latent tendencies?

"Free from ego" (*nirahaṅkāram*) means devoid of the gross egoism that thinks "I am the body. That which is consciousness (*cit*) is the nature of consciousness itself. "Being" (*sattvam*) refers to the mind known as *sattva*. By means of that [mind], there arises a noble fortitude—a state of nobility and steadfastness resulting from the absence of fear regarding death and so forth. Where indeed does such a thing exist? It has arisen through the "possession" (*āveśa*), that is, by the influence of those false latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*).
The "evil construction of ego" (*ahaṅkārakukalpanā*) refers to the contemptible conceptualization consisting of the ego in the form "the body is I. Where does it exist?
The intended meaning is: "See for yourself the difference between these two."
This vast and spreading cluster of the miseries of saṃsāra, dense with its branches and tendrils, arises from the very sprout of egoism.
This [world], flashing forth before us, is expansive and wide-stretching with its clusters of branches consisting of various objects;

it is dense and difficult to traverse. Saṃsāra itself is a poisonous creeper with dangerous blossoms. Egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) alone is the sprout—the seed—from which it arises and manifests. In the absence of egoism, whose would saṃsāra be, and what would its form be? As in deep sleep (*suṣupti*).
For the meaning is that when the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) dissolves, no one experiences saṃsāra.
It declares that the fruit is egoism; therefore, O Rāma, cleanse it from within with effort. Having cleansed [the mind] with the thought "I am indeed nothing at all," be happy.

O Rāma, since egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) itself is the calamity, you must therefore wipe away—by means of the effort known as right knowledge—the gross egoism consisting of "I am the body" and so forth, within the internal mind (*antaḥ*). To the question, "What will be achieved for me by that?", he says: "I am... [and continues] "I am not at all [the one] whose form is the gross body and so forth."

"I am someone" [only] because of the association with the existence of the reality that is pure consciousness alone; thus it is so. Consequently, having wiped away the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), you become happy, endowed with the great bliss produced by independence from the body and so forth. For it is precisely due to dependence on the body and such that a person becomes miserable. Now, one might ask: "Where does the dependence on the body go? To this, we say: no.
It proceeds; however, because it is devoid of the sense of "I" (ahaṃkāra) regarding its objects, reflections on the existence or non-existence of those objects do not disturb it.
As for the effort that arises spontaneously as a mere concomitant of that movement, it does not possess such power to cause suffering—enough said.
Now, what fault is produced by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) by which a person becomes miserable? To this he replies:
"The orb of the moon of ultimate reality, consisting of an elixir and cool, is covered by the cloud of the ego-sense and has thus become invisible. (MU 4.31.8)

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the supreme object of attainment. Because He brings delight, He is the Moon (*indu*). His orb (*maṇḍala*) is His all-pervading essential nature. Egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) itself is the body; egoity is precisely that which takes the form of "I. It is like a cloud (*ambuda*, *megha*). Being covered or veiled by that [cloud], it has attained invisibility—that is, the state of being unfit as an object of the reflective awareness of "I" (*aham-parāmarśa*).

For a person who is possessed by the conceit of a body does not, from the perspective of ultimate reality, perceive through the sense of "I" that which is his own essential nature, the principle of pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Of what nature is that? It consists of an elixir (*rasāyanamaya*), being of the nature of nectar (*amṛta*) as the support for great self-sufficiency. For this very reason, it is cool (*śīta*), meaning free from the feverish torment of the nature of desire. And therefore, because it veils the Supreme Self whose nature is bliss—
The sense is that it is indeed logical for the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) to produce faults that cause torment.
With the intention that "you have indeed manifested through the power of egoism (ahaṅkāra)," he said:
"Seized by the demon of egoism, the three—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—though non-existent, attained existence as demons through the greatness of illusion. (MU 4.31.9)

By the majesty—that is, the power—of Māyā employed by Śambara, the Dānavas attained the form of Dānavas. Therefore, although they were non-existent, the three—Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa—became possessed by the Piśāca that is egoism (ahaṅkāra). Being seized by it, they attained existence in the form of "we are Dāma and the others. You too are likewise.

Through the power of illusion (*māyā*), he has assumed a human form; therefore, the intended meaning is that although he does not exist [in reality], he experiences his own existence solely by virtue of his own ego-inflation (*svāhaṅkāra*).

"But surely those Dāma and the others were at some small pond in Kaśmīra? To this he replied: "In Kaśmīra, at a small pond on the shore of the Mahāpadma lake, O Rāma, fish remain today, greedily longing for bits of moss."
This is clear.
In this regard, Śrī Rāma asks: "The non-existent has no being, and the existent has no non-being. How then did those who were non-existent become existent? Tell me this."

For indeed: non-existence (*abhāva*), which does not partake in being the agent of existence (*sattā*) for that which is non-existent—where "existence" (*bhāva*) means presence—is not found, because it is never observed in cases such as the horns of a rabbit. Likewise, existence (*bhāva*), which does partake in being the agent of existence for that which is already existent, is not found, because it is not observed when a seed is cast into mud. Therefore, even though non-existent things do not partake in being the agent of existence by virtue of being produced through the illusory power of Śambara; [they nevertheless appear].
Those [beings] such as Dāma and others are "existent," meaning they are endowed with being (*sattā*). How have they come to be so? Tell me—this means "explain it thus."

The venerable Vasiṣṭha replies: "It is so, O mighty-armed one; for that which is non-existent never comes into being anywhere. At some time or other, this [universe] may become either vast or minute."

This matter has been stated by you: "It is so. For indeed, because a non-existent thing (*asat vastu*)—in any place or at any time—is not existent, it does not possess existence (*sattā*). By implication, it should be understood as being either existent or non-existent. [Objection:

But then, how can there be a relationship between atoms, which are non-existent because they are beyond the range of the senses (*indriyāgocaratva*), and a jar, which is existent by nature because it is perceivable by the senses (*indriyalabhyatva*)?

The existence of a real jar is perceived, and by the power of time, its state as non-existent atoms is also perceived. To this, he says "kadācit" (at some time): even though something exists in reality as an indefinable essence of pure being (*sanmātra*), this form of the jar, atoms, and so forth—which manifests before us and is known through perception and inference—is understood in terms of both existence and non-existence.
An entity may be large or it may be small; likewise, the point here is that there is no non-existence of what exists, nor existence of what does not exist.
And so, what logic applies to the case of Dāma and the others? To this he says:

"Tell me, how can that which is non-existent be established as existent, or how can that which is existent be established as non-existent? By this very illustration, I shall bring about your awakening."

"You speak first. When the expectation arises, "What shall I say?", he says: "What?"—meaning what object? "Being" (*sat*) has become; "non-being" (*asat*) has become established, having attained the nature of non-existence. Or rather, "non-being" has become; "being" has become established, having attained the nature of existence. [The opponent asks: "But what will be accomplished by my speaking? To this he replies: "By way of illustration. Therefore, I—
By this illustration spoken by you, that is, by the example you have provided, I shall bring about your awakening; the sense is that otherwise you would not listen.
Śrī Rāma says: "O Brahmin, it is indeed true that we who are here—Dāma and the others—are virtuous; yet I say that even those who are not virtuous are established as virtuous."

*Kila* indicates certainty: O Brahmin, we here, who are manifest before your eyes, exist as truly real beings (*santa eva santah*). Indeed, it is not possible for us to be non-existent in any way, because mutual activities such as conversation and so forth are possible among us. But on the other hand (*tu*), Dāma and the others, though non-existent—being produced by the illusion (*māyā*) of Śambara—are nonetheless [perceived] as existent.
The peaceful ones remain established in this way: "I"—thus I speak, thus I say.
The venerable Vasiṣṭha provides this illustration to awaken Śrī Rāma:
"Just as Dāma and the others who stand here before you, O Rāma, are composed of illusion; they are truly unreal, yet appear real, like the flood of water in a mirage."
In the very same way, we too—along with the gods, asuras, and dānavas—are entirely unreal as we leap about, go, and come.
"Consisting of illusion" means having the nature of illusion. "In this world" refers to this saṃsāra. Having stated the illustration, he states the illustrated point:
"In the same way, we here. These [beings] are conversing with one another; "we go," "we come"—this is an elliptical expression for all actions; the meaning is "we do everything."

[Objection: But how can we be of an unreal nature, like a rope-snake and so forth? To this he says: "Your existence is indeed false, and my existence is indeed false; even though experienced, it is of an unreal nature, just like one's own death in a dream. (MU 4.31.17)

Your existence—that is, your being as the name "Rāma"—is indeed false, that is, unreal. My existence—that is, my being as the name "Vasiṣṭha"—is also indeed false. Of what nature is this existence of yours and mine? Even though it has been experienced, even though it is being experienced at this very moment, it is of the nature of non-existence. Here, a simile that produces conviction [is provided].

He says, "It is a dream. The meaning is this: just as a person sees his own death in a dream even though it is unreal—for otherwise, in the absence of the dreamer, who would see his own death?—so too do we two perceive both your existence and my non-existence; for otherwise, since you are established solely in your own selfhood (*tvattā*) and I am established solely in my own selfhood (*mattā*), you [would not perceive me].

"You should not perceive [the self] as 'you' with respect to me, nor as 'I' with respect to yourself; for the state of being 'you' (tvattva) resides in you, and the state of being 'me' (mattva) resides in me.
The use of the past participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) here, despite the action being present, is intended to indicate that [these states] are established as enduring characteristics.
He explains this very point by means of another illustration:
"Just as a deceased kinsman, though experienced even in a dream, consists of unreality, and there arises the cognition 'this one is dead'—so too is this world. (MU 4.31.18)

Just as a deceased relative, even when experienced in a dream, is composed of unreality and is indeed false; and [the word] "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a reason—meaning because—the cognition that "this one is dead," which is the awareness belonging to the waking state, exists; in this manner, the world, though experienced, becomes unreal. For the wise, it does not exist, and thus their awareness has no such object; whereas for the ignorant, it is otherwise.
But [the self] belongs to the time of deep sleep; otherwise, there would be no possibility of the reflective awareness during the waking state that "it was not," such is the meaning.
[Objection: "In that case, why is it that everyone does not possess an understanding that accords precisely with what I have said? To this he replies:
"For this statement, which concerns the domain of the deluded, does not shine forth at all; it arises without practice, yet there is no denial of experience. (MU 4.31.19)

"Hi" signifies certainty. [This state] pertains only to the ignorant, not to those who know that [reality]. "This statement is yours"—this is the ellipsis. It does not shine, it does not appear beautiful, for you; the implication is that this is because you are a knower of that [reality]. [Objection: "In that case, what should I do regarding the experience of your state? To this he says: "By practice. By practice—that is, by the practice of contrary experience—without [such practice], there is no experience [of the truth].

The denial of a prior experience does not arise; therefore, you too must simply experience the unreality of the existence of your own being, so that there may be no experience of the existence of your own being—this is the intended meaning.
[Objection: But how can the denial of experience be accomplished without practice? To this he says:
"In this world, no one's conviction that has taken deep root within ever perishes without effortful practice. (MU 4.31.20)
Certainty is experience; it has taken root and become firm within the mind. The sense is that this is its very nature.
[Objection: "In that case, why do those who know this and are overcome by compassion not teach this very thing to everyone? To this he replies:
"The insane laugh excessively at that madman who says, 'This world is unreal; Brahman alone is real. (MU 4.31.21)

"This world manifesting before us is unreal; that reality called Brahman—which is beyond the external and internal organs, consisting of pure existence and consciousness—is real. He who speaks or declares this is a knower of That (Tajjña). Those who laugh at him like madmen are themselves mad, being devoid of self-knowledge, and are deluded ignorants.
What, then, can be said of hearing his instruction? Therefore, the implication is that he does not speak at all.
"Now, for what reason do they laugh at him? To this he replies:

"Where indeed could there be identity between one who is blind and one who is not, between the ignorant and the knower? It would be like [the identity] of shadow and sunlight within a single perception, or of darkness and light. (MU 4.31.22)

Of the two—the intoxicated and the non-intoxicated—whose natures are characterized respectively by forgetting and not forgetting the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) through the drinking of the honey called the bliss of one's own self and the absence of such drinking;
how could there be unity in their awakening or experience? That is to say, there could be no unity in the form of mutual agreement.
For the meaning is that no agreement regarding the realization of truth is observed here between the intoxicated and the non-intoxicated. Therefore...
The intention is that these two laugh. Of which two? Like shadow and light.
Just as there is no unity in the cognition of shadow and light—which consist of darkness and illumination—within the cognition known as the manifestation of objects; such is the meaning.
"Now, why is there no unity in the cognition of those two? To this he says:
"Even with effort, neither the knower nor the ignorant can deny an object that has been experienced as real, just as one cannot deny the assault of a corpse. (MU 4.31.23)

In the case of that which has been experienced—that is, when the truth is known as truth, regarding both the reality called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) and the reality called the world—the knower and the ignorant alike cannot, even with effort, deny it, because it manifests before them. Indeed, no one is able to deny a thing that manifests before them. For this very reason, there is no identity between the cognition of these two.
The state [of being]. What is it that cannot? It is like a corpse; as a corpse is unable to perform an "approach"—that is, the approach toward objects—it is in that same way, such is the meaning.
[Objection: "In that case, why not let even an ignorant person say this? To this, he says:
It is appropriate for one who knows Brahman to declare that "the entire world is Brahman," because, through the non-experience of ignorance, he has experienced that very [Brahman]. (MU 4.31.24)
It is appropriate for one who knows that—that is, for one who knows the nature of Brahman called pure consciousness—to say, "The entire world becomes Brahman.
For it is he alone, the knower of that, who has experienced and seen that Brahman. Under what condition?
When there is no experience of ignorance—that is, when there is no perception of ignorance characterized by existence and non-existence in the form of the objects of the world.
When there is existence.
Furthermore, he says this very thing:
"O Rāma, this speech shines forth indeed within the sphere of the awakened; for in the form of 'I am the Buddha,' there is truly nothing at all."

O Rāma! This speech, "All is Brahman," is speech itself. It shines forth intensely in that object known as the awakened, which is the fit location; by implication, it should be understood that it does not shine in the object of the unawakened. Now, one might ask: why does it shine only there? To this he says, "of the awakened" (*buddhasya*). The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied [as the reason]. Since for the awakened, even the slightest thing, such as the body and so forth—

The phrase "I am" does not exist as a form, nor does it exist as an object of knowledge. This is the meaning: the ignorant person is certain that "I am the body," and thus perceives even those things useful to it as real; otherwise, they would not be intent on exerting effort day and night for its sake. The wise person, however, due to the absence of the conceit of "I" regarding the body, does not perceive reality in those things useful to it.
Otherwise, equanimity toward that object would be impossible; therefore, it is proper to say that "all is Brahman" only for one who knows that, not for one who does not know it.
Now, one might ask: "Is there ever a denial of this experience by one who knows it, or not? To this he says:
"The wise man, experiencing that 'this supreme Brahman alone is peace,' cannot possibly deny his own experience. (MU 4.31.26)

The wise one is the knower. This world becomes nothing but the peaceful Supreme Brahman; it is exactly thus, indeed so. Experiencing it in this very way, he becomes [that]. Therefore, for that knower, it is not proper—that is, it is not fitting—to deny this self-experience.
"But then, how is it that you are worthy of the name Śrī Vasiṣṭha? To this he replied:
"Apart from the Supreme, there is nothing whatsoever in me as a self; just as a ring and so forth do not exist apart from gold, the state of being Vasiṣṭha does not exist in me."

"I am the one called Vasiṣṭha; I do not exist as something distinct from the Supreme, which is pure Consciousness transcending all else. The sense is: "As for you, see that which you perceive [as 'you']. Therefore, in me, there is no "Vasiṣṭha-ness"—that is, no fitness for the name 'Vasiṣṭha. How so? Just like the state of being a ring or the like. The meaning is: just as the state of being a ring and so forth does not exist in gold, so it is here.
Therefore, the sense is that "I, too, am not Vasiṣṭha."
"Now, if you are such as this in your own self, then what kind of person is a fool? To this he says:

"Apart from the state of being [the elements], there is nothing at all in the self that is a fool; just as gold does not exist in the cognition of waves and so forth, there is no ultimate reality in the ignorant one."

The fool is one who lacks knowledge of the Supreme Self, whose nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Apart from the state of being an actual entity (*bhūtatva*), there is nothing whatsoever—nothing at all—in the Self, since it is devoid of the condition of being a body. The intention is that let the knower of That see the Self in its true form; for in the ignorant person, the ultimate reality—the state of being pure consciousness as the ultimate truth—does not exist. Indeed, he...

It does not perceive its own nature as pure consciousness. What is it like? It is like gold. Just as when there is the cognition of a wave and so forth, or the cognition of a bracelet and so forth, the gold is not [perceived as such]; such is the meaning.
Summarizing this, he says:
"The fool consists of the disease of false ego, while the wise man consists of the single reality of the True Self; indeed, it is never possible for the nature of these two to be denied."

The fool is ignorant; he becomes absorbed in that egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) which is unreal and has the body as its object. The wise man is a knower of that [reality]; he becomes absorbed in that which is real, the true Self (*satya*), the one Self that pervades all, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This is certain. Between these two—the fool and the wise man—there is a difference of nature, namely between that called false egoism and that called the ultimate reality.
And the denial—that is, the repudiation—of its own nature is not tenable in any case; for no one is able to deny their own nature as it manifests before them.

He states this very point with an illustration: "How could there be a denial of that which belongs to someone? For the statement 'I am a pot' on the part of a person is indeed nothing but madness. (MU 4.31.30)

For a person who, by way of certainty, possesses a certain nature—that person, in that very nature, how could there be a denial? For indeed, for a person, the statement "I am a pot" is nothing but madness.
Therefore, this applies to the wise one who is certain of the identity with Brahman, and to the ignorant one who is certain of the identity with the gross body.
The sense is that it is not logical to deny one's own experience.
He recalls the subject at hand by way of its fruition:
"Therefore, neither we nor Dāma and the others are real anywhere; they and we are unreal, for indeed there is no origination of us."
Since our own nature, as well as that of Dāma and the others, is established solely by our own cognition, for that reason we are not real,
nor are Dāma and the others real; on the contrary, those Dāmas and others are unreal, and we too are unreal, because there is no actual origination of us who possess gross forms.

The suitability for existence does not exist; for a non-existent entity cannot become existent merely by being perceived, because that would entail the absurd consequence (prasaṅga) that even things such as a hare's horn would possess existence—this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "In that case, even for one who knows that [reality], their own nature—which is called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*)—must exist as something established by perception just like ours; therefore, he too would be non-existent. To this, [the author] replies: "Pure, stainless, and untainted, the space of awareness (*bodhākāśa*) is true consciousness. It is real, all-pervading, peaceful, and neither sets nor rises. (MU 4.31–32)
That which is consciousness is reality; that is to say, its nature is the form of consciousness untainted by the objects of cognition such as jars and the like.

For it is not logical that consciousness conditioned by objects of cognition such as jars should possess reality, since with the destruction of the object of cognition, that [conditioned] consciousness too becomes as good as destroyed. Nor is it logical for the object of cognition to possess reality, because its essence consists merely in being perceived. It is pure.
It is defiled by the impurity known as the objective world (*cetya*); for this very reason, it is stainless (*nirañjana*) and untainted (*nirlepa*).

It is the True (*satya*), because it exists as the essence of all things; it is the Form (*rūpa*). It is omnipresent (*sarvagata*), because it pervades everything by existing as the witness and as the essence. It is tranquil (*śānta*), resting in its own true nature. It is the sky of consciousness (*bodhākāśa*), the sky of pure awareness (*cinmātra*), which neither sets nor rises. It exists in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

It possesses existence; therefore, because it lacks the status of being established by mere cognition, the sense is that there is no unreality for the knower who has ascertained as his own the nature of pure consciousness, which is ultimately real.

The conscious self alone repeatedly qualifies itself as "all that exists," yet it is utterly empty, established as if being nothing at all; within that void, O dear one, these perceptions shine forth as its own innate radiance.
Because it exists as the substratum of all appropriation (*upādāna*), its nature is "existent" (*sat*). Indeed, that which is non-existent cannot serve as a substratum.

For this very reason, it is "not empty" (*niḥśūnya*), meaning its nature is other than emptiness. Nevertheless, because it is beyond the range of both external and internal faculties, it remains as if it were nothing at all, abiding like emptiness. That reality is called "pure consciousness" (*cinmātra*). It becomes the entire, totality of the world (*jagat*). In this regard—

He states the latter half [of the verse] as the reason for this, beginning with "therein" (*tatra*). The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Since, therein—in that sky which is the space of pure consciousness (*cinmātra-ākāśa*)—these visions, these perceptions in the form of the world, manifest and flash forth before one's eyes; what are these visions? They are one's own radiance, one's own splendors. The meaning is that they are not distinct from oneself. This is witnessed by all consciousness.
Since this is already established for us in the analogy of the dream, no further effort has been made here.
He explains this very point with an illustration:
"Just as for one with cataracts, innate visual perceptions appear like clusters of hair and so forth, so too do these creations appear therein."

Just as for one with "timira" eyes—a person whose vision is impaired by the disease of *timira*—the visual rays (the sight) are innate and not adventitious; they appear and flash like a mass of hair or a tuft of hair [seen by the diseased]. In the same way, these creations appear there in the space called pure consciousness (*cinmātra*); these too are indeed of the nature of the rays of pure consciousness.
The term "existence" (bhāvaḥ); by the word "etc. (ādi), the apprehension of a double moon and so forth is included.
[Objection: But by what effort does he make the world take on the form of his own rays? [Reply: To this he says:
He experiences himself in whatever way he knows it; therefore, the space of consciousness (cidākāśa) is truly real, for it becomes real through his very perception of it.
That consciousness-space (cidākāśa) knows its own self, its true nature, in whatever manner it is joined;

in that very manner, it experiences and directly perceives it. Therefore, even though the world is unreal, through the vision of that—that is, the vision of the consciousness-space—it becomes real, just as the dream-world becomes real for the dreamer.
From this observation, the sense is that he performs this very effortlessly.
He declares the established conclusion:
there is neither truth nor untruth here in the three worlds; whatever the nature of consciousness perceives, that arises exactly in that way, without a doubt.

Therefore, for that reason, here in these three worlds there is nothing that is real, nor is there anything that is unreal. Whatever object exists in the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) and has consciousness as its essence (*cidātman*), it arises without doubt exactly as one perceives it; the word "like a dream" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
By this, he declares that his own similarity to the fetter and so forth has borne fruit:
"Just as the fetters and so forth [were], so too have we arisen; whether they are real or unreal—my friend, what room is there here for conceptualization regarding them? (MU 4.31.37)

The word "ataḥ" (therefore) is to be supplied. Therefore, just as the ropes and other such things are both real and unreal—real insofar as they appear, but unreal from the perspective of ultimate reality—they arise, that is, they manifest; in the same way, we here arise as both real and unreal. The sense is that this is due to the application of the same principle. O dear one! Therefore, in this world (*ihaloka*), those...

"Even toward them," that is, toward those very people; "conceptualization" means the conceptualization of their reality. What is it? The sense is: if you imagine a reality for yourself, then do so for them as well.
[Objection: But how can there be a mutual equality between Dāma and the rest and ourselves? To this, he says:
"Of this infinite, all-pervading, formless sky of consciousness, consciousness arises in whatever manner; in that very way, it shines forth therein abundantly. (MU 4.31.38)
Of this [Reality], which manifests as the Self; which is infinite because it exists even as the witness within the end [of all things] and is thus devoid of an end;

which is omnipresent, pervading everything; which is formless, lacking any delimited shape; and which is the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoman*), the space of consciousness—the consciousness that is its attribute, the vibration known as *cit*—arises and flashes forth in whatever manner or form upon its own inner wall.
That very [consciousness] shines—that is, it manifests—in that manner, in that form, upon that wall of pure consciousness; the word "like a dream" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
[Objection: "Even so, what relevance does this have to the present topic? To this he says:
"Where consciousness itself shines forth in the form of a rope and so on, it is accomplished there as such, because of the experience of its having that form. (MU 4.31.39)
The experience of the form of the letter *ta*, such as the form of the letter *da* and so forth, arises from that [experience].
Wherever consciousness itself has arisen in the form of ourselves and others, it has become established there in that very way, due to the experience of its corresponding forms.
The experience of having such a form—that is, a form like our own—is what follows from that; and thus, the intended meaning is that we indeed possess equality with Dāma and the others.
The world is designated as the manifestation of one's own dream, just as the sky-like void of consciousness, whose nature is space, appears like the water of a mirage to a weary traveler.

Of that which has the sky as its body—because it is of the nature of space due to its absolute purity—and which belongs to the sky of consciousness (cidvyoman): its own dream-appearance is given the designation "the world" (jagat), that is, the name "world. This is the sense: it was made by the sky of consciousness. Like what? Like the state of being a mirage-water (mṛgāmbutā). Just as the name "mirage-water" is applied to the water [seen] by one who is tormented by heat, so too is this the case; such is the meaning.
If that is so, then does the entire expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*) exist as nothing other than the world? To this he replies:

"Where the expanse of consciousness is awakened, there the designation 'the visible' (*dṛśya*) is applied; but where it is asleep by that very same [consciousness], there the designation 'liberation' (*mokṣa*) is applied. (MU 4.31.42)

In whichever part of the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*) it is awakened—that is, endowed with the reflective awareness of the world-form as both self and other—it is by that very same sky of consciousness that the designation "the visible" (*dṛśya*) is made. In whichever part it is asleep—that is, devoid of reflective awareness of its own nature as the world-form—it is by that very same [sky] that the designation "liberation" (*mokṣa*) is made. Thus, it is not the case that the entire sky of consciousness exists as the temporal state of the world.
Existence.
"Is it not then the case that the sky of consciousness (cidvyoman) has come to possess parts? To this he says:
"And that [sky of consciousness] is never asleep, nor is it ever awakened; let it be understood that the sky of consciousness alone is the visible world. (MU 4.31.43)

When ultimate reality is investigated, that space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*)—in any part whatsoever, at any time at all—is neither asleep nor awake. This is because sleep and waking, which are witnessed by it, cannot exist apart from it. Nor can that very [space] be its own qualifier; for if it were, it would follow absurdly that a pot could also be its own qualifier.

Therefore, by you who are engaged in the investigation of ultimate reality, the visible world should be understood and known as nothing but the space of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), devoid of attributes such as sleep and waking; for, according to the reasoning already stated, sleep and waking— which produce the states of liberation and the world— cannot exist apart from their locus in pure consciousness alone.
Because it is an ultimate secret, he explains once again the very same meaning stated in the first half of the preceding verse:
"Nirvāṇa itself is the glory of creation; the glory of creation itself is liberation. There is no difference in meaning between these two words, just as there is none between synonyms."

Nirvāṇa is pure consciousness devoid of thought; *nirvṛti* is *nirvāṇa*. Just as a distinction between a wave and water is not tenable, so too a distinction between creation (*sarga*) and *nirvāṇa* is not tenable; such is the meaning.
If that is so, what then is the status of the word and the cognition "the world"? To this he says:
In the ultimate sense, one perceives one's own form as "the world," just as a person with cataracts sees a mass of hair where none exists. (MU 4.31.45)

This one, whose nature is consciousness devoid of objective thought (*acetayitṛ*), perceives the form "the world" within its own true nature (*svasvarūpa*), which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) among all ultimate realities. That is to say, it perceives the state of being the world. How is this? It is like the eye; just as the eye of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*) perceives its own ray-like nature as a mass of floating hairs (*keśoṇḍuka*), so too [does this consciousness]. This is the meaning. Its own...

Of what nature is it? It is "observed" (*īkṣita*), seen by its outward diffusion from itself; otherwise, its status as supersensible (*atīndriyatva*) would be lost, for supersensibility is indeed asserted by all to belong to the sense faculty.

[Objection: "In that case, since the world appears like a mass of hair [seen by one with cataracts], does it not exist in some way? How then can it be said to have the nature of nirvāṇa? [Reply: To this he says: "That mass of hair is nothing at all; rather, it is the vision that exists in such a manner. This visible world is not anything real in this way; it is established as the sky of consciousness. (MU 4.31.46)

That which appears as a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*) does not exist as anything at all. For that vision is a vision of one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), and it persists in the form of a mass of hair. Since, even when searched for a thousand times, the mass of hair cannot be grasped by the hand, nor is there any other object there capable of serving as its substratum; therefore—

The point is that it is known that the very perception itself appears as suchness (*tathātva*). He applies the logic previously stated to the present case as well: "It is not thus. This world is nothing at all; it is the sky of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), the space of consciousness. Thus, it exists in the form of the world.
For in a dream, the existence of the sky of consciousness in the form of the world is observed; therefore, there is no contradiction.
Such is the intended meaning.
He states the established conclusion:

"Everything exists everywhere exactly as it is experienced; nothing whatsoever exists here that has not been experienced. This peaceful, existent, and singular reality remains thus, pervasive, free from doubt, and devoid of differentiation.
Therefore, remain [in this state]."

Just as it has been experienced, so too has it been experienced in its various forms. All this exists everywhere because it is manifest. That which has not been experienced—that which has not entered the domain of experience—does not exist anywhere at all, in any place, even in the slightest degree, because it is unmanifest. Thus, the state of being experienced and the state of not being experienced belong to the world in states such as waking and states such as deep sleep.

And since all this is witnessed by one's own direct experience (*svapratītisākṣika*), no effort is required here [to prove it]. [Objection: "In that case, what is it that exists eternally? To this he says: "It is tranquil" (*śāntam*). It is tranquil because it abides as the experiencer; it is devoid of the modifications known as "experienced" and "not experienced.
It is one (*ekam*), without a second. It is pervasive (*ātatam*), extending everywhere. This [Reality] flashes forth before us as the Self (*ātman*). Thus...
The ellipsis is that [the world] manifests as having a nature seized by the modifications of being experienced and not being experienced. "Sat" refers to the reality known as Pure Being (*sanmātra*);

it "abides," meaning it remains forever, because even in the state of non-experience, it persists as the experiencer of its own non-experience. He states the conclusion with the words "having abandoned": therefore, you are "free from doubt regarding the reality of the world," meaning devoid of the suspicion that the world is real.
"Non-differentiation" means being devoid of the cognition of difference; "āssva" means remain or stay.
He expresses this very point with a concluding verse at the end of the chapter:

This form of the Great Consciousness is as dense as a solid stone, tranquil, and as clear as the sky; the two views that "it exists" or "it does not exist" do not apply anywhere. That which exists is real, and it is that alone which shines forth. (MU 4.31.48)

This is the clear, stainless sky called the world, because it has no form whatsoever; it is the form, the very nature, of the Great Consciousness (*mahācit*). What is the nature of the Great Consciousness? It is as dense as the interior of a rock; the meaning is that it is a mass of consciousness (*cidghana*). For this very reason, it is perfectly tranquil, devoid of the agitation known as the object of thought (*cetya*); it is clearly [the source] of the dream-world.

The intended meaning is: "Because [all things] are seen to have the nature of pure consciousness alone. Now, one might ask: "In that case, how can there be the cognition of existence and non-existence?

To this he replies: "They do not exist at all. The cognitions of existence and non-existence are the perceptions of "it exists" and "it does not exist"; they do not exist anywhere at all. The meaning is that they consist merely of appearances. Now, even so, how can the denial of existence and non-existence—which are nevertheless appearing—be possible?

Thus [it is said]. Here he says: "And that which exists" (yac cāsti). Whatever exists according to your view, having the nature of both existence and non-existence—that is well and correct. That very thing is indeed the Great Consciousness-form (*mahācidrūpa*). It exists, because without that [Consciousness], anything devoid of a witness would be like something non-existent; whereas if its cognition is established, then—like objects in a dream—it does not lose its reality. May there be auspiciousness! (*śivam*) // MT 4.31.48 //
Thus ends the thirty-first canto in the Sthitiprakaraṇa of the Śrīmokṣopāya-ṭīkā composed by the venerable Bhāskarakaṇṭha.
Oṃ! Śrī Rāma asks:
How can there be an end to the suffering of Dāma, Vyālakaṭa, and the others—who, though they are virtuous, appear like children, yakṣas, and piśācas to those who are not? MU 4.32.1.
Of suffering, which consists in wandering through various wombs.

Śrī Vasiṣṭha relates the sequel for the sake of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa: "O scion of Raghu, listen to this which was spoken by Yama when he was thus entreated by those very servants of Yama at that very time."
This is clear.
When Yama speaks these words, and Dāma and the others hear their own story— that they shall attain liberation— they will undoubtedly be set free.
The word "iti" marks the conclusion of Yama’s statement.
Here Śrī Rāma asks:
"O Blessed One, tell me where, when, and how they shall hear this account of my own life being described by you in due order."
"O Blessed One, please relate this in due order: in which country, at what time, by whom being described, and in what manner will those Dāmas and others hear this account of their own history?"
The venerable Vasiṣṭha says in reply:
"In the marshlands on the shore of the great lotus lake in Kaśmīra, these two have repeatedly experienced a succession of births as fish."
With their intentions bound by desire and fickle, they will at the time of death go to their dissolution; right there in that lotus lake, they will become cranes.
With their intentions tethered, their minds bound. //5-6//
There, amidst garlands of white water-lilies and clusters of lotuses, among the excellent creeping vines of moss and the undulations of the waves;
Upon the swings of blooming white lotuses and upon the creepers of blue water-lilies, amidst streaks of clouds formed by masses of spray, and within the movements of cool whirlpools;
Having enjoyed the delights of the lake with the cranes, those ornaments of the world, having sported for a very long time, have now attained complete purity.

Having attained the proper means for liberation, they will become dissociated from it, just as the qualities of passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas) are separated by chance through the attainment of differentiation.

In those particular swings (*dolā*) which take the form of waves; [therein] are the enjoyments of the cranes (*sārasa*) of the lake—the meaning is: the enjoyments appropriate for cranes. Having attained purity means having reached the ripening of the saffron robes (*kāṣāya*). For this very reason, they are ornaments of the world (the masculine gender is used in the sense of the *ārṣa* tradition).
Those by whom the "method" (*yukti*)—namely, the method consisting of separation—has been obtained; such are they. [This occurred] by chance, and not otherwise.

"With effort"—of what are they like? "Like passion (*rajas*), goodness (*sattva*), and darkness (*tamas*). The meaning is: just as these, by chance, through their attainment of distinction, will become separated; so it shall be.
Within the region of Kaśmīra, there will be a glorious city adorned by mountains, known by the name Adhiṣṭhāna.
This is clear.
In its center there will be a peak named Pradyumnaśikhara, like the small bud of a lotus within the whorl of its petals.
The pericarp is the wheel of the treasury.
Upon the summit of that mountain, some king will build a palace—a great *sāla* tree scraping the clouds—like another peak upon a peak.
This is clear.
In the interior of a hole in the wall at the northeast corner of the house, which was marked by grasses tossed incessantly and without rest by the wind; MU_4,32.14.
In the storehouse-consciousness (ālaya), the demon will become like a *kalaviṅka* bird; it shrieks without meaning, just as a student who has heard little at the outset makes empty noise.
In what manner is the *kalaviṅka*? It is "one that cries out devoid of meaning" (*artharahitāraṭi*), meaning it warbles without [conveying] meaning. Like what?

Like a student who has little learning at first—a "first-time, little-learned student" (*prathamālpaśrutacchāttra*). It is like him; for a little-learned student indeed cries out only what is devoid of meaning. However, after some time, he cries out even that which possesses meaning; thus, the inclusion of the word "first" (*prathama*) is used.
At that very time, there will be a king there named Śrī Yaśaskaradeva, like another Śakra in heaven.
This is clear.
But a Dānava named Dāma will become a mosquito in his house, making a soft sound from within a hole in the back of a large pillar.
This is clear.
He introduces the stage of the "waist" (the middle part): "At that very time, in that city called Adhiṣṭhāna, there will also be a monastery named the Ratnāvalī-vihāra."
A *vihāra* is a place for recreation.
In that place, there will be a minister of that land known as Narasiṃha, who will perceive bondage and liberation as clearly as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of his hand.
In that monastery, the minister of that local ruler is "tadbhūmipāmātyaḥ."
In his house there will be a bird that acts as a plaything—a magical demon named Kaṭa, who has fashioned a cage for himself.
One for whom a cage of iron fetters has been fashioned; such a person [is he].
That Nṛsiṃha, the minister of the king, will relate this narrative composed in verses concerning Dāma, Vyāla, Kaṭa, and the others.
*Nṛsiṃha* means *narasiṃha*. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes Śambara and others, [referring to] the story related to Dāma, Vyālakaṭa, and so forth.
Having heard that discourse, Kaṭa Krakara will remember his true self; with the false sense of "I" stilled within, he will attain supreme nirvāṇa.

Krakara is a specific kind of bird. Having heard that story concerning himself, he was one by whom his own origin—his birth as a self—was remembered. Being thus, and being one whose false sense of "I" had become stilled, he will go to, that is, attain, the supreme, most excellent Nirvāṇa, which is absolute absorption into Brahman.
The kalaviṅka bird dwelling on the edge of the Pradyumna peak, having likewise heard its own story, will attain supreme nirvāṇa.
In the very same way, just like a mat.
Even a mosquito, having come to dwell within a wound inside the wood of a royal palace, shall attain peace by chance upon hearing [the teaching].
By way of consequence; by way of the course of conversation.
Having gathered them together, he says:
"O Rāghava, the sparrow shall come from Pradyumnaśṛṅga, the mosquito from the royal palace, and the quail from the monastery; thus they shall attain liberation."
This is clear.
He makes this summary:
"This entire sequence of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa has been told to you; this very cycle of existence is an illusion, utterly empty and exceedingly radiant."
When not fully understood, it causes one to wander like a mirage perceived as an ocean; when fully understood, it subsides like a mirage perceived as an ocean.
Thus, like a rope and so forth, it remains uncomprehended—meaning its true nature has not been investigated as to what form it actually takes.
Even from a great height, fools who are deluded fall downward by the power of their ignorance regarding the True Self, just like Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa.
Thus, it is like a rope and so forth.
From his very footfall, he speaks of nothing but downfall;
for where is the capacity to endure the crushing of Mount Meru and Mandara by the knitting of his brows, and where is the state of being a mere speck in a wound within the wood of Rājagṛha?
This is clear.
How vast the difference between having the orbs of the sun and moon felled by a mere slap of the hand, and becoming a bird in a hole in the wall within the house on Mount Pradyumna!
This is clear.
Where is the state of being a Meru mountain lifted by hands trembling with the play of flowers, and where is the state of being a tiny fledgling in the den of the Man-Lion at Arṣyaśṛṅga?
On the Ṛṣyaśṛṅga mountain, on the Pradyumna peak.
"But how can the cessation of a falling that is actually occurring be accomplished? To this he says:
"For the space of consciousness, though its luster is falsely colored by passion (rajas), perceives itself as if it were deformed, even while not abandoning its own true nature."

For indeed, because the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), its radiance stained—that is, its light defiled—by the false dust known as the *rajas* quality, perceives—that is, experiences—as if it were something else, even while not abandoning its own nature called "consciousness. This is an expression emphasizing the state of being; that is, as if it were a state of deformity, or as if it were insentience, which is contrary to its own nature. This occurs from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*).

The inclusion of the word "itīva" (as if) indicates that [the self] does not realize this. Therefore, the meaning is that, like the fall of a snake imagined upon a rope, the fall into lower realms—which is synonymous with "having a different form"—is not difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, it says this very thing:
by its own delusion of latent impressions, whether they be real or unreal, a living being passes from one state to another, like the perception of water in a mirage.

The living being (*jantu*), whose sole essence is consciousness, is the individual soul (*jīva*) that identifies with the body. By its own delusion of latent impressions (*vāsanā-bhrānti*)—that is, by the error consisting of the impression of selfhood within the body—it goes to a secondary location distinct from the place of ultimate rest, namely the secondary location called the egoity of the body. In what manner? Although it is ultimately unreal, it appears as such.

By means of truth: this is the meaning. Just as a man desiring to go to a certain place travels through intermediate regions due to an error produced by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of that place, so too the individual soul (*jīva*), desiring to reach its own self which is of the nature of consciousness, remains within the self in the form of the body due to an error produced by those latent impressions. Therefore, the downward fall is indeed caused by latent impressions; [it occurs] by means of latent impression.

"By what indeed? means "as if by the notion of water in a mirage. Just as a deer, desiring to go to a place of water that serves as a resting spot, stands in a desert region with the notion that it is the water of a mirage—such is the meaning.
[Objection: "By what means, then, is falling back down prevented? To this, he says:
"Those who, by the very intellect of their own natural flow, cross the ocean of existence—remaining free from latent impressions through the teaching that 'this visible world is unreal'—" MU 4.32.34.

Those persons, by means of their own mental flow alone—that is, by means of the intellect established in its own natural current, and not by that intellect which is impelled by a teacher or others—cross the ocean of existence. Who are they? They are those who, by means of the scripture that serves as a means, namely the *adhyātma-śāstra*, [attain] the state free from latent impressions (*nirvāsana*), devoid of the residual traces of the visible world. As for the word "established" (*sthitāḥ*), what is it? It is this very thing being experienced.

The visible world is non-existent, being devoid of true reality; it exists only insofar as its essence consists in mere cognition—this is the meaning. Therefore, the intention is that the treatise alone possesses the primary status of being the means [to liberation] in this context.

This [teaching] excludes dry reasoning as a means for those whose views on dry logic are subject to the fluctuations of the cries of stars; they quickly go to the waters of the abyss, yet they do not destroy their own misfortune.
Those persons who possess a loud and forceful clamor—that is, a discourse which is itself a distortion—and who are joined with such distortions of loud clamor;

who are "dry," being like something parched due to the absence of the aesthetic flavor known as the determination of the reality of the Supreme Self, and due to the harshness of determining things such as jars and cloths; those views consisting of mere sophistry and fallacious reasoning—those views go [to destruction].

They rely on those very [views] as a means; these people do not eliminate the misfortune called saṃsāra, which is impure, but rather, because they are seized by various conceptual constructions, they only increase it—this is the sense. What are the doctrines of dry logic?
They mean that they are like the waters of a chasm. Even the waters of a chasm are parched and difficult to reach, characterized by the agitation of the sound of falling stars.
And they become destroyers of impurities.
[Objection: "In that case, for whom is the destruction of impurity accomplished? To this he says:

"O dear one, there is no destruction [of impurity] for those who proceed by the path established through one's own experience and leading back to the scriptures, just as there is none for those who are falling. (MU 4.32.36)

O friend! That experience which is one's own—that is, experience established by one's own direct perception, meaning established through one's own self-evident realization—and likewise that which accords with the *āgama*, the true scripture; for those who proceed by such a path, there is no destruction in the form of the destruction of the inauspicious.
The meaning is that for them, the inauspicious is not destroyed [in the sense of being eliminated]. For them...

Of what, like what? Like birds; just as for birds that have fallen onto a wrong path destruction occurs, so it does not happen for these—this is a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). It was stated "by means of what is established through one's own experience" in order to turn away from what is contrary to one's own doctrine. [...]

Now, one might object: "If the adoption of the views of the logicians (tārkika) leads to such misfortune, then worldly conduct alone is better than that. To this, he says: "The thought of the wise is: 'May this be mine, may that be mine'; yet, due to their own wretchedness and misery, not even ashes remain for them. (MU 4.32.37)

"This thing, let it be mine"—such is the thought, the intellect, of the wise, those endowed with intelligence. Due to their own wretchedness and misery—that is, the dejection caused by the poverty known as *mamatā* (the sense of "mine")—even ashes do not attend them; they do not obtain even that. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the prefix *upa-* is used here with the root *sthā*.

It functions for the sake of attainment. The sense is that since worldly activity, which consists of hope, is not even fit to be called a means for attaining the Self, what need is there to mention the superiority of dry logic?

It is said that all calamities abandon one who is free from the worldly dealings of saṃsāra and has attained auspiciousness— him whose noble self always regards even the three worlds as a blade of grass, just as moisture leaves behind withered grass.

That noble-souled person who is free from the poverty known as possessiveness (*mamatā*)—and not merely at the time of obtaining a desired object—regards even the three worlds as a blade of grass; all calamities abandon that man. This is because the very state of dissatisfaction is the cause for the application of the term "calamity. What are these calamities like? They are like "taste" (*rasatā*). The abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used here for the sake of metrical completion. It is like "taste" (*rasa*); just as [people avoid] taste... [the rest of the verse follows].
It casts off old grass; such is the meaning of "tathā" (so).
[Objection: But how can the maintenance of the body be accomplished for one who renounces everything? To this he says:
"The lords of the world protect him in whom there constantly flashes forth within the wonder of pure being (*sattva*), like the indivisible cosmic egg of Brahmā. (MU 4.32.39)

The lords of the world protect perfectly and without fail that person in whose heart there flashes a wonder—a marvelous manifestation—of *sattva*, which is the fortitude consisting of total renunciation; it flashes within the mind and not merely in words due to hypocrisy, laziness, or the like. How so? Just as they protect the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*). [This applies to one who is] utterly free from greed.
The sense is that the task accomplishes itself, just as the task of creating the cosmic egg does.
Now, one might ask: "If at some point he should encounter a calamity that has no end, what then should be done? To this he replies:
"Even in the face of a calamity that has no end, one must never act out of sequence; for even Rāhu died while drinking the nectar, precisely because he acted out of sequence."

"Even when it has ended and has vanished"—that is, even when it has lasted for a long time—"in times of distress, by a person endowed with discernment, one should not take pleasure in, nor should one adhere to, an improper sequence that contradicts the scriptures and so forth. By implication, it should be understood that "one should take pleasure in a sequence that arises spontaneously from one's own flow. Therefore, the intended meaning is that the sequence itself must be maintained.
He praises the true scriptures and the like which show the proper sequence:
"Those who take refuge in the sun of true scripture and association with the virtuous, which bestows fierce light, do not again fall under the sway of the blindness of delusion. (MU 4.32.41)
The meaning is: "of that which is blinded by delusion and lacks sequential form."
He praises the qualities such as loving-kindness that arise from following true scriptures and the like:
"Those who are not under control come under control, and all calamities go to their destruction; for one whose fame is purchased by virtues, well-being becomes inevitable."
Enemies are unavoidable; the highest good known as liberation (*mokṣa*) is the supreme auspiciousness (*paramakalyāṇa*). It is "to be acquired" (*kreya*), meaning it is to be grasped or produced.

This is by means of qualities (*guṇaiḥ*)—namely, the qualities of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth—produced through the practice of true scriptures and the like. Therefore, the intended meaning is that one should rely solely upon those qualities that produce fame.
He praises the desire for virtues:
"Those who have no satiety regarding virtues, those whose passion is for sacred learning, and those who are devoted to truth—those men are [truly] human; others are merely beasts."
Dissatisfaction is a state of incompleteness. "Learning" refers to the inner science (adhyātma-śāstra); others are distinct from these.
Hari surely resides in the embodied form of those oceans of milk, whose fame— produced by their virtues— is praised, and by the moonlight of whose glory the sky of the people's hearts is illuminated.
The sky of the hearts of people was illuminated by the moonlight of their fame— the moonlight of fame produced from virtues such as loving-kindness belonging to those men. Of them,
who are like the Ocean of Milk because they share the quality of producing moonlight, Lord Hari, the illustrious Nārāyaṇa, surely dwells within their physical forms.
The sense is that the Blessed One constantly manifests within their minds; and it is fitting that the glorious Hari should abide in the form of the milk ocean.
All that is to be enjoyed has been enjoyed, and all that is to be seen has been seen; what else remains but non-attachment toward enjoyments for the sake of breaking the cycle of existence?

Everything that was to be enjoyed has been enjoyed by you; the meaning is that, through some form of enjoyment, all enjoyments—which share the same nature as that [previous experience]—have been experienced. Those things to be seen have been seen; those views have been viewed. Here too, the application is exactly as before.
Again—that is, once more—is there anything else, other than this, to be enjoyed or to be seen? Is there anything at all?

The meaning is "even not [existent]. Therefore, for the sake of the destruction of existence—that is, for the destruction of *saṃsāra*—let there be freedom from greed, which is the absence of avarice; "let it be maintained" is the ellipsis.
Abide according to the sequence, according to the scriptures, according to custom, and according to established order; let go of the unreal internal greed for enjoyments.

"According to one's conduct" means in accordance with one's own established practice, but not by being intent on a different kind of conduct; for if that were the case, the performance [of the rite] would be improper. "As it stands" means that one who is a householder does not act as a forest-dweller, nor does one who is a forest-dweller act as a householder.
"Within" means in the mind. "One who craves enjoyments" refers to one who has a longing for or greed regarding sense-objects (*bhoga*). Such a person is "one who craves enjoyments."
The state of that [is] "tat" (that).
Cultivate intimacy with fame through virtues that reach the heavens; objects of enjoyment can never protect one who has encountered death.

"By you, through qualities that travel through the sky—namely, qualities such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and so forth—together with the fame that has arisen, let intimacy (*saṃstava*) and familiarity be cultivated. [Objection: Why indeed should we cultivate intimacy with fame, having abandoned intimacy with enjoyments?
To this, he says: 'They protect. For what is the use of those things which are of no avail in such a state of death?"
The meaning is: "together with familiarity."

The beautiful women of the Siddhas praise and sing of those whose fame has been produced by their virtues; their fame is as white as the moon. Through these songs throughout the expanse of the sky, they truly live, while others are dead.
Others are devoid of proclaimed glory.
Now, one might ask: "If nothing at all will be accomplished even by acquiring the aforementioned qualities, then what should be done? To this he replies:
"Who would not be a possessor of success, provided they apply supreme human effort, undertake excellent exertion, and act according to the scriptures without weariness? (MU 4.32.49)
From conduct—that is, from conduct consisting in the acquisition of virtues.
"Is it not true that at some time or other I have indeed made an effort to acquire virtues? What has been accomplished by that? To this he replies:
"One who practices according to the scriptures should not be in a hurry for successes; success ripened over a long period of time will yield abundant fruit. (MU 4.32.50)
This is clear.
It declares that the fruit is free from sorrow, fear, and fatigue; it is without greed and without constraint. Let worldly conduct be performed according to the scriptures; let it not come to ruin.
Free from greed, it is devoid of covetousness; free from constraint, it is devoid of bondage.
The living soul has fallen into disappearance within the decaying wells of worldly existences; let it now be raised up from there by you, who possess abundant skill in breaking through them.
